items.title: Home
items.text:
Latest release: v0.5.3

5.6×faster than PyTorch Geometric on the GPU (MPS) 5.8×faster than PyTorch Geometric on the CPU 58×faster at best, over 35 training benchmarks 31×faster at best for one GNN layer than PyG on the Mac's GPU (M5 Pro) 
import mlx.core as mx
from mlx_graphs.nn.linear import Linear
from mlx_graphs.nn.message_passing import MessagePassing, fused_message_passing


@fused_message_passing  # aggregate with one SpMM instead of gather-scatter
class SAGEConv(MessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, node_features_dim: int, out_features_dim: int, bias: bool = True):
        super().__init__(aggr="mean")
        self.neigh_proj = Linear(node_features_dim, out_features_dim, bias=False)
        self.self_proj = Linear(node_features_dim, out_features_dim, bias=bias)

    def __call__(self, edge_index: mx.array, node_features: mx.array, edge_weights: mx.array) -> mx.array:
        # Message passing directly on GPU. The default message is
        # edge_weights * source features, which the fused kernel computes.
        neigh_features = self.propagate(
            edge_index=edge_index,
            node_features=node_features,
            message_kwargs={"edge_weights": edge_weights},
        )
        return self.self_proj(node_features) + self.neigh_proj(neigh_features)


# 3 nodes, 3 weighted edges, 8 features -> 16
edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 0]])
conv = SAGEConv(8, 16)
out = conv(edge_index, mx.random.normal((3, 8)), mx.array([1.0, 0.5, 2.0]))
print(out.shape)  # (3, 16)

Layers that override message() with something other than a weighted sum of neighbour features (e.g. attention computed per edge) simply drop the decorator, and propagate gathers per-edge messages and scatters them.

Write your own layers

items.title: Graph neural networks,fast on Apple silicon
items.text:
MLX-graphs is a library for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) built upon Apple's MLX, with the API of PyTorch Geometric.

pip install mlx-graphs

Quickstart Tutorials API reference Join the Discord

items.title: Faster than PyG, at the same accuracy
items.text: On a Mac, MLX-graphs trains GNNs 5.6× faster than PyTorch Geometric on the GPU (MPS) and 5.8× faster than PyTorch Geometric on the CPU, and the models reach the same accuracy (medians over 35 training benchmarks, up to 58× faster). See the benchmarks.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Fast GNN training and inference on Apple Silicon

    MLX-graphs has been designed to run fast on Apple Silicon chips. All GNN operations fully leverage the GPU and CPU hardware of Macs thanks to the efficient low-level primitives available within the MLX core library, and message passing aggregates neighbours with fused sparse kernels. On an M5 Pro, one GNN layer runs up to 31× faster than PyTorch Geometric on the Mac's GPU (MPS). See the benchmarks.

  • Scalability to large graphs

    With unified memory architecture, objects live in a shared memory accessible by both the CPU and GPU. This setup allows Macs to leverage their entire memory capacity for storing graphs. Consequently, Macs equipped with substantial memory can efficiently train GNNs on large graphs, spanning tens of gigabytes, directly using the Mac's GPU, and features larger than the memory stay on disk in a memory-mapped feature store. See the large graphs guide.

  • PyTorch Geometric's API, on MLX

    The layers, models, samplers and loaders, transforms and datasets of PyG are available under the same names: mini-batch training with NeighborLoader and ClusterLoader, heterogeneous models with to_hetero, temporal graphs with TGN, graph transformers with GPSConv, point clouds with PointNetConv, and hierarchical pooling. Each was checked against PyG. See Coming from PyG.

  • Multi-device

    Unified memory eliminates the need for time-consuming device-to-device transfers. This architecture also enables specific operations to be run explicitly on either the CPU or GPU without incurring any overhead, facilitating more efficient computation and resource utilization.

items.title: Example usage
items.text:
This library has been designed to build GNNs with ease and efficiency. Building new GNN layers is straightforward by implementing the MessagePassing class. This approach ensures that all operations related to message passing are properly handled and processed efficiently on your Mac's GPU. As a result, you can focus exclusively on the GNN logic, without worrying about the underlying message passing mechanics.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
MLX-graphs is compared with PyTorch Geometric (PyG) on the same Mac, on both PyTorch backends: MPS (the Apple GPU) and CPU. Every framework trains the same models, with the same hyperparameters, on the same data, and the training loss and test accuracy are recorded alongside the times: being faster only counts at the same results.

Each section below is one machine. Click a figure to see it at full size.

items.title: What is measured
items.text:
• One layer: one forward + backward pass of GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, GAT and GATv2 on random graphs of 100k, 500k and 2M edges.
  • Node classification: full-batch training of GCN, GraphSAGE and GAT on Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, Amazon Photo / Computers, Coauthor CS / Physics and ogbn-arxiv, 3 seeds.
  • Graph classification: mini-batch training of GCN, GraphSAGE and GIN on the TU datasets MUTAG, PROTEINS, NCI1 and DD, 3 seeds.

The scripts are in benchmarks/pyg_comparison. Its README describes how the comparison is kept fair, and every number of the figures is in a table in the results.md file next to them.

items.title: Reproducing
items.text:
pip install -e '.[benchmarks]'
python benchmarks/pyg_comparison/run.py    # ~1.5 hours, results/<chip>/<version>/
python benchmarks/pyg_comparison/plot.py   # figures, results.md and this page's section

Every configuration runs in its own process under a 16 GB memory cap; a run over the cap is reported as out of memory.

items.title: Changelog
items.text: Every release of mlx-graphs, newest first, with the notes of its GitHub release and, for some versions, hand-written notes from CHANGELOG.rst. The packages are on PyPI.

items.title: Unreleased
items.text: Merged after v0.5.3 · changes since v0.5.3

items.title: Large graphs
items.text:
• Datasets: Reddit, Reddit2, Flickr, Yelp, AmazonProducts and PPI, with PyG's files, edges, labels and splits (checked equal to PyG's, benchmarks/quality/dataset_parity.py). Single large graphs are stored as safetensors after processing. PPI is read from the GraphSAGE release, as DGL's server is down.
  • Temporal sampling: NeighborLoader and LinkNeighborLoader take PyG's time_attr, input_time / edge_label_time and temporal_strategy ("uniform" / "last"): only neighbors not later than their seed are sampled, with node- or edge-level timestamps, each seed getting its own subgraph (disjoint=True, also available without time). Implemented as a vectorized numpy sampler; "last" gives the same mini-batches as PyG with pyg-lib.
  • Feature and graph stores: FeatureStore / GraphStore (PyG's remote backend API) with in-memory and on-disk (MemmapFeatureStore, MemmapGraphStore) implementations. NeighborLoader((feature_store, graph_store), ...) gathers only the rows of the sampled nodes, so node features larger than the memory can be used for training.

items.title: Features
items.text: • Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) datasets: TGBLinkPropPredDataset (tgbl-wiki, tgbl-review, tgbl-coin, tgbl-comment, tgbl-flight) with TGB's chronological splits and precomputed one-vs-many negative samples (TGBNegativeEdgeSampler), and TGBNodePropPredDataset (tgbn-trade, tgbn-genre, tgbn-reddit, tgbn-token) with its label stream. TGBEvaluator computes MRR / Hits@k and NDCG@10 as py-tgb. The events, splits, negative samples and labels of tgbl-wiki, tgbl-review, tgbn-trade and tgbn-genre were checked to be identical to py-tgb's. New examples tgn_tgbl.py and tgn_tgbn.py train TGN with the TGB protocol (compared with py-tgb's PyG examples in benchmarks/tgn_comparison).

items.title: New API
items.text:
• Hierarchical and dense pooling, checked against PyG (outputs, auxiliary losses and gradients) and by training on PROTEINS in both frameworks (benchmarks/quality/pooling_quality.py):

    • dense pooling dense_diff_pool, dense_mincut_pool and DMoNPooling, with the dense layers DenseGCNConv, DenseSAGEConv, DenseGINConv and DenseGraphConv;
    • sparse hierarchical pooling EdgePooling (with unpool), ASAPooling, MemPooling and PANPooling (with PANConv), and the GraphUNet model;
    • GCNConv(improved=True) (self-loops of weight 2).

items.title: Point clouds and meshes
items.text:
• Layers PointNetConv (alias PointConv), PointTransformerConv, PPFConv, XConv, SplineConv (B-spline basis in MLX, any degree up to 3), GMMConv and FeaStConv, checked against PyG with copied weights (outputs and gradients).
  • Sampling and clustering: fps (farthest point sampling, one Metal threadgroup per point cloud; the same points as PyG with random_start=False), voxel_grid, nearest, graclus (parallel matching), consecutive_cluster, and the cluster poolings avg_pool, max_pool, avg_pool_x and max_pool_x.
  • Transforms SamplePoints, FixedPoints, NormalizeScale, Center, LinearTransformation, RandomJitter, RandomRotate, RandomScale, FaceToEdge, Cartesian, Distance, Polar and PointPairFeatures.
  • Datasets ModelNet (ModelNet10 and ModelNet40) and ShapeNet (part segmentation, downloaded from a Hugging Face mirror since the original URL is offline).
  • GraphData gets its number of nodes from pos when it has no node features, and offsets mesh triangles face in batches, as PyG does.
  • benchmarks/quality/pointcloud_quality.py trains PointNet++ and DGCNN on ModelNet10 with mlx-graphs and PyG.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Molecular and 3D models, checked against PyG with copied weights (outputs and gradients) and by training both on QM9 and ESOL (benchmarks/quality/molecular_quality.py): SchNet, DimeNet, DimeNetPlusPlus and AttentiveFP.
  • Molecular datasets matching PyG's: QM9, ZINC (subset and full) and MoleculeNet (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, BACE, BBBP, HIV, Tox21, ...).
  • from_smiles, to_smiles, from_rdmol and to_rdmol with PyG's x_map / e_map featurization (rdkit is an optional dependency).

items.title: 0.2.0: PyG parity
items.text:
2026-11-22 · GitHub release · Full diff · PyPI

Detailed notes (CHANGELOG.rst)

This release brings mlx-graphs close to PyTorch Geometric in features and API: about 235 new public classes and functions, samplers and loaders for mini-batch training, heterogeneous and temporal graphs, graph transformers, and 18 new datasets. Every addition was checked against PyG: layers with copied weights (outputs and gradients), samplers statistically, and models by training them in both frameworks on the same data (benchmarks/quality/).

Highlights

  • Samplers and loaders: LinkNeighborLoader, HGTLoader, ClusterData / ClusterLoader, the GraphSAINT samplers, ShaDowKHopSampler, RandomNodeLoader, ImbalancedSampler, DynamicBatchSampler, DataListLoader, DenseDataLoader; Dataloader gains drop_last, follow_batch, sampler, batch_sampler, transform and collate_fn.
  • Heterogeneous graphs: to_hetero and to_hetero_with_bases turn a homogeneous model into a heterogeneous one, as in PyG (without torch.fx: see the docstring for the supported model patterns); HANConv, HGTConv, RGATConv, FastRGCNConv; the OGBMAG dataset.
  • Temporal graphs: TemporalData, TemporalDataLoader, TGNMemory and its building blocks, LastNeighborLoader, JODIEDataset, and the new mlx_graphs.metrics package (link prediction ranking metrics, AUC, AP).
  • Graph transformers: GPSConv, SGFormer, Polynormer, MultiheadAttention, PerformerAttention, positional encodings (LapPEEncoder, RWSEEncoder, PositionalEncoding, TemporalEncoding), LRGBDataset and GNNBenchmarkDataset.
  • Aggregations: the mlx_graphs.nn.aggr module (sum, mean, max, min, mul, var, std, median, quantile, softmax, power mean, LSTM, GRU, set transformer, graph multiset transformer, sort, MLP, LCM, deep sets, equilibrium, degree scaler, ...). MessagePassing(aggr=...) accepts a name, a list of aggregations (concatenated or combined with aggr_kwargs={"mode": ...}) or an Aggregation module.
  • PyG names: GraphData has the x, edge_attr and y aliases, GraphDataBatch has batch and ptr, and the norm layers are also exported under their PyG names (GraphNorm, PairNorm, ...).

  • Documentation:

    • new tutorials, each compared with PyG on accuracy and runtime: mini-batch training on large graphs, link prediction, temporal graph networks, heterogeneous graphs with to_hetero, and graph transformers with GPS; node2vec is now a single tutorial;
    • new pages: "Creating message passing layers" (user guide) and "Validation against PyG"; an updated "Coming from PyTorch Geometric"; an overview figure at the top of every tutorial.

New API

  • mlx_graphs.nn:

    • Message passing layers:

      • AGNNConv, ARMAConv, CGConv, ClusterGCNConv, DirGNNConv, DynamicEdgeConv, ECConv, FAConv, FastRGCNConv, FiLMConv;
      • GCN2Conv, GENConv, GINEConv, GPSConv, GatedGraphConv, GeneralConv, HANConv, HGTConv, LEConv, LGConv, MFConv;
      • MixHopConv, NNConv, PNAConv, RGATConv, ResGatedGraphConv, SSGConv.

    • Models:

      • PNA, EdgeCNN, DeepGCNLayer, LINKX, LightGCN, LabelPropagation, CorrectAndSmooth, MaskLabel, RECT_L;
      • graph autoencoders: GAE, VGAE, ARGA, ARGVA, InnerProductDecoder;
      • DeepGraphInfomax;
      • knowledge graph embeddings: KGEModel, TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, RotatE, KGTripletLoader;
      • SGFormer, Polynormer, TGNMemory.

    • Norms: BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm, PairNorm, DiffGroupNorm, MessageNorm, MeanSubtractionNorm, GraphSizeNorm, HeteroBatchNorm, HeteroLayerNorm.

    • Pooling and graph construction: TopKPooling, SAGPooling, global_sort_pool, knn, knn_graph, radius, radius_graph.

  • mlx_graphs.transforms: AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE, AddRemainingSelfLoops, FeaturePropagation, IndexToMask, KNNGraph, LineGraph, LocalDegreeProfile, MaskToIndex, NormalizeFeatures, RadiusGraph, RemoveDuplicatedEdges, RemoveTrainingClasses, SIGN, SVDFeatureReduction, TargetIndegree, ToDense, TwoHop, VirtualNode.

  • mlx_graphs.utils:

    • graph generators;
    • subgraph, mask and self-loop helpers;
    • negative sampling for batches;
    • get_ppr;
    • assortativity, normalized_cut;
    • scipy conversions;
    • the scatter reductions var, std, mul, median and quantile.

  • mlx_graphs.datasets:

    • citation and web graphs: CitationFull, CoraFull, WikiCS, WebKB, WikipediaNetwork, Actor, HeterophilousGraphDataset;
    • knowledge graphs: FB15k_237, WordNet18, WordNet18RR;
    • synthetic graphs: FakeDataset, FakeHeteroDataset;
    • JODIEDataset, LRGBDataset, GNNBenchmarkDataset, OGBMAG;
    • a torch-free reader for .pt files (load_torch_file), which uses a restricted unpickler.

  • Dataset, GraphData and HeteroGraphData gain PyG conveniences, among them num_classes (inferred as in PyG), shuffle, to_homogeneous and the feature counts.

Changes that can affect existing code

  • Self-loops now default to PyG's behaviour.

    • GCNConv defaults to add_self_loops=True (it was False).
    • GATConv and GATv2Conv gain add_self_loops=True and fill_value="mean".
    • To keep the previous results, pass add_self_loops=False.

  • GIN: the act and norm arguments now also apply to the MLP inside every GINConv, as in PyG. Before, that MLP always used ReLU and no normalization.

    • Models with the defaults (act="relu", norm=None) are unchanged.
    • With norm="batch" or "layer", the MLPs gain norm layers, so weights saved before this change will not load as-is.

  • GAT: dropout now also applies to the attention coefficients of every GATConv / GATv2Conv, as in PyG's GAT. Before, it only applied between layers. Models with dropout=0 are unchanged.

  • LayerNormalization:

    • mode="graph" (the default) was broken and now matches PyG's LayerNorm.
    • mode="node" now uses the layer's own weight and bias. Its unused layernorm.* parameters are gone, so older checkpoints do not load strictly.

  • Index dtypes are int32 throughout. This covers:

    • the n_id, e_id and edge_index returned by NeighborLoader;
    • GraphDataBatch.batch_indices, batch and ptr;
    • the follow_batch vectors.

    Indexing with them works as before. int64 is used only for graphs with more than 2^31 - 1 nodes or edges.

  • GraphDataBatch indexes like a Python list of graphs.

    • Slices are clipped instead of raising: batch[:101] on a smaller batch, or batch[3:2], which gives [].
    • Negative steps work.
    • batch[num_graphs] raises IndexError.
    • Index arrays, lists and boolean masks are accepted.

  • MessagePassing(aggr="softmax") is now the softmax aggregation (SoftmaxAggregation), as in PyG and as aggr=["softmax", ...] already was. Plain string aggregations given with aggr_kwargs now use them instead of ignoring them.

  • Max and min aggregations split the gradient equally among tied values, as PyG does (e.g. with duplicate edges). Before, every tied value got the full gradient. The backward pass of the fused max/min kernels is slower as a result; forward passes are unchanged.

  • Initialization: HeteroDictLinear now initializes like torch.nn.Linear, as in PyG, instead of Glorot.

Fixes to previously released code

  • SAGEConv with a max, min, std or list aggregation and more input than output features projected before aggregating (max(Wx) instead of W max(x)).
  • SAGEConv gains PyG's root_weight. Without it, DirGNNConv(SAGEConv) kept a root projection in both directions and trained 2-3 points below PyG.
  • TUDataset dropped edge labels.
  • IMDB keyed its labels by "movies" instead of the "movie" node type.
  • NeighborLoader with out-of-range seed nodes read past the sampler's buffers. It now raises IndexError.
  • Batching graphs whose first graph has no nodes broke the edge offsets.
  • Unbatching turned int32 edge_index into int64.
  • QM7b downloads failed: the old http URL returns 400. It now uses PyG's https URL.
  • Tar extraction is now protected against path traversal and symlink escapes.

Tips when porting PyG code

  • mlx.optimizers.Adam has no bias correction by default, unlike torch.optim.Adam. Use Adam(learning_rate=..., bias_correction=True) to train the same way.
  • Batches of graphs of varying sizes create arrays of many different shapes. To bound memory, cap MLX's buffer cache with mx.set_cache_limit(...).

Known limitations

  • to_hetero:

    • It does not detect operations that mix rows across node types inside the model's __call__ (e.g. x.mean(0), sorting). PyG traces these per node type.
    • Copies without a reset_parameters() method are re-initialized by shuffling their weights.

  • GPS, SGFormer, Polynormer and the LSTM, GRU, set transformer and sort aggregations read the batch layout on the host. They work with nn.value_and_grad but not with mx.compile, unless the precomputed layout= argument is given (GPS, SGFormer, Polynormer).

  • TGNMemory's memory is not saved by save_weights. Use memory_state() and load_memory_state().
  • MLX 0.32.4 crashes when a compiled activation is applied to an empty matmul result. CGConv, NNConv and EdgeConv are guarded against it. Most layers still fail on graphs with zero nodes.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
This brings mlx-graphs close to PyTorch Geometric in features and API, as release 0.2.0. It adds about 235 public classes and functions, each checked against PyG. The full list is in CHANGELOG.rst, which the docs show as the Changelog page.

  • Mini-batch training:
    • LinkNeighborLoader, HGTLoader, ClusterData / ClusterLoader, the GraphSAINT samplers, ShaDowKHopSampler, RandomNodeLoader, ImbalancedSampler, DynamicBatchSampler, DataListLoader, DenseDataLoader.
    • Dataloader gains drop_last, follow_batch, sampler, batch_sampler, transform and collate_fn.
  • Heterogeneous graphs: to_hetero and to_hetero_with_bases (without torch.fx), HANConv, HGTConv, RGATConv, FastRGCNConv, OGBMAG.
  • Temporal graphs: TemporalData, TemporalDataLoader, TGNMemory, LastNeighborLoader, JODIEDataset, and a new mlx_graphs.metrics package with ranking metrics, AUC and AP.
  • Graph transformers: GPSConv, SGFormer, Polynormer, MultiheadAttention, PerformerAttention, and positional encodings (AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE, RWSEEncoder, LapPEEncoder).
  • Layers and models:
    • 26 new convolutions;
    • aggregation modules, usable in MessagePassing(aggr=...) by name, as a list or as a module;
    • 11 norms, plus TopK / SAG pooling;
    • autoencoders, DeepGraphInfomax, knowledge-graph embeddings, LINKX, LightGCN, CorrectAndSmooth, PNA, EdgeCNN, and more.
  • Transforms, utilities and 18 datasets.
  • Docs:
    • seven tutorials (each compares accuracy and runtime with PyG);
    • a guide to writing message passing layers;
    • a "Validation against PyG" page;
    • an examples index;
    • the changelog;
    • an updated "Coming from PyTorch Geometric" page.

items.title: Changes that can affect existing code
items.text:
The changelog explains each change and how to keep the old behaviour.

  • GCNConv, GATConv and GATv2Conv add self-loops by default, as in PyG. Pass add_self_loops=False for the previous results.
  • GIN: act and norm now also apply to the MLP inside each GINConv. Models with the defaults are unchanged.
  • GAT: dropout now also applies to the attention coefficients.
  • LayerNormalization:
    • mode="graph", the default, was broken; it now matches PyG.
    • mode="node" no longer has its unused layernorm.* parameters.
  • Index arrays are int32 throughout: NeighborLoader outputs, GraphDataBatch.batch and ptr.
  • GraphDataBatch indexing behaves like a Python list: slices are clipped, batch[num_graphs] raises IndexError, and masks and index arrays work.
  • aggr="softmax" is now SoftmaxAggregation.
  • Max/min aggregations split the gradient among tied values, as PyG does. The fused backward pass is slower as a result; forward passes are unchanged.
  • HeteroDictLinear initializes like torch.nn.Linear.

items.title: Fixes to released code
items.text:
• SAGEConv projected before aggregating for max, min, std and list aggregations.
  • SAGEConv gains root_weight. Without it, DirGNNConv(SAGEConv) trained 2–3 points below PyG.
  • TUDataset dropped edge labels.
  • IMDB keyed its labels by the wrong node type.
  • NeighborLoader read out of bounds on out-of-range seeds.
  • Batching broke edge offsets when the first graph was empty.
  • QM7b downloads failed.
  • Tar extraction allowed path traversal.

  • Training (benchmarks/quality/, results on the Validation page):
    • Models are trained in both frameworks on the same data and splits.
    • Node level: 96 of 99 configurations match PyG. Of the other three, two are PNA runs, which are unstable in both frameworks, and one is DirGNN(GCN) on CiteSeer, where mlx-graphs scores higher.
    • Graph level: 34 of 34 configurations match.
  • TGN, GPS and to_hetero comparisons are in benchmarks/tgn_comparison, benchmarks/gps_peptides and benchmarks/to_hetero.

items.title: mlx-graphs 0.1.0: faster message passing, PyG-parity layers and models, PyG benchmarks
items.text: On an M5 Pro, mlx-graphs now trains GNNs 5.6× faster than PyTorch Geometric on MPS and 5.8× faster than on CPU, with the same accuracy (median of 35 training benchmarks on 12 datasets, up to 58×). Compared with 0.0.11 (current main), a single layer is 1.5–2.7× faster on large graphs.

items.title: Performance
items.text:
• Fused message passing: layers whose message is a weighted sum of neighbour features aggregate with one sparse × dense matmul on the GPU (mlx-cluster kernels) instead of gather-scatter, so the [num_edges, features] message array is never built. This includes GAT/GATv2 (one SpMM per head). format="auto" switches from COO to the faster CSR kernel when the conversion pays off; it can be turned off globally or per block of code.
  • Cached GCN normalization for GCN, SGConv, APPNP, TAGConv and ChebConv on a fixed graph.
  • Vectorized coalesce, to_undirected, batching/collate and scatter_softmax.

items.title: New features
items.text:
• Layers: TransformerConv, GraphConv, SGConv, APPNP, ChebConv, TAGConv, EdgeConv, RGCNConv.
  • Models: GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, GAT (v1/v2), MLP, with dropout, batch/layer norm and Jumping Knowledge.
  • Pooling / readout: AttentionalAggregation, Set2Set, JumpingKnowledge.
  • Transforms: Compose, structure transforms (self-loops, undirected, isolated nodes, largest connected component, …), RandomNodeSplit, RandomLinkSplit, feature transforms (OneHotDegree, Constant, AddRandomWalkPE, GCNNorm).
  • Utilities: subgraph, k_hop_subgraph, negative sampling, dropout_edge / dropout_node, to_dense_batch, to_dense_adj, get_laplacian, homophily, from_pyg / to_pyg.
  • Datasets: Amazon (Computers, Photo) and Coauthor (CS, Physics).

items.title: Fixes
items.text:
• Layers are initialized as in PyG (Glorot for GCN/GAT, PyTorch's default Linear init for GraphSAGE/GraphConv). GraphSAGE no longer collapses on Amazon: 72% → 91% test accuracy on Photo, 63% → 78% on Computers.
  • GAT attention vectors use Glorot initialization.
  • Dataloader reshuffles on every pass and has a len() (number of batches).

items.title: Behaviour changes
items.text:
Code written for 0.0.11 may behave differently:

  • Layers initialize as in PyG, so trained results can differ slightly.
  • coalesce sorts edges by (source, destination) and no longer swaps the rows of edge_index.
  • Dataloader reshuffles on every pass when shuffle=True.
  • Requires mlx>=0.32 and mlx_cluster>=0.1.2. Dependencies are now minimum versions instead of exact pins.

items.title: Benchmarks against PyG
items.text:
benchmarks/pyg_comparison compares mlx-graphs with PyG on MPS and on CPU, using the same models, data and hyperparameters:

  • Isolation: each configuration runs in its own process under a 16 GB memory cap.

items.title: Validation against PyG
items.text:
mlx-graphs follows PyTorch Geometric (PyG), and every layer, sampler and model added for PyG parity was checked against PyG: layers by copying PyG's weights and comparing outputs and gradients, samplers statistically, and models by training them in both frameworks on the same data. This page describes how, summarizes the results, lists the bugs these checks found, and shows how to rerun them.

The full result tables are in the repository, under benchmarks/quality. The speed comparison is on the Benchmarks page.

items.title: Method
items.text:
The checks work at three levels:

Level What is compared Where Layers The same layer is built in both frameworks and PyG's weights are copied into the mlx-graphs one. Both run on the same random graph, with duplicate edges, self-loops and isolated nodes, and the outputs (and for many layers the gradients) must agree. The unit tests, tests/ Samplers and loaders Exact comparisons with PyG's pure-Python code paths where they exist, and otherwise statistical properties: coverage of every node once per epoch, uniform neighbour sampling, unbiased normalizations. Then mini-batch training against full-batch training. benchmarks/quality/sampler_quality.py Training quality The same model is trained in both frameworks, with the same data, splits and hyperparameters, over several seeds. The test metric is read at the epoch of best validation metric. benchmarks/quality/node_quality.py, benchmarks/quality/graph_quality.py, and the TGN, GPS and to_hetero comparisons

A training configuration passes when the gap between the means is within 1 point, or within 2 standard deviations of PyG's results: \(|\mathrm{gap}| \le 1\) or \(|\mathrm{gap}| \le 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{PyG}}\). The node classification table also marks pass (noise) a gap within 2 standard errors of the difference of the means.

Keeping the comparison fair

  • Same model and data. Both frameworks train the same architecture with the same hyperparameters, on identical arrays: the data is loaded once and handed to both, and the splits are the same. Each framework keeps its own default initialization, and mlx-graphs layers are initialized as in PyG.
  • Adam's bias correction. MLX's Adam is created with bias_correction=True, which is the update rule of torch.optim.Adam. MLX's default has no bias correction and takes much larger first steps: it lowered GAT's accuracy on Cora by about 4 points in the speed benchmarks, and gave GPS on Peptides-func a clearly higher training loss.
  • L2 penalty vs weight decay. torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=...) adds weight_decay * p to the gradients (an L2 penalty), which is not the decoupled weight decay of AdamW. The harnesses reproduce it in MLX by adding the same term to the gradients. Where the PyG script uses AdamW (the to_hetero comparison), both frameworks use AdamW.
  • Devices. mlx-graphs runs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU (with one or two torch threads per run), except for the slow deep models of the node classification harness (GCNII, DeeperGCN), for which PyG runs on MPS. The device changes the speed, not what is compared.
  • One process per run. Every configuration and seed runs in its own process under a memory cap.

Numerical tolerance

MLX's float32 matmul on the Mac's GPU has a relative error of about 1e-3, where NumPy and torch on the CPU have about 1e-7. This is MLX behaviour, not mlx-graphs', and it is the source of the ~1e-3 differences of the forward passes. It can be larger for gradients that go through a cancellation: EdgeConv's first layer, whose inputs are differences x_j - x_i, has gradient differences of up to about 10 %. The layer tests therefore use a tolerance of 2e-2: a wrong formula is off by far more. It did not change any training result.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
108 of the 151 test files compare mlx-graphs with PyG or use PyG as a reference:

Tests Files using PyG Examples Convolution layers (tests/nn/conv) 39 of 44 test_gat_conv.py, test_gine_conv.py, test_pna_conv.py Models (tests/nn/models) 7 of 8 autoencoders, KGE, LightGCN, label propagation, TGN Norms (tests/nn/norm) 8 of 9 GraphNorm, PairNorm, LayerNorm, MessageNorm Pooling (tests/nn/pooling) 5 of 6 TopK pooling, Set2Set, global pooling Aggregations (tests/nn/aggr) 2 of 2 the aggregation modules, including the learnable ones Message passing, to_hetero, graph transformers (tests/nn) 3 of 5 test_to_hetero.py, test_message_passing_aggr.py Transforms, utilities, data, loaders, metrics 27 of 52 test_scatter_reductions.py, test_pyg_reference.py Datasets (slow tests, pytest --datasets) 17 of 23 a dataset's arrays against PyG's version of it Other (tests/algorithms, tests/test_hetero_linear.py) 0 of 2 (mlx-graphs only)

12 of these files also compare gradients with torch's autograd, among them the GAT, GATv2, AGNN, GEN, MF and DirGNN convolutions, the aggregations, the scatter reductions and TGNMemory. The to_hetero tests copy PyG's weights into converted models, including on the full DBLP and IMDB graphs (slow tests). tests/pyg_copy.py holds the helpers that convert PyG state dicts. Message passing shows how to write such a test.

Some layers were also checked with copied weights on full datasets:

  • On Cora: PairNorm, GraphNorm and GENConv (with and without MessageNorm) agree with PyG to GPU matmul precision, forward and input gradients; CorrectAndSmooth agrees to 3e-5; LabelPropagation gives identical accuracies.
  • On PubMed: PNAConv's output and input gradients agree with PyG's to 1e-4 and 1e-8 (relative ~1e-3).
  • On DBLP: the HGT model's forward pass matches PyG's on the full graph.
  • On Peptides-func: the full GPS model gives the same train-mode loss (0.70363 vs 0.70362 on 16 graphs) and gradients within ~1 %.

items.title: Hierarchical pooling on PROTEINS
items.text:
benchmarks/quality/pooling_quality.py trains the same architectures in both frameworks on PROTEINS, with the same data and splits (5 seeds, 100 epochs; test accuracy in % at the best validation epoch):

Model PyG mlx-graphs Gap DiffPool 71.4 ± 4.8 74.1 ± 4.8 +2.8 MinCutPool 73.0 ± 4.3 74.5 ± 5.0 +1.4 DMoN 72.7 ± 4.7 73.9 ± 4.2 +1.2 ASAPooling 68.2 ± 6.8 70.7 ± 4.1 +2.5 EdgePooling 70.2 ± 7.2 71.1 ± 4.0 +0.9 GraphUNet 73.4 ± 3.7 75.5 ± 2.5 +2.1

All six are within 2 PyG standard deviations (3 to 7 points with 5 random splits of PROTEINS). MinCut and DMoN hit non-finite gradients in both frameworks on nearly empty clusters; those steps are skipped in both (about twice as many in mlx-graphs, with the same final accuracy). The dense and sparse pooling layers are also compared with PyG with copied weights (outputs, auxiliary losses and gradients) in the test suite. Full table: pooling_results.md.

items.title: Point clouds on ModelNet10
items.text: PointNet++ (PyG's examples/pointnet2_classification.py: fps, radius, PointNetConv) trained for 5 epochs on ModelNet10, on the same fixed clouds of 1024 points sampled through mlx-graphs' ModelNet and SamplePoints, reaches a test accuracy of 80.9 % in mlx-graphs and 82.5 % in PyG (best epoch: 80.9 % and 82.9 %), with training losses of 0.26 and 0.31. DGCNN (DynamicEdgeConv, PyG's examples/dgcnn_classification.py) reaches 78.0 % and 80.2 % after 3 epochs. The point cloud layers, fps, voxel_grid, nearest, graclus and the point cloud transforms are also compared with PyG in the test suite (fps picks the same points as PyG with random_start=False, in 1.9 ms with its Metal kernel against 132 ms for torch_cluster on the CPU, for 32 clouds of 1024 points). Full table: pointcloud_results.md.

items.title: Molecular models
items.text:
SchNet, DimeNet, DimeNet++ and AttentiveFP match PyG with copied weights (outputs, and gradients with respect to the parameters and to the atom positions, tests/nn/models/test_molecular.py). They were also trained in both frameworks (benchmarks/quality/molecular_quality.py, small budget): SchNet and DimeNet++ on the HOMO-LUMO gap of a random QM9 subset, AttentiveFP on ESOL (one-hot from_smiles features, random 80/10/10 splits).

Model Task PyG mlx-graphs SchNet QM9 gap, 10k molecules, 10 epochs, test MAE (eV), 2 seeds 0.377 ± 0.004 0.384 ± 0.019 DimeNet++ QM9 gap, 5k molecules, 6 epochs, test MAE (eV), 1 seed 0.270 0.279 AttentiveFP ESOL, 100 epochs, test RMSE, 3 seeds 0.606 ± 0.058 0.593 ± 0.034

Full table, with the time per epoch: molecular_results.md.

items.title: Samplers and loaders
items.text:
PyG's own neighbour samplers, GraphSAINT, ShaDow, ClusterData and knn / radius need compiled extensions (pyg-lib, torch_sparse, torch_cluster), so the samplers are checked against references that don't:

  • Exactly, in the test suite: RandomNodeLoader, ClusterLoader, DynamicBatchSampler and ImbalancedSampler against PyG's pure-Python classes; ShaDow subgraphs and full-fan-out NeighborLoader against PyG's k_hop_subgraph; knn / radius against SciPy's KD-tree; KNNGraph / RadiusGraph against PyG's transforms.
  • Statistically: every seed node or item covered exactly once per epoch (NeighborLoader, LinkNeighborLoader, ShaDowKHopSampler, RandomNodeLoader, ClusterLoader); uniform neighbour sampling (chi-squared tests on the highest-degree nodes of Cora); class balance of ImbalancedSampler; batch budgets of DynamicBatchSampler; and the bias of GraphSAINT's normalizations.
  • By training: a 2-layer GraphSAGE trained with each mini-batch method against full-batch training.

Every mini-batch method lands within one standard deviation of full-batch training (test accuracy in %, 5 seeds):

Training Cora PubMed Full batch, PyG 80.3 ± 0.7 76.9 ± 0.8 Full batch, mlx-graphs 80.2 ± 0.7 77.3 ± 0.8 NeighborLoader [10, 10] 80.3 ± 0.9 76.6 ± 0.4 GraphSAINTRandomWalkSampler 80.3 ± 1.1 77.0 ± 0.9 ClusterLoader (20 parts, 5 per batch) 79.4 ± 1.4 76.9 ± 0.6 ShaDowKHopSampler (depth 2, 10) 80.2 ± 0.8 76.9 ± 0.5

For link prediction, LinkNeighborLoader reaches a test AUC of 84.3 ± 1.4 % on Cora (full batch: 84.4 ± 3.2 % in mlx-graphs, 83.3 ± 1.6 % in PyG) and 89.2 ± 0.7 % on PubMed (full batch: 90.1 % in both). Full results: sampler_results.md.

items.title: Large graphs
items.text:
Results of benchmarks/quality/ for the large datasets, temporal neighbour sampling and the memory-mapped feature store (Apple M5 Pro, 64 GB, shared with other jobs, so the times are indicative). Full results: large_graph_results.md.

The datasets are identical to PyG's. dataset_parity.py loads Flickr, Reddit, Reddit2, Yelp, AmazonProducts and PPI with both libraries and compares the edges (in the same order), features, labels and split masks: all equal. PPI is read from the GraphSAGE release (DGL's server, which PyG uses, is down) and gives exactly PyG's 20 / 2 / 2 graphs.

GraphSAGE mini-batch training (2 layers, NeighborLoader with fan-outs [25, 10], batches of 1,024; PyG on the CPU with 8 threads):

Dataset Framework Seeds × epochs Test accuracy s / epoch Flickr mlx-graphs 3 × 10 0.5095 ± 0.0001 3.6 Flickr mlx-graphs, MemmapFeatureStore 3 × 10 0.5101 ± 0.0026 8.7 Flickr PyG 3 × 10 0.5120 ± 0.0015 11.5 Reddit mlx-graphs 1 × 3 0.9558 27.6 Reddit PyG 1 × 3 0.9583 79.7

Temporal sampling (temporal_sampler_quality.py, a random graph of 20,000 nodes and 400,000 timestamped edges): with temporal_strategy="last", the mini-batches are identical to PyG's with pyg-lib (8 of 8, with node- and edge-level time); neither library samples an edge later than its seed; with "uniform", the sampling frequencies are as close to uniform as PyG's (mean deviation 0.0267 against 0.0266 with node-level time, no seed rejected by a chi-squared test in either). pyg-lib's C++ sampler is 1.2 to 2.3 times faster than the vectorized numpy one.

Memory-mapped features (feature_store_memory.py): a NeighborLoader over a MemmapFeatureStore of 6.1 GB (1.5M nodes × 1,024 features) and a MemmapGraphStore gathers 250 MB of features per mini-batch and peaks at 2.8 GB of resident memory over 100 mini-batches, where loading the features in a GraphData would take 6.1 GB. See the large graphs guide.

items.title: Temporal graph networks
items.text:
TGN link prediction on JODIE Wikipedia, examples/tgn_jodie.py against PyG's examples/tgn.py, with the same hyperparameters, 8 epochs, seeds 0 and 1:

Run Test AP, seeds 0 / 1 Test AUC, seeds 0 / 1 mlx-graphs 0.957 / 0.955 0.953 / 0.951 PyG 0.950 / 0.949 0.946 / 0.948 PyG with the torch-scatter scatter_argmax 0.952 / 0.952 0.949 / 0.952

Without torch-scatter, PyG's fallback scatter_argmax gives empty groups the index dim_size - 1, so its LastAggregator copies an unrelated message to the nodes that have none instead of zeros. mlx-graphs follows the torch-scatter semantics, so the comparison also runs PyG with that function patched. Results: results.json. The TGN tutorial compares the two in more detail.

items.title: Temporal Graph Benchmark
items.text:
The TGB datasets are checked against the official py-tgb package (tests/datasets/test_tgb.py): for tgbl-wiki, tgbl-review, tgbn-trade and tgbn-genre, the events (src, dst, t, msg, w), the split masks, the negative samples of every validation and test event and the node label streams are identical to py-tgb's. The large datasets (tgbl-coin, tgbl-comment, tgbl-flight, tgbn-reddit, tgbn-token) are checked on the first 200,000 events of their raw files (benchmarks/tgn_comparison/check_tgb_slices.py), without their negative samples. TGBEvaluator returns the same MRR, Hits@10 and NDCG@10 as py-tgb's evaluators, ties included.

TGN with the TGB protocol (examples/tgn_tgbl.py / tgn_tgbn.py against py-tgb's PyG TGN examples, benchmarks/tgn_comparison/compare_tgb.py), same hyperparameters, 10 epochs, seeds 1 to 5 (mean ± sample std; time per epoch on a shared M-series machine, PyG on the CPU with 4 threads):

Run Val Test Train s/epoch Val s/epoch tgbl-wiki MRR, mlx-graphs 0.312 ± 0.039 0.281 ± 0.042 6.5 2.0 tgbl-wiki MRR, PyG 0.275 ± 0.062 0.253 ± 0.062 15.6 10.7 tgbn-trade NDCG@10, mlx-graphs 0.394 ± 0.002 0.374 ± 0.003 7.2 1.0 tgbn-trade NDCG@10, PyG 0.388 ± 0.009 0.368 ± 0.010 9.8 2.1

The differences are within seed noise (Welch's t-test: p = 0.30 and 0.43 for the tgbl-wiki validation and test MRR, p = 0.24 and 0.27 for tgbn-trade). On tgbl-wiki both are still improving at epoch 10, the best epoch is 9 or 10 in every run, and the MRR at a fixed early epoch varies a lot with the seed (validation 0.25 to 0.35 in mlx-graphs, 0.18 to 0.34 in PyG). PyG scores the events of a mini-batch together; on the same seed this gives the same MRR as the edge-by-edge loop of the TGB example (val 0.0513, test 0.0559 after one epoch), whose validation pass takes 275 s instead of 7 s. Results: results_tgb.json.

items.title: GPS on Peptides-func
items.text:
GPSConv (examples/graph_gps_peptides.py) against a PyG twin of the same model: 4 GPS layers (GINE and 4-head attention), the same data with random-walk encodings, Adam (lr 1e-3, L2 1e-5), 10 epochs, seeds 0 and 1. Average precision over the 10 tasks:

Run Final train loss Best val AP Test AP PyG, seed 0 0.2522 0.4044 0.3881 PyG, seed 1 0.2613 0.4194 0.4079 mlx-graphs, seed 0 0.2588 0.4447 0.4288 mlx-graphs, seed 1 0.2553 0.4437 0.4268

The full-model gradient check (above) gives the same loss and gradients within ~1 %. Details: benchmarks/gps_peptides.

items.title: to_hetero on DBLP
items.text: benchmarks/to_hetero/compare_dblp.py trains to_hetero(GraphSAGE) and to_hetero(GAT) for author classification on DBLP, full batch, in both frameworks with the same data, architecture and optimizer (AdamW, lr 0.005, weight decay 0.001), and reports the test accuracy at the best validation epoch over several seeds. Mini-batch training (NeighborLoader, HGTLoader) runs in mlx-graphs only, since PyG's heterogeneous samplers need pyg-lib or torch-sparse. Its results are not committed to the repository. The models it converts are also checked with copied weights in tests/nn/test_to_hetero.py, including on the full DBLP and IMDB graphs.

items.title: Remaining mismatches
items.text:
Three node classification configurations don't pass.

PNAConv on Cora (-4.6) and CiteSeer (+6.8). The gaps have opposite signs. PNAConv on raw features, with amplification scalers, trains with large loss spikes in both frameworks: PyG's seed 0 on PubMed jumps to a loss of 3.0, and mlx-graphs' seed 3 to 4.9 near the end. With copied weights on PubMed, the layer's output and input gradients agree with PyG's to 1e-4 and 1e-8 (relative ~1e-3): the layer computes the same function, which points to the unstable training rather than to the layer. The PubMed row passes (-0.2), and so do the PNA model on Cora and CiteSeer (+1.7, +3.1) and PNA on MUTAG and PROTEINS.

DirGNNConv(GCNConv) on CiteSeer (+1.8). mlx-graphs is ahead: 68.7 ± 1.4 % against PyG's 66.9 ± 0.7 %, beyond 1 point and twice PyG's small standard deviation. The training losses are close (0.006 / 0.008 over epochs 25-75, 0.011 / 0.008 at the end, PyG / mlx-graphs), the Cora (+0.6) and PubMed (-0.4) rows pass, and with copied weights the layer gives the same outputs as PyG's DirGNNConv (tests/nn/conv/test_dir_gnn_conv.py). No cause has been identified.

items.title: Bugs found and fixed
items.text:
Found by the training and sampler comparisons, each fixed with a regression test:

  • SAGEConv with a non-linear aggregation ("max", "min", "std", lists, modules) and more input than output features projected the features before aggregating (max(W x) instead of PyG's W max(x)), a trick only valid for sum and mean. Max error against PyG with copied weights: 1.7.
  • Lists of aggregations: SAGEConv crashed, and GENConv did not accept them. Both now size their projections like PyG's. The other layers with a projection after the aggregation crashed with a shape error, or for GATConv / GATv2Conv returned twice as many rows; they now refuse concatenating lists with a clear error (supports_concat_aggr).
  • NaN gradients from L2 norms at zero in AGNNConv, MessageNorm and GENConv(msg_norm=True): a node whose features are all zero (common after ReLU and dropout) made every gradient NaN. Seen as AGNN on PubMed going NaN at epoch 145, and GENConv with MessageNorm reaching 66 % instead of 79 % on Cora (one seed).
  • MixHopConv stored its per-power layers in a dict that load_weights could not load.
  • AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE did not converge on Cora (float64 eigensolver on float32 values).
  • DirGNNConv(GCNConv(...)), PyG's usual way to build it, raised an error.
  • DirGNNConv(SAGEConv) trained 2-3 points below PyG with twice its training loss: SAGEConv had no root_weight, so both directions kept a root projection. SAGEConv now has PyG's root_weight, and the rows pass (+0.9 / +0.7 / +0.5).
  • TUDataset dropped edge labels (e.g. MUTAG's bond types) and did not reorder edge features with the edges. MUTAG, PROTEINS and NCI1 now equal PyG's arrays.
  • IMDB stored its labels under "movies" instead of the "movie" node type.
  • HeteroDictLinear (used by HGTConv) initialized with Glorot weights instead of torch.nn.Linear's: HGT on DBLP reached 76.9 ± 2.3 % against PyG's 71.8 ± 1.8 %. With PyG's initialization it reaches 73.0 ± 2.5 %.
  • GINEConv's edge projection was also initialized with Glorot weights (GINE on MUTAG: 80.0 ± 10.5 % before the fix, 82.0 ± 7.1 % after, 78.0 ± 13.6 % in PyG).
  • GraphSAINT's edge_norm used the count of the edge's source node, as PyG does, instead of its target (the paper's definition). On Cora, the median relative error of the normalized aggregation was about 50 % with the source count; with the target count it is sampling noise that shrinks with sample_coverage.

Other differences from PyG fixed in the same release (see the changelog):

  • LayerNormalization(mode="graph") gave wrong shapes with batch indices, and mode="node" ignored its own weight and bias. Both now match PyG's LayerNorm.
  • Max and min aggregations gave the full gradient to every tied value (e.g. the identical messages of duplicate edges). They now split it equally, as PyG does.
  • MultiAggregation(mode="std") had a NaN gradient for sets of a single element.
  • GIN and EdgeCNN did not apply the model's act and norm to the MLPs inside their convolutions, as PyG does.

items.title: Where mlx-graphs differs from PyG on purpose
items.text:
• GraphSAINT normalization: target count in edge_norm (see above).
  • GraphSAINT edge sampler: mlx-graphs samples edges with the paper's probabilities, \(1/\deg(u) + 1/\deg(v)\). PyG's GraphSAINTEdgeSampler computes the inverse weighting, which favours edges between hubs. At the same number of edges, the paper's probabilities give a 3.5-4.4x smaller standard deviation of the estimated aggregation.
  • DynamicBatchSampler with skip_too_big=True yields every graph once; PyG re-yields the graphs that follow a skipped one. Without skip_too_big, the batches are the same as PyG's.
  • TGN's LastAggregator gives zeros to nodes without messages, as PyG does with torch-scatter (see above).
  • TopK and SAG pooling break ties between equal scores differently. Both are valid, and training quality is the same.

items.title: Reproducing
items.text:
Install the test and benchmark dependencies (some harnesses also use scikit-learn), then run:

pip install -e '.[test,benchmarks]'

# layer-level parity (add --datasets for the slow tests that download data)
pytest tests

# node classification (--configs gcn arma ... for a subset, --summarize for the table only)
python benchmarks/quality/node_quality.py

# graph-level, heterogeneous, link and KG models (--groups tu kge ... for a subset)
python benchmarks/quality/graph_quality.py

# hierarchical and dense pooling on PROTEINS (--models diffpool asap ... for a subset)
python benchmarks/quality/pooling_quality.py

# PointNet++ and DGCNN on ModelNet10 (--models pointnet2 --epochs 5 for a subset)
python benchmarks/quality/pointcloud_quality.py

# SchNet and DimeNet++ on QM9, AttentiveFP on ESOL (--tasks attentivefp for a subset)
python benchmarks/quality/molecular_quality.py

# large graphs: datasets equal to PyG's, GraphSAGE training, temporal sampling, feature store
python benchmarks/run_capped.py --gb 24 -- python benchmarks/quality/dataset_parity.py \
    --data-dir .mlx_graphs_data --datasets flickr reddit2 yelp reddit ppi amazon_products
python benchmarks/run_capped.py --gb 16 -- python benchmarks/quality/large_graph_training.py \
    --datasets flickr --seeds 0 1 2 --epochs 10
PYTHONPATH=<pyg-lib dir> python benchmarks/quality/temporal_sampler_quality.py
python benchmarks/quality/feature_store_memory.py --dir /tmp/fs_bench \
    --num-nodes 1500000 --num-features 1024

# samplers and loaders (about 15 minutes)
python benchmarks/run_capped.py --gb 6 -- python benchmarks/quality/sampler_quality.py \
    --data-dir .mlx_graphs_data --seeds 0 1 2 3 4

# TGN on JODIE Wikipedia
python benchmarks/tgn_comparison/compare.py --data <data_dir> --epochs 8

# GPS on Peptides-func: export the data, train both, check the gradients
python benchmarks/gps_peptides/export_npz.py <data_dir>
python examples/graph_gps_peptides.py --data_dir <data_dir> --epochs 10 --seed 0
python benchmarks/gps_peptides/gps_pyg.py --data_dir <data_dir> --epochs 10 --seed 0
python benchmarks/gps_peptides/grad_parity.py <data_dir>

# to_hetero on DBLP
python benchmarks/to_hetero/compare_dblp.py --data_dir .mlx_graphs_data

Note

The harnesses run every configuration in its own process under a hard memory cap, and kill it above the cap: 6 GB by default for the node and graph harnesses (--memory-gb), 4 GB for the TGN and to_hetero comparisons. The memory is the process' physical footprint, as shown by Activity Monitor, which, unlike RSS, includes the GPU (Metal) allocations of MLX and PyTorch MPS. Run any other script the same way with python benchmarks/run_capped.py --gb <cap> -- <command>. Mini-batches of varying shapes make MLX's buffer cache grow: the sampler harness caps it with mx.set_cache_limit.

The node and graph harnesses append one line per run to node_results.jsonl / graph_results.jsonl and skip the runs already there, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped.

items.title: Not covered
items.text:
• Training quality on the largest graphs (AmazonProducts, Yelp, ogbn): out of the memory budget of these checks; Flickr and Reddit are covered above. They are part of the speed Benchmarks, which also record accuracy.
  • Mini-batch training in the node classification harness, which trains full batch only. Mini-batch training is checked for GraphSAGE by the sampler harness, and for to_hetero models in mlx-graphs only.
  • PyG's compiled samplers and operations: PyG's neighbour samplers, GraphSAINT, ShaDow, ClusterData (METIS), DynamicEdgeConv and knn_graph need pyg-lib, torch_sparse or torch_cluster, which were not installed. The samplers were checked against references instead, and ClusterLoader was trained with the dependency-free balanced partitioner, not METIS.
  • NCI1 graph classification, which did not fit in the time budget.
  • Converged knowledge graph embeddings: the KGE models trained for 20-40 epochs instead of PyG's 500, so the comparison covers the early training trajectories, not converged models.
  • Attention variants of GeneralConv on CiteSeer and PubMed (Cora only).
  • Compilation: mx.compile for mlx-graphs and torch.compile for PyG.

items.title: Algorithms
items.text: Class Description Node2Vec The Node2Vec model from the "node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks" paper where random walks of length walk_length are sampled in a given graph, and node embeddings are learned via negative sampling optimization. MetaPath2Vec The MetaPath2Vec model from the "metapath2vec: Scalable Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Networks" paper.

items.title: MetaPath2Vec
items.text:
MetaPath2Vec(
    edge_index_dict: Mapping[EdgeType, array],
    embedding_dim: int,
    metapath: Sequence[EdgeType],
    walk_length: int,
    context_size: int,
    walks_per_node: int = 1,
    num_negative_samples: int = 1,
    num_nodes_dict: Optional[Mapping[NodeType, int]] = None,
    use_gpu: bool = True,
)

Bases: Module

The MetaPath2Vec model from the "metapath2vec: Scalable Representation Learning for Heterogeneous Networks" paper.

Random walks that follow a given meta-path (a sequence of edge types) are sampled in a heterogeneous graph, and node embeddings are learned with a skip-gram objective and negative sampling. Negative samples respect node types: each position of a negative walk gets a random node of the type the meta-path puts at that position.

All node types visited by the meta-path share one embedding table, so they are embedded in the same space. Use model(node_type) to get the embeddings of one node type.

Note

This feature is experimental and requires mlx_cluster>=0.1.2.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default edge_index_dict Mapping[EdgeType, array]

(src, rel, dst) -> [2, num_edges] edge indices, with node ids local to each node type, e.g. HeteroGraphData.edge_index_dict.

required embedding_dim int

The size of each embedding vector.

required metapath Sequence[EdgeType]

The meta-path, a list of (src, rel, dst) edge types. Each edge type must start at the node type the previous one ends at.

required walk_length int

Number of steps per random walk, so every walk has walk_length + 1 nodes. If it is longer than the meta-path, the meta-path must be cyclic (end at the node type it starts from).

required context_size int

Size of the context windows cut out of each walk; the first node of a window is paired with the other context_size - 1 nodes as positive samples.

required walks_per_node int

Number of walks to start from each node of type metapath[0][0]. (default: 1)

1 num_negative_samples int

Number of negative walks per positive walk. (default: 1)

1 num_nodes_dict Optional[Mapping[NodeType, int]]

Optional number of nodes per node type, e.g. HeteroGraphData.num_nodes. Types not given are inferred from the largest node id in edge_index_dict. (default: None)

None use_gpu bool

Whether to sample the random walks on the GPU. (default: True)

True

Example:

metapath = [
    ("author", "writes", "paper"),
    ("paper", "published_in", "venue"),
    ("venue", "publishes", "paper"),
    ("paper", "written_by", "author"),
]
model = MetaPath2Vec(
    edge_index_dict,
    embedding_dim=128,
    metapath=metapath,
    walk_length=20,
    context_size=7,
)
optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=0.01)
loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, model.loss)
for pos, neg in model.dataloader(batch_size=128):
    loss, grads = loss_and_grad(pos, neg)
    optimizer.update(model, grads)

author_embeddings = model("author")

def __init__(
    self,
    edge_index_dict: Mapping[EdgeType, mx.array],
    embedding_dim: int,
    metapath: Sequence[EdgeType],
    walk_length: int,
    context_size: int,
    walks_per_node: int = 1,
    num_negative_samples: int = 1,
    num_nodes_dict: Optional[Mapping[NodeType, int]] = None,
    use_gpu: bool = True,
):
    super().__init__()
    if walk_length < 1:
        raise ValueError("walk_length must be >= 1")
    if not 2 <= context_size <= walk_length + 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"context_size ({context_size}) must be between 2 and "
            f"walk_length + 1 ({walk_length + 1})"
        )
    if walks_per_node < 1 or num_negative_samples < 1:
        raise ValueError("walks_per_node and num_negative_samples must be >= 1")

    # Validates the meta-path and sorts every relation into a CSR once.
    # Attributes starting with "_" are not treated as model parameters.
    self._csr = build_metapath_csr(edge_index_dict, metapath, num_nodes_dict)
    metapath = self._csr.metapath
    m = len(metapath)
    if walk_length > m and metapath[-1][2] != metapath[0][0]:
        raise ValueError(
            f"walk_length ({walk_length}) is longer than the metapath ({m}), "
            "so the metapath must be cyclic: it ends at "
            f"'{metapath[-1][2]}' but starts at '{metapath[0][0]}'"
        )
    num_nodes = self._csr.num_nodes_dict

    # One embedding table for all node types on the meta-path; node type t
    # owns rows [start[t], end[t]).
    node_types: List[NodeType] = []
    for t in [metapath[0][0]] + [et[2] for et in metapath]:
        if t not in node_types:
            node_types.append(t)
    self._start: Dict[NodeType, int] = {}
    self._end: Dict[NodeType, int] = {}
    offset = 0
    for t in node_types:
        n = int(num_nodes.get(t, 0))
        if n == 0:
            raise ValueError(f"Node type '{t}' on the metapath has no nodes")
        self._start[t], self._end[t] = offset, offset + n
        offset += n

    # Node type of every walk position, as embedding offsets and sizes.
    self._walk_types = metapath_node_types(metapath, walk_length)
    self._walk_offset = mx.array(
        [self._start[t] for t in self._walk_types], dtype=mx.int64
    )
    self._walk_count = mx.array(
        [self._end[t] - self._start[t] for t in self._walk_types],
        dtype=mx.int64,
    )

    self.metapath = metapath
    self.embedding_dim = embedding_dim
    self.walk_length = walk_length
    self.context_size = context_size
    self.walks_per_node = walks_per_node
    self.num_negative_samples = num_negative_samples
    self.use_gpu = use_gpu
    self.embedding = nn.Embedding(offset, embedding_dim)

def __call__(
    self, node_type: NodeType, batch: Optional[mx.array] = None
) -> mx.array:
    """Returns the embeddings of the nodes of type ``node_type``.

    Args:
        node_type: The node type.
        batch: Optional local node ids of that type. All nodes of the type
            are returned if omitted.
    """
    if node_type not in self._start:
        raise KeyError(
            f"Node type '{node_type}' is not on the metapath; "
            f"embedded types are {self.node_types}"
        )
    emb = self.embedding.weight[self._start[node_type] : self._end[node_type]]
    return emb if batch is None else emb[batch]

def pos_sample(self, batch: mx.array) -> mx.array:
    """Samples positive context windows from meta-path random walks.

    Args:
        batch: Local ids of start nodes, of type ``metapath[0][0]``.

    Returns:
        ``[num_windows, context_size]`` global embedding indices. Windows
        that run past the end of a walk that hit a dead end (a node with
        no neighbor of the next edge type) are dropped.
    """
    batch = mx.repeat(batch.astype(mx.int64).reshape(-1), self.walks_per_node)
    nodes, _ = metapath_random_walk(
        self._csr,
        batch,
        self.walk_length,
        stream=mx.gpu if self.use_gpu else mx.cpu,
    )
    # Local ids -> embedding rows; dead-end padding (-1) stays -1.
    walks = mx.where(nodes >= 0, nodes + self._walk_offset, -1)
    windows = self._windows(walks)
    keep = np.asarray(mx.all(windows >= 0, axis=1))
    if keep.all():
        return windows
    return windows[mx.array(np.flatnonzero(keep))]

Each negative walk starts at a node of batch and continues with random nodes of the type the meta-path puts at each position.

def neg_sample(self, batch: mx.array) -> mx.array:
    """Samples negative context windows.

    Each negative walk starts at a node of ``batch`` and continues with
    random nodes of the type the meta-path puts at each position.

    Args:
        batch: Local ids of start nodes, of type ``metapath[0][0]``.

    Returns:
        ``[num_windows, context_size]`` global embedding indices.
    """
    batch = batch.astype(mx.int64).reshape(-1)
    batch = mx.repeat(batch, self.walks_per_node * self.num_negative_samples)
    u = mx.random.uniform(shape=(batch.shape[0], self.walk_length))
    counts = self._walk_count[1:]
    rest = mx.minimum((u * counts).astype(mx.int64), counts - 1)
    walks = mx.concatenate([batch[:, None], rest], axis=1) + self._walk_offset
    return self._windows(walks)

def dataloader(
    self, batch_size: int, shuffle: bool = True
) -> Iterator[Tuple[mx.array, mx.array]]:
    """Yields ``(pos, neg)`` samples for mini-batches of start nodes.

    Every node of type ``metapath[0][0]`` is used as a start node once per
    pass.

    Args:
        batch_size: Number of start nodes per mini-batch.
        shuffle: Whether to shuffle the start nodes. (default: :obj:`True`)
    """
    start_type = self.metapath[0][0]
    n = self._end[start_type] - self._start[start_type]
    order = np.random.permutation(n) if shuffle else np.arange(n)
    for s in range(0, n, batch_size):
        batch = mx.array(order[s : s + batch_size], dtype=mx.int64)
        yield self.pos_sample(batch), self.neg_sample(batch)

def loss(self, pos_rw: mx.array, neg_rw: mx.array) -> mx.array:
    """Skip-gram loss with negative sampling.

    Args:
        pos_rw: Positive windows from :meth:`pos_sample`.
        neg_rw: Negative windows from :meth:`neg_sample`.
    """
    # log_sigmoid is the numerically stable log(sigmoid(x)).
    loss = -nn.log_sigmoid(-self._skipgram_scores(neg_rw)).mean()
    if pos_rw.shape[0] > 0:
        loss = loss - nn.log_sigmoid(self._skipgram_scores(pos_rw)).mean()
    return loss

def dataloader(self, batch_size):
    r"""Dataloader for nodes"""
    data_array = mx.arange(self.num_nodes).astype(mx.int64)
    perm = mx.array(np.random.permutation(self.num_nodes))

    for s in range(0, self.num_nodes, batch_size):
        ids = perm[s : s + batch_size]
        yield (
            self.pos_sample(data_array[ids]),
            self.neg_sample(data_array[ids]),
        )

Computes the loss given positive and negative random walks.

Source code in mlx_graphs/algorithms/node2vec.py 
def loss(self, pos_array, neg_array):
    r"""Computes the loss given positive and negative random walks."""

    # Positive loss
    start, rest = pos_array[:, 0], pos_array[:, 1:]
    h_start = self.embedding(start).reshape(pos_array.shape[0], 1, -1)

    h_rest = self.embedding(rest.reshape(-1)).reshape(
        pos_array.shape[0], -1, self.embedding_dim
    )

    out = (h_start * h_rest).sum(axis=-1)
    pos_loss = -mx.mean(mx.log(mx.sigmoid(out) + self.EPS))

    # Negative loss
    start, rest = neg_array[:, 0], neg_array[:, 1:]
    h_start = self.embedding(start).reshape(neg_array.shape[0], 1, -1)
    h_rest = self.embedding(rest.reshape(-1)).reshape(
        neg_array.shape[0], -1, self.embedding_dim
    )
    out = (h_start * h_rest).sum(axis=-1)
    neg_loss = -mx.mean(mx.log(1 - mx.sigmoid(out) + self.EPS))

    return pos_loss + neg_loss

The first available source is used:

y: Optional[array]

PyG-style alias of the labels of the graph.

Reading y returns node_labels if they are set, and graph_labels otherwise (None if neither is set). Edge labels are never returned.

Assigning y replaces the labels that reading y returns. If the graph has no labels yet, the value becomes node_labels if it has one entry per node and graph_labels otherwise, which is the rule used by from_pyg(). On a single-node graph, a one-entry y is ambiguous and becomes graph_labels, so that graph classification datasets with single-node graphs keep the same attributes in every graph (and can be batched): set node_labels directly for the node labels of a single-node graph. Assigning None clears the labels that reading y returned.

def keys(self) -> list[str]:
    """Names of the attributes that are set (not ``None``).

    Private attributes are omitted, and ``"num_nodes"`` is included when
    the number of nodes was set explicitly. PyG-style aliases (``x``,
    ``edge_attr``, ``y``) are not listed, only the attributes they refer
    to.

    Returns:
        The list of attribute names.
    """
    keys = [
        key
        for key, value in vars(self).items()
        if value is not None and not key.startswith("_")
    ]
    if getattr(self, "_num_nodes", None) is not None:
        keys.append("num_nodes")
    return keys

def subgraph(self, subset: IndexLike) -> "GraphData":
    """Returns the subgraph induced by the nodes ``subset``.

    The edges between nodes of ``subset`` are kept and relabeled, and every
    node-level and edge-level attribute (see :meth:`is_node_attr` and
    :meth:`is_edge_attr`) is sliced accordingly. Other attributes are
    shared with the original graph.

    Args:
        subset: The nodes to keep, as an array (or list) of node indices or
            as a boolean mask of shape ``[num_nodes]``. With indices, the
            nodes of the subgraph follow the order of ``subset``.

    Returns:
        A new graph with ``len(subset)`` nodes (or ``subset.sum()`` nodes
        for a mask).

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        graph = GraphData(
            edge_index=mx.array([[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 3]]),
            node_features=mx.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]),
        )
        sub = graph.subgraph(mx.array([1, 2, 3]))
        sub.edge_index
        # mx.array([[0, 1], [1, 2]])
        sub.node_features
        # mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
    """
    num_nodes = self._full_num_nodes()
    node_keys, edge_keys = self._node_and_edge_keys()
    keep_nodes = _to_host_index(subset, num_nodes, "subset")

    data = copy.copy(self)
    if self.edge_index is not None:
        edge_index, _, edge_mask = _node_subgraph(
            keep_nodes,
            self.edge_index,
            relabel_nodes=True,
            num_nodes=num_nodes,
            return_edge_mask=True,
        )
        keep_edges = np.nonzero(np.asarray(edge_mask))[0]
        for key in edge_keys:
            setattr(data, key, _take(getattr(self, key), keep_edges))
        data.edge_index = edge_index
    for key in node_keys:
        setattr(data, key, _take(getattr(self, key), keep_nodes))
    if self._needs_explicit_num_nodes():
        data.num_nodes = keep_nodes.size
    return data

def edge_subgraph(self, subset: IndexLike) -> "GraphData":
    """Returns the subgraph made of the edges ``subset``.

    Every node is kept, even if it becomes isolated, and every edge-level
    attribute (see :meth:`is_edge_attr`) is sliced accordingly.

    Args:
        subset: The edges to keep, as an array (or list) of edge indices
            or as a boolean mask of shape ``[num_edges]``.

    Returns:
        A new graph with the selected edges.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        graph = GraphData(
            edge_index=mx.array([[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 3]]),
            edge_features=mx.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0]]),
        )
        sub = graph.edge_subgraph(mx.array([0, 2]))
        sub.edge_index
        # mx.array([[0, 2], [1, 3]])
        sub.num_nodes
        # 4
    """
    num_nodes = self._full_num_nodes()
    _, edge_keys = self._node_and_edge_keys()
    keep = _to_host_index(subset, self.num_edges, "subset")
    data = copy.copy(self)
    for key in edge_keys:
        setattr(data, key, _take(getattr(self, key), keep))
    data.edge_index = _take(self.edge_index, keep, axis=1)
    if self._needs_explicit_num_nodes():
        data.num_nodes = num_nodes
    return data

items.text:
validate(raise_on_error: bool = True) -> bool

Checks the consistency of the graph.

The following properties are checked:

  • edge_index has shape [2, num_edges] and an integer dtype;
  • edge_index has no negative node id, and no node id greater than or equal to the number of nodes when it is known (set explicitly or given by node_features);
  • node-level default attributes (node_features, node_labels) have one entry per node, if the number of nodes is set explicitly;
  • edge_features and edge_labels have one entry per edge.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default raise_on_error bool

def validate(self, raise_on_error: bool = True) -> bool:
    """Checks the consistency of the graph.

    The following properties are checked:

    - ``edge_index`` has shape ``[2, num_edges]`` and an integer dtype;
    - ``edge_index`` has no negative node id, and no node id greater than
      or equal to the number of nodes when it is known (set explicitly or
      given by ``node_features``);
    - node-level default attributes (``node_features``, ``node_labels``)
      have one entry per node, if the number of nodes is set explicitly;
    - ``edge_features`` and ``edge_labels`` have one entry per edge.

    Args:
        raise_on_error: If ``True``, raises a ``ValueError`` on the first
            failed check. Otherwise, emits a warning for every failed check.
            Default: ``True``

    Returns:
        ``True`` if every check passed, ``False`` otherwise.
    """
    name = type(self).__name__
    errors = []
    edge_index = self.edge_index
    known_num_nodes = getattr(self, "_num_nodes", None)
    if known_num_nodes is None and self.node_features is not None:
        known_num_nodes = self.node_features.shape[0]

    if edge_index is None:
        errors.append(f"'edge_index' is undefined in '{name}'")
    elif edge_index.ndim != 2 or edge_index.shape[0] != 2:
        errors.append(
            f"'edge_index' needs to be of shape [2, num_edges] in '{name}' "
            f"(found {tuple(edge_index.shape)})"
        )
    else:
        if not mx.issubdtype(edge_index.dtype, mx.integer):
            errors.append(
                f"'edge_index' needs an integer dtype in '{name}' "
                f"(found {edge_index.dtype})"
            )
        if edge_index.size > 0:
            min_id = int(mx.min(edge_index).item())
            max_id = int(mx.max(edge_index).item())
            if min_id < 0:
                errors.append(
                    f"'edge_index' contains negative indices in '{name}' "
                    f"(found {min_id})"
                )
            if known_num_nodes is not None and max_id >= known_num_nodes:
                errors.append(
                    "'edge_index' contains larger indices than the number "
                    f"of nodes ({known_num_nodes}) in '{name}' "
                    f"(found {max_id})"
                )
        for key in ("edge_features", "edge_labels"):
            value = getattr(self, key)
            if value is not None and (
                value.ndim == 0 or value.shape[0] != edge_index.shape[1]
            ):
                errors.append(
                    f"'{key}' needs one entry per edge ({edge_index.shape[1]}) "
                    f"in '{name}' (found shape {tuple(value.shape)})"
                )

    explicit = getattr(self, "_num_nodes", None)
    if explicit is not None:
        for key in ("node_features", "node_labels"):
            value = getattr(self, key)
            if value is not None and (
                value.ndim == 0 or value.shape[0] != explicit
            ):
                errors.append(
                    f"'{key}' needs one entry per node ({explicit}) in "
                    f"'{name}' (found shape {tuple(value.shape)})"
                )

    for error in errors:
        if raise_on_error:
            raise ValueError(error)
        warnings.warn(error, stacklevel=2)
    return len(errors) == 0

def is_coalesced(self) -> bool:
    """Whether ``edge_index`` is sorted by source then destination node and
    contains no duplicate edge."""
    if self.edge_index.shape[1] < 2:
        return True
    edges = np.asarray(self.edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    src, dst = edges[0], edges[1]
    return bool(
        np.all(
            (src[1:] > src[:-1]) | ((src[1:] == src[:-1]) & (dst[1:] > dst[:-1]))
        )
    )

def coalesce(self, reduce: str = "add") -> "GraphData":
    """Sorts ``edge_index`` by source then destination node and merges
    duplicate edges.

    Every edge-level attribute (see :meth:`is_edge_attr`, e.g.
    ``edge_features``, ``edge_weights``) follows the edges, and the values
    of merged edges are combined with ``reduce``. The original graph is
    left unchanged.

    Args:
        reduce: How the attributes of merged edges are combined: ``"add"``,
            ``"mean"``, ``"max"`` or ``"min"``. Default: ``"add"``

    Returns:
        A coalesced copy of the graph (the graph itself if it is already
        coalesced).

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        graph = GraphData(
            edge_index=mx.array([[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0]]),
            edge_features=mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]),
        )
        graph = graph.coalesce()
        graph.edge_index
        # mx.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
        graph.edge_features
        # mx.array([[2.0], [4.0]])
    """
    if self.is_coalesced():
        return self
    num_nodes = self._full_num_nodes()
    _, edge_keys = self._node_and_edge_keys()
    data = copy.copy(self)
    for key in edge_keys:
        _, values = _coalesce_edges(
            self.edge_index, getattr(self, key), num_nodes, reduce
        )
        setattr(data, key, values)
    data.edge_index = _coalesce_edges(self.edge_index, num_nodes=num_nodes)
    if self._needs_explicit_num_nodes():
        data.num_nodes = num_nodes
    return data

def __inc__(self, key: str, *args, **kwargs) -> Union[int, None]:
    """This method can be overriden when batching is used with custom attributes.
    Given the name of a custom attribute `key`, returns an integer indicating the
    incrementing value to apply to the elemnts of the attribute.

    By default, all attribute names containing "index" (and ``face``) will be
    incremented based on
    the number of nodes in previous batches to avoid duplicate nodes in the index,
    e.g. `edge_index`. Other attributes are cnot incremented and keep their original
    values, e.g. node features.
    If incrementation is not used, the return value should be set to `None`.

    Args:
        key: Name of the attribute on which change the default incrementation
            behavior while using batching.

    Returns:
        Incrementing value for the given attribute or None.
    """
    if "index" in key or key == "face":
        return self.num_nodes
    if key in ("batch", "batch_indices"):
        # A graph's own assignment of nodes to sub-batches (e.g. ShaDow
        # subgraphs): offset by its number of groups, as PyG does.
        value = self.to_dict().get(key)
        if isinstance(value, mx.array):
            return int(value.max().item()) + 1 if value.size > 0 else 0
    return None

Bases: GraphData

Concatenates multiple GraphData into a single unified GraphDataBatch for efficient computation and parallelization over multiple graphs.

All graphs remain disconnected in the batch, meaning that any pairs of graphs have no nodes or edges in common. GraphDataBatch can be especially used to speed up graph classification tasks, where multiple graphs can easily fit into memory and be processed in parallel.

@_BatchAlias
def ptr(self) -> mx.array:
    """Offsets of the nodes of each graph in the batch, as in PyG: the nodes
    of graph ``i`` are ``ptr[i]`` to ``ptr[i + 1] - 1``. Has
    ``num_graphs + 1`` entries (int32)."""
    cumsum = getattr(self, "_cumsum_edge_index", None)
    if cumsum is not None:
        return cumsum.astype(mx.int32)
    counts = np.bincount(np.asarray(self.batch_indices), minlength=self.num_graphs)
    ptr = np.zeros(self.num_graphs + 1, dtype=np.int32)
    np.cumsum(counts, out=ptr[1:])
    return mx.array(ptr)

def put_edge_index(
    self,
    edge_index: Union[mx.array, np.ndarray, tuple],
    edge_type: Any = None,
    layout: EdgeLayout = "coo",
    size: Optional[tuple[int, int]] = None,
    is_sorted: bool = False,
) -> bool:
    """Adds edges, as a ``[2, num_edges]`` array or a pair of arrays
    (``(row, col)`` for COO, ``(row, colptr)`` for CSC, ``(rowptr, col)``
    for CSR).

    Args:
        edge_index: The edges.
        edge_type: Their type (``None`` for homogeneous graphs).
        layout: ``"coo"``, ``"csc"`` or ``"csr"``.
        size: ``(num_src_nodes, num_dst_nodes)``. Inferred from the
            largest node ids if not given (isolated nodes with larger
            ids are then missed).
        is_sorted: Whether COO edges are sorted by destination.
    """
    first, second = (_host(edge_index[0]), _host(edge_index[1]))
    if size is None:
        if layout == "coo":
            n = int(max(first.max(initial=-1), second.max(initial=-1))) + 1
            size = (n, n)
        elif layout == "csc":
            size = (int(first.max(initial=-1)) + 1, second.size - 1)
        else:
            size = (first.size - 1, int(second.max(initial=-1)) + 1)
    attr = EdgeAttr(edge_type, layout, is_sorted, size)
    self._csc_cache.pop(edge_type, None)
    return self._put_edge_index((first, second), attr)

def get_edge_index(
    self, edge_type: Any = None, layout: Optional[EdgeLayout] = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """The edges of ``edge_type`` as stored (``layout=None``) or
    converted to ``layout``."""
    attr = self._get_attr(edge_type)
    if layout is None or layout == attr.layout:
        out = self._get_edge_index(attr)
        assert out is not None
        return out
    if layout == "coo":
        return self.coo(edge_type)
    if layout == "csc":
        colptr, row, _ = self.csc(edge_type)
        return row, colptr
    rowptr, col, _ = self.csr(edge_type)
    return rowptr, col

def coo(self, edge_type: Any = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """``(row, col)`` of ``edge_type``, in the original edge order for
    edges stored as COO."""
    attr = self._get_attr(edge_type)
    first, second = self._get_edge_index(attr)  # type: ignore
    if attr.layout == "coo":
        return first, second
    if attr.layout == "csc":
        col = np.repeat(np.arange(second.size - 1), np.diff(second))
        return first, col
    row = np.repeat(np.arange(first.size - 1), np.diff(first))
    return row, second

Source code in mlx_graphs/data/graph_store.py 
def csc(
    self, edge_type: Any = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, Optional[np.ndarray]]:
    """``(colptr, row, perm)`` of ``edge_type``: the in-edges of every
    node, and the position in the stored COO edges of every CSC entry
    (``None`` if the stored edges need no permutation). Cached."""
    if edge_type in self._csc_cache:
        return self._csc_cache[edge_type]
    attr = self._get_attr(edge_type)
    first, second = self._get_edge_index(attr)  # type: ignore
    num_dst = attr.size[1]  # type: ignore
    if attr.layout == "csc":
        out = (second, first, None)
    else:
        row, col = self.coo(edge_type)
        if attr.layout == "coo" and attr.is_sorted:
            perm = None
        else:
            perm = np.argsort(col, kind="stable")
            row, col = row[perm], col[perm]
        out = (_ptr(col, num_dst), row, perm)
    self._csc_cache[edge_type] = out
    return out

def csr(
    self, edge_type: Any = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, Optional[np.ndarray]]:
    """``(rowptr, col, perm)`` of ``edge_type`` (out-edges of every
    node)."""

    if attr.layout == "csr":
        rowptr, col = self._get_edge_index(attr)  # type: ignore
        return rowptr, col, None
    row, col = self.coo(edge_type)
    perm = np.argsort(row, kind="stable")
    return _ptr(row[perm], attr.size[0]), col[perm], perm  # type: ignore

Nodes are stacked by node type in the order of node_types, and the edges of every edge type (in the order of edge_types) are offset accordingly and concatenated.

Per-type attributes are the dict attributes named <name>_dict whose keys are node types (e.g. node_features_dict, node_labels_dict, train_mask_dict) or edge types (e.g. edge_features_dict). They are merged into a single <name> attribute (e.g. node_features) if every type has them with the same number of dimensions and the same shape beyond the first one (2D node attributes of different widths are zero-padded to the widest one). With dummy_values, types missing an attribute are first filled with NaN (floats), False (booleans) or -1 (integers), provided the types that have it agree on its shape.
