    edge_features: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    relabel_nodes: bool = False,
    size: Optional[tuple[int, int]] = None,
    return_edge_mask: bool = False,
) -> Union[
    tuple[mx.array, Optional[mx.array]],
    tuple[mx.array, Optional[mx.array], mx.array],
]:
    """
    Returns the subgraph of a bipartite graph induced by a subset of the
    source nodes and a subset of the destination nodes, i.e. the edges whose
    source is in ``subset[0]`` and destination is in ``subset[1]``.

    Args:
        subset: A tuple ``(src_subset, dst_subset)`` of the source and
            destination nodes to keep, each given as an array (or list) of
            node indices or as a boolean mask.
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target
            nodes of each edge
        edge_features: Optional features of each edge, of shape
            ``[num_edges, ...]``. Default: ``None``
        relabel_nodes: If ``True``, the source (destination) nodes of the
            returned ``edge_index`` are relabeled to their position in
            ``src_subset`` (``dst_subset``), or their rank among the selected
            nodes for a boolean mask. Default: ``False``
        size: The number of source and destination nodes ``(num_src,
            num_dst)``. Inferred from ``edge_index`` if not given.
        return_edge_mask: If ``True``, also returns the boolean mask of shape
            ``[num_edges]`` of the edges that were kept. Default: ``False``

    Returns:
        A tuple ``(edge_index, edge_features)`` with the edges of the subgraph
        and their features (``None`` if ``edge_features`` was not given),
        followed by the edge mask if ``return_edge_mask`` is ``True``.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        edge_index = mx.array(
            [[0, 5, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 3, 5, 5, 6], [0, 0, 3, 2, 0, 0, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]]
        )
        subset = (mx.array([2, 3, 5]), mx.array([2, 3]))

        bipartite_subgraph(subset, edge_index, relabel_nodes=True)
        # (mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 2], [1, 0, 0, 1]]), None)
    """
    sub_edge_index, sub_edge_features, edge_mask = _bipartite_subgraph(
        edge_index, subset, edge_features, relabel_nodes, size
    )
    if return_edge_mask:
        return sub_edge_index, sub_edge_features, mx.array(edge_mask)
    return sub_edge_index, sub_edge_features

@validate_edge_index_and_features
def to_adjacency_matrix(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    edge_features: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    num_nodes: Optional[int] = None,
) -> mx.array:
    """
    Converts an edge index representation to an adjacency matrix.

    Args:
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target nodes
            of each edge
        edge_features: a 1-dimensional array representing the features corresponding
            to the edges in edge_index. Defaults to None.
        num_nodes: the number of nodes in the graph. Defaults to the number of nodes
            in edge_index

    Returns:
        The resulting adjacency matrix
    """
    if num_nodes is not None:
        if mx.max(edge_index) > num_nodes - 1:
            raise ValueError(
                "num_nodes must be >= than the number of nodes in the edge_index ",
                f"(got num_nodes={num_nodes} and {mx.max(edge_index) + 1}",
                "nodes in index",
            )
    else:
        num_nodes = (mx.max(edge_index) + 1).item()

    if edge_features is not None:
        if edge_features.ndim != 1:
            raise ValueError(
                "edge_features must be 1-dimensional",
                f"(got {edge_features.ndim} dimensions)",
            )

    adjacency_matrix = mx.zeros((num_nodes, num_nodes), dtype=edge_index.dtype)
    if edge_features is None:
        adjacency_matrix[edge_index[0], edge_index[1]] = 1
    else:
        adjacency_matrix[edge_index[0], edge_index[1]] = edge_features
    return adjacency_matrix

@validate_edge_index
def to_dense_adj(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    batch_indices: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    edge_features: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    max_num_nodes: Optional[int] = None,
) -> mx.array:
    """
    Converts the edges of a batch of graphs to dense adjacency matrices of
    shape ``[batch_size, max_num_nodes, max_num_nodes]``.

    Entry ``[b, i, j]`` holds the edge from the ``i``-th to the ``j``-th node
    of graph ``b``. Duplicate edges are summed.

    Args:
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target
            nodes of each edge
        batch_indices: Array of shape ``[num_nodes]`` with the graph of each
            node (e.g. ``GraphDataBatch.batch_indices``). Default: ``None``
            (a single graph, whose size is inferred from ``edge_index``).
        edge_features: Optional features of each edge, of shape
            ``[num_edges, ...]``, used as the values of the adjacency
            matrices. Default: ``None`` (ones).
        max_num_nodes: Number of nodes per graph in the output. Edges of nodes
            beyond that size are dropped. Default: ``None`` (the size of the
            largest graph).

    Returns:
        The dense adjacency matrices, of shape
        ``[batch_size, max_num_nodes, max_num_nodes, ...]`` (the trailing
        dimensions are those of ``edge_features``). The dtype is the one of
        ``edge_features``, or float32 if they are not given.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        edge_index = mx.array([[0, 0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 0, 3, 2]])
        batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 1, 1])

        to_dense_adj(edge_index, batch_indices)
        # mx.array([[[1, 1], [1, 0]], [[0, 1], [1, 0]]])
    """
    num_edges = edge_index.shape[1]
    if edge_features is not None and edge_features.shape[0] != num_edges:
        raise ValueError(
            "edge_features must be 1 per edge "
            f"(got {num_edges} edges and {edge_features.shape[0]} features)"
        )
    edges = _to_numpy(edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    max_node = int(edges.max()) if edges.size > 0 else -1
    if batch_indices is None:
        num_nodes = max_node + 1
    else:
        num_nodes = batch_indices.size
        if max_node >= num_nodes:
            raise ValueError(
                f"batch_indices has {num_nodes} entries but `edge_index` "
                f"contains node {max_node}"
            )
    batch, local, batch_size, largest = _batch_layout(batch_indices, num_nodes)
    if max_num_nodes is None:
        max_num_nodes = largest

    graph, row, col = batch[edges[0]], local[edges[0]], local[edges[1]]
    keep = np.nonzero((row < max_num_nodes) & (col < max_num_nodes))[0]

    if edge_features is None:
        feature_shape: tuple = ()
        dtype = mx.float32
    else:
        feature_shape = tuple(edge_features.shape[1:])
        dtype = edge_features.dtype
    adj = mx.zeros((batch_size * max_num_nodes * max_num_nodes, *feature_shape), dtype)

    if keep.size > 0:
        flat = (graph[keep] * max_num_nodes + row[keep]) * max_num_nodes + col[keep]
        if edge_features is None:
            values = mx.ones((keep.size,), dtype=dtype)
        elif keep.size < num_edges:
            values = edge_features[mx.array(keep)]
        else:
            values = edge_features
        adj = adj.at[mx.array(flat)].add(values)

    return adj.reshape(batch_size, max_num_nodes, max_num_nodes, *feature_shape)

def to_dense_batch(
    node_features: mx.array,
    batch_indices: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    fill_value: float = 0.0,
    max_num_nodes: Optional[int] = None,
) -> tuple[mx.array, mx.array]:
    """
    Converts the node features of a batch of graphs to a dense array of shape
    ``[batch_size, max_num_nodes, num_features]``, padded with ``fill_value``.

    Args:
        node_features: Array of shape ``[num_nodes, ...]`` with the features of
            the nodes of all the graphs.
        batch_indices: Array of shape ``[num_nodes]`` with the graph of each
            node (e.g. ``GraphDataBatch.batch_indices``). Default: ``None``
            (all the nodes belong to a single graph).
        fill_value: Value of the padded entries. Default: ``0.0``
        max_num_nodes: Number of nodes per graph in the output. Graphs with
            more nodes are truncated. Default: ``None`` (the size of the
            largest graph).

    Returns:
        A tuple ``(dense, mask)`` with the dense features of shape
        ``[batch_size, max_num_nodes, ...]`` and a boolean mask of shape
        ``[batch_size, max_num_nodes]`` which is ``True`` for real nodes and
        ``False`` for padding.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        node_features = mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
        batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 1])

        dense, mask = to_dense_batch(node_features, batch_indices)
        # dense: mx.array([[[1.0], [2.0]], [[3.0], [0.0]]])
        # mask: mx.array([[True, True], [True, False]])
    """
    num_nodes = node_features.shape[0]
    batch, local, batch_size, largest = _batch_layout(batch_indices, num_nodes)
    if max_num_nodes is None:
        max_num_nodes = largest

    feature_shape = node_features.shape[1:]
    # `mx.full` ignores an integer dtype for a float fill value.
    dense = mx.full(
        (batch_size * max_num_nodes, *feature_shape),
        fill_value,
        dtype=node_features.dtype,
    ).astype(node_features.dtype)
    mask = np.zeros(batch_size * max_num_nodes, dtype=bool)

    keep = np.nonzero(local < max_num_nodes)[0]
    if keep.size > 0:
        flat = batch[keep] * max_num_nodes + local[keep]
        if keep.size < num_nodes:
            node_features = node_features[mx.array(keep)]
        dense[mx.array(flat)] = node_features
        mask[flat] = True

    return (
        dense.reshape(batch_size, max_num_nodes, *feature_shape),
        mx.array(mask.reshape(batch_size, max_num_nodes)),
    )

@validate_adjacency_matrix
def to_edge_index(
    adjacency_matrix: mx.array, *, dtype: mx.Dtype = mx.uint32
) -> mx.array:
    """
    Converts an adjacency matrix to an edge index representation.

    Args:
        adjacency_matrix: the input adjacency matrix
        dtype: type of the output edge_index. Default to uint32.

    Returns:
        A [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target nodes of each edge

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        matrix = mx.array(
            [
                [0, 1, 2],
                [3, 0, 0],
                [5, 1, 2],
            ]
        )
        edge_index = to_edge_index(matrix)
        # mx.array([[0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2], [1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2]])
    """
    edge_index = mx.stack(
        [
            mx.array(x, dtype=dtype)
            for x in np.nonzero(np.array(adjacency_matrix, copy=False))
        ]
    )
    return edge_index

def to_networkx(
    data: GraphData,
    remove_self_loops: bool = False,
) -> nx.DiGraph:
    r"""Converts a :class:`mlx_graphs.data.GraphData` instance to a
    a directed :obj:`networkx.DiGraph` otherwise.

    Args:
        data: Graph data object
        remove_self_loops: If set to :obj:`True`, will not
            include self-loops in the resulting graph. (default: :obj:`False`)

    Returns:
        A networkx graph

    Examples:

    .. code-block:: python

        import mlx.core as mx

        edge_index = mx.array(
            [
                [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3],
                [1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2],
            ]
        )
        node_features = mx.array([[1], [1], [1], [1]])
        data = GraphData(node_features=node_features, edge_index=edge_index)
        G = to_networkx(data)
        print(G.edges)
        >>> OutEdgeView([(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)])

    """

    G = nx.DiGraph()

    if data.graph_features is not None:
        G.graph["graph_features"] = data.graph_features.tolist()

    if data.graph_labels is not None:
        G.graph["graph_labels"] = data.graph_labels.tolist()

    if data.num_nodes is None:
        return G

    node_attrs = {}
    for i in range(data.num_nodes):
        if data.node_features is not None:
            node_attrs["features"] = data.node_features[i].tolist()
        if data.node_labels is not None:
            node_attrs["label"] = data.node_labels[i].item()
        G.add_node(i, **node_attrs)

    edge_attrs = {}
    for i, (v, w) in enumerate(data.edge_index.T.tolist()):
        if remove_self_loops and v == w:
            continue
        if data.edge_features is not None:
            edge_attrs["features"] = data.edge_features[i].tolist()
        G.add_edge(v, w, **edge_attrs)

    return G

def to_pyg(graph: "GraphData") -> "Data":
    """
    Converts a :class:`mlx_graphs.data.GraphData` to a
    :class:`torch_geometric.data.Data` object.

    The attributes are renamed as follows:

    - ``node_features`` -> ``x``
    - ``edge_features`` -> ``edge_attr``
    - ``edge_weights`` -> ``edge_weight``
    - ``node_labels`` -> ``y``, or ``graph_labels`` -> ``y`` if the graph has
      no node labels (if it has both, ``graph_labels`` keeps its name)

    Every other array attribute is converted to a tensor and kept under the
    same name, and plain Python scalars and strings are carried over as they
    are. ``num_nodes`` is always set explicitly. Integer arrays (indices and
    labels) become int64 tensors, as PyG expects.

    ``torch`` and ``torch_geometric`` are optional dependencies, imported when
    the function is called.

    Args:
        graph: The graph to convert.

    Returns:
        The converted PyG graph.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        graph = GraphData(
            edge_index=mx.array([[0, 1], [1, 2]]),
            node_features=mx.ones((3, 4)),
            node_labels=mx.array([0, 1, 0]),
        )
        to_pyg(graph)
        # Data(edge_index=[2, 2], x=[3, 4], y=[3], num_nodes=3)
    """
    torch, Data = _import_pyg()

    def to_torch(array: mx.array) -> Any:
        array_np = np.array(array)
        if np.issubdtype(array_np.dtype, np.integer):
            array_np = array_np.astype(np.int64)
        return torch.from_numpy(array_np)

    num_nodes = graph.num_nodes
    if graph.edge_index.size > 0:
        num_nodes = max(num_nodes, int(graph.edge_index.max().item()) + 1)

    attributes = graph.to_dict()
    label_key = "node_labels" if "node_labels" in attributes else "graph_labels"

    data = Data()
    for key, value in attributes.items():
        if key.startswith("_"):
            continue
        if key == label_key:
            key = "y"
        key = _MLX_TO_PYG_NAMES.get(key, key)
        if isinstance(value, mx.array):
            data[key] = to_torch(value)
        elif isinstance(value, _SCALAR_TYPES):
            data[key] = value
    data.num_nodes = num_nodes
    return data

def to_rdmol(data: "GraphData", kekulize: bool = False) -> Any:
    r"""Converts a :class:`~mlx_graphs.data.GraphData` with the features of
    :func:`from_rdmol` back to an RDKit molecule, as PyG's ``to_rdmol``.

    Args:
        data: The molecular graph.
        kekulize: Whether to convert the aromatic bonds to single and double
            bonds. Default: ``False``

    Returns:
        The sanitized ``rdkit.Chem.Mol``.
    """
    Chem, _ = _import_rdkit()
    if data.node_features is None or data.edge_features is None:
        raise ValueError("The graph needs node_features and edge_features")

    x = _numpy(data.node_features).astype(np.int64)
    edge_index = _numpy(data.edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    edge_attr = _numpy(data.edge_features).astype(np.int64)

    mol = Chem.RWMol()
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        atom = Chem.Atom(int(x[i, 0]))
        atom.SetChiralTag(Chem.rdchem.ChiralType.values[int(x[i, 1])])
        atom.SetFormalCharge(x_map["formal_charge"][int(x[i, 3])])
        atom.SetNumExplicitHs(x_map["num_hs"][int(x[i, 4])])
        atom.SetNumRadicalElectrons(x_map["num_radical_electrons"][int(x[i, 5])])
        atom.SetHybridization(Chem.rdchem.HybridizationType.values[int(x[i, 6])])
        atom.SetIsAromatic(bool(x[i, 7]))
        mol.AddAtom(atom)

    visited = set()
    for k, (src, dst) in enumerate(edge_index.T.tolist()):
        key = (min(src, dst), max(src, dst))
        if key in visited:
            continue
        mol.AddBond(src, dst, Chem.BondType.values[int(edge_attr[k, 0])])

        stereo = Chem.rdchem.BondStereo.values[int(edge_attr[k, 1])]
        if stereo != Chem.rdchem.BondStereo.STEREONONE:
            bond = mol.GetBondBetweenAtoms(src, dst)
            bond.SetStereoAtoms(dst, src)
            bond.SetStereo(stereo)

        mol.GetBondBetweenAtoms(src, dst).SetIsConjugated(bool(edge_attr[k, 2]))
        visited.add(key)

    mol = mol.GetMol()
    if kekulize:
        Chem.Kekulize(mol)
    Chem.SanitizeMol(mol)
    Chem.AssignStereochemistry(mol)
    return mol

@validate_edge_index_and_features
def to_scipy_sparse_matrix(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    edge_features: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    num_nodes: Optional[int] = None,
) -> Any:
    """
    Converts a graph given by ``edge_index`` (and optional scalar edge
    features) to a ``scipy.sparse.coo_matrix``. Requires ``scipy``.

    Args:
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target
            nodes of each edge
        edge_features: Optional scalar weight of each edge, of shape
            ``[num_edges]`` or ``[num_edges, 1]``. Default: ``None`` (all
            ones)
        num_nodes: Number of nodes in the graph. Inferred from ``edge_index``
            if not given.

    Returns:
        A ``scipy.sparse.coo_matrix`` of shape ``[num_nodes, num_nodes]``.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 2]])
        to_scipy_sparse_matrix(edge_index).toarray()
        # array([[0., 1., 0.],
        #        [1., 0., 1.],
        #        [0., 0., 0.]], dtype=float32)
    """
    import scipy.sparse as sp

    edges = _to_numpy(edge_index)
    if edge_features is None:
        values = np.ones(edges.shape[1], dtype=np.float32)
    else:
        values = np.asarray(edge_features).reshape(-1)
        if values.size != edges.shape[1]:
            raise ValueError(
                "`edge_features` must hold one scalar per edge "
                f"(got shape {edge_features.shape})"
            )
    n = _infer_num_nodes(edge_index, num_nodes)
    return sp.coo_matrix((values, (edges[0], edges[1])), shape=(n, n))

def to_smiles(data: "GraphData", kekulize: bool = False) -> str:
    r"""Converts a :class:`~mlx_graphs.data.GraphData` with the features of
    :func:`from_smiles` to a (canonical, isomeric) SMILES string, as PyG's
    ``to_smiles``.

    Args:
        data: The molecular graph.
        kekulize: Whether to convert the aromatic bonds to single and double
            bonds. Default: ``False``

    Returns:
        The SMILES string.
    """
    Chem, _ = _import_rdkit()
    mol = to_rdmol(data, kekulize=kekulize)
    return Chem.MolToSmiles(mol, isomericSmiles=True)

@validate_edge_index_and_features
def to_undirected(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    edge_features: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    coalesce: bool = False,
    num_nodes: Optional[int] = None,
    reduce: str = "add",
) -> Union[mx.array, tuple[mx.array, mx.array]]:
    """
    Converts a graph given as `edge_index` and, optionally, `edge_features`
    to an undirected one, by adding the reverse of every edge.

    Args:
        edge_index: The edge index of the graph.
        edge_features: Edge features associated with each edge.
        coalesce: If ``True``, duplicate edges are merged afterwards (see
            :func:`coalesce`), so an edge that already had its reverse is kept
            once per direction. This is the behavior of PyG's
            ``to_undirected``. Default: ``False`` (plain concatenation).
        num_nodes: Number of nodes, only used when ``coalesce=True``.
        reduce: How the features of merged edges are combined when
            ``coalesce=True``. Default: ``"add"``.

    Returns:
        The undirected `edge_index` (and `edge_features`)
    """

    src, dst = edge_index
    undirected_edge_index = mx.concatenate(
        [mx.stack([src, dst]), mx.stack([dst, src])], 1
    )
    undirected_edge_features = None
    if edge_features is not None:
        undirected_edge_features = mx.concatenate([edge_features, edge_features], 0)

    if coalesce:
        return _coalesce(
            undirected_edge_index, undirected_edge_features, num_nodes, reduce
        )
    if undirected_edge_features is not None:
        return undirected_edge_index, undirected_edge_features
    return undirected_edge_index

Splits the edges of an undirected graph into positive and negative training, validation and test edges.

Its edge_index and edge_features are set to None. The input graph is not modified.

Randomness comes from mx.random, so results are reproducible with mx.random.seed.

def train_test_split_edges(
    data: "GraphData",
    val_ratio: float = 0.05,
    test_ratio: float = 0.1,
) -> "GraphData":
    """
    Splits the edges of an undirected graph into positive and negative
    training, validation and test edges.

    Only the edges ``(i, j)`` with ``i < j`` are considered (one per
    undirected edge). ``floor(val_ratio * num)`` of them become validation
    edges, ``floor(test_ratio * num)`` test edges and the others training
    edges, which are returned in both directions. As many negative edges
    (pairs ``i < j`` that are not edges) as positive ones are sampled for the
    validation and test sets.

    The returned graph has the attributes ``train_pos_edge_index``,
    ``val_pos_edge_index``, ``test_pos_edge_index``, ``val_neg_edge_index``,
    ``test_neg_edge_index`` and ``train_neg_adj_mask`` (a boolean
    ``[num_nodes, num_nodes]`` upper-triangular mask of the pairs that can
    still be used as training negatives), plus ``*_pos_edge_features`` if the
    graph has ``edge_features``. Its ``edge_index`` and ``edge_features`` are
    set to ``None``. The input graph is not modified.

    Randomness comes from ``mx.random``, so results are reproducible with
    ``mx.random.seed``.

    .. note::

        Prefer :class:`~mlx_graphs.transforms.RandomLinkSplit`, which this
        function predates (it is deprecated in PyG).

    Args:
        data: The graph to split.
        val_ratio: Ratio of validation edges. Default: ``0.05``
        test_ratio: Ratio of test edges. Default: ``0.1``

    Returns:
        A copy of ``data`` with the splits.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        graph = GraphData(
            edge_index=mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], [1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2]]),
            num_nodes=4,
        )
        graph = train_test_split_edges(graph, val_ratio=0.34, test_ratio=0.34)
        graph.val_pos_edge_index
        # e.g. mx.array([[1], [2]])
    """
    num_nodes = data.num_nodes
    data = copy.copy(data)
    edge_index = data.edge_index
    edge_features = data.edge_features
    data.num_nodes = num_nodes

    edges = _to_numpy(edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    upper = np.nonzero(edges[0] < edges[1])[0]
    row, col = edges[0][upper], edges[1][upper]

    n_v = int(math.floor(val_ratio * row.size))
    n_t = int(math.floor(test_ratio * row.size))

    perm = _permutation(row.size)
    row, col = row[perm], col[perm]
    dtype = edge_index.dtype
    features = None
    if edge_features is not None:
        features = edge_features[mx.array(upper[perm])] if upper.size else None

    def pos_edges(start: int, end: int) -> mx.array:
        return mx.array(np.stack([row[start:end], col[start:end]]), dtype=dtype)

    data.val_pos_edge_index = pos_edges(0, n_v)
    data.test_pos_edge_index = pos_edges(n_v, n_v + n_t)
    train_pos = pos_edges(n_v + n_t, row.size)
    if features is not None:
        data.val_pos_edge_features = features[:n_v]
        data.test_pos_edge_features = features[n_v : n_v + n_t]
        data.train_pos_edge_index, data.train_pos_edge_features = to_undirected(
            train_pos,
            features[n_v + n_t :],
            coalesce=True,
            num_nodes=num_nodes,
        )
    else:
        data.train_pos_edge_index = to_undirected(
            train_pos, coalesce=True, num_nodes=num_nodes
        )

    # Negative edges.
    neg_adj_mask = np.triu(np.ones((num_nodes, num_nodes), dtype=bool), k=1)
    neg_adj_mask[row, col] = False
    neg_row, neg_col = np.nonzero(neg_adj_mask)
    neg_perm = _permutation(neg_row.size)[: n_v + n_t]
    neg_row, neg_col = neg_row[neg_perm], neg_col[neg_perm]
    neg_adj_mask[neg_row, neg_col] = False
    data.train_neg_adj_mask = mx.array(neg_adj_mask)

    data.val_neg_edge_index = mx.array(
        np.stack([neg_row[:n_v], neg_col[:n_v]]), dtype=dtype
    )
    data.test_neg_edge_index = mx.array(
        np.stack([neg_row[n_v : n_v + n_t], neg_col[n_v : n_v + n_t]]), dtype=dtype
    )

    data.edge_index = None
    data.edge_features = None
    return data

def unbatch(
    src: mx.array,
    batch_indices: mx.array,
    axis: int = 0,
    batch_size: Optional[int] = None,
) -> list[mx.array]:
    """
    Splits ``src`` into one array per graph, according to ``batch_indices``.

    This is the array-level counterpart of
    :func:`mlx_graphs.data.batch.unbatch`, which splits a whole
    :class:`~mlx_graphs.data.GraphDataBatch`.

    Args:
        src: The array to split, e.g. node features of shape
            ``[num_nodes, ...]``.
        batch_indices: The graph of each entry of ``src`` along ``axis``, of
            shape ``[src.shape[axis]]``, with the entries of each graph stored
            contiguously and in graph order.
        axis: The axis along which to split. Default: ``0``
        batch_size: Number of graphs. Inferred from ``batch_indices`` if not
            given (graphs after the last one in ``batch_indices`` are then
            missing).

    Returns:
        A list with one array per graph.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        src = mx.arange(7)
        batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2])
        unbatch(src, batch_indices)
        # [mx.array([0, 1, 2]), mx.array([3, 4]), mx.array([5, 6])]
    """
    return _split(src, _graph_sizes(batch_indices, batch_size), axis)

@validate_edge_index
def unbatch_edge_index(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    batch_indices: mx.array,
    batch_size: Optional[int] = None,
) -> list[mx.array]:
    """
    Splits the ``edge_index`` of a batch of graphs into one ``edge_index`` per
    graph, with the node ids of each graph starting at 0.

    Args:
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target
            nodes of each edge of the batch, with the edges of each graph
            stored contiguously and in graph order.
        batch_indices: The graph of each node, of shape ``[num_nodes]``, with
            the nodes of each graph stored contiguously and in graph order.
        batch_size: Number of graphs. Inferred from ``batch_indices`` if not
            given.

    Returns:
        A list with the ``edge_index`` of each graph.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], [1, 0, 2, 1, 5, 4, 6, 5]])
        batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
        unbatch_edge_index(edge_index, batch_indices)
        # [mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]]),
        #  mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]])]
    """
    num_nodes = _graph_sizes(batch_indices, batch_size)
    ptr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(num_nodes)[:-1]])
    batch = _to_numpy(batch_indices).astype(np.int64).reshape(-1)
    edges = _to_numpy(edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    edge_batch = batch[edges[0]]
    local = mx.array(edges - ptr[edge_batch], dtype=edge_index.dtype)
    sizes = np.bincount(edge_batch, minlength=num_nodes.size)
    return _split(local, sizes, axis=1)

required batch_size Optional[int]

Number of graphs. Inferred from batch_indices if not given.

None

Returns:

Type Description list[array]

A list with the edge_index of each graph.

Example:

edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], [1, 0, 2, 1, 5, 4, 6, 5]])
batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
unbatch_edge_index(edge_index, batch_indices)
# [mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]]),
#  mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]])]
Source code in mlx_graphs/utils/unbatch.py 
@validate_edge_index
def unbatch_edge_index(
    edge_index: mx.array,
    batch_indices: mx.array,
    batch_size: Optional[int] = None,
) -> list[mx.array]:
    """
    Splits the ``edge_index`` of a batch of graphs into one ``edge_index`` per
    graph, with the node ids of each graph starting at 0.

    Args:
        edge_index: a [2, num_edges] array representing the source and target
            nodes of each edge of the batch, with the edges of each graph
            stored contiguously and in graph order.
        batch_indices: The graph of each node, of shape ``[num_nodes]``, with
            the nodes of each graph stored contiguously and in graph order.
        batch_size: Number of graphs. Inferred from ``batch_indices`` if not
            given.

    Returns:
        A list with the ``edge_index`` of each graph.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], [1, 0, 2, 1, 5, 4, 6, 5]])
        batch_indices = mx.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
        unbatch_edge_index(edge_index, batch_indices)
        # [mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]]),
        #  mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1]])]
    """
    num_nodes = _graph_sizes(batch_indices, batch_size)
    ptr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(num_nodes)[:-1]])
    batch = _to_numpy(batch_indices).astype(np.int64).reshape(-1)
    edges = _to_numpy(edge_index).astype(np.int64)
    edge_batch = batch[edges[0]]
    local = mx.array(edges - ptr[edge_batch], dtype=edge_index.dtype)
    sizes = np.bincount(edge_batch, minlength=num_nodes.size)
    return _split(local, sizes, axis=1)

def validate_adjacency_matrix(func):
    """Decorator function to check the validity of an adjacency matrix."""

    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(adjacency_matrix, *args, **kwargs):
        if adjacency_matrix.ndim != 2:
            raise ValueError(
                "Adjacency matrix must be two-dimensional",
                f"(got {adjacency_matrix.ndim} dimensions)",
            )
        if not mx.equal(*adjacency_matrix.shape):
            raise ValueError(
                "Adjacency matrix must be a square matrix",
                f"(got {adjacency_matrix.shape} shape)",
            )
        return func(adjacency_matrix, *args, **kwargs)

    return wrapper

def validate_edge_index_and_features(func):
    """Decorator function to check the validity of an edge_index and edge_features."""

    @functools.wraps(func)
    @validate_edge_index
    def wrapper(edge_index, edge_features=None, *args, **kwargs):
        if edge_features is not None:
            if edge_index.shape[1] != edge_features.shape[0]:
                raise ValueError(
                    "edge_features must be 1 per edge ",
                    f"(got {edge_index.shape[1]} edges",
                    f"and {edge_features.shape[0]} features)",
                )
        return func(edge_index, edge_features, *args, **kwargs)

    return wrapper

Example:

import mlx.core as mx

pos = mx.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.4, 0.2], [1.5, 0.1], [0.2, 1.7]])
>>> voxel_grid(pos, size=1.0)

Source code in mlx_graphs/utils/clustering.py 
def voxel_grid(
    pos: mx.array,
    size: Union[float, Sequence[float], mx.array],
    batch: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    start: Optional[Union[float, Sequence[float], mx.array]] = None,
    end: Optional[Union[float, Sequence[float], mx.array]] = None,
) -> mx.array:
    r"""Voxel grid pooling from the `"Dynamic Edge-Conditioned Filters in
    Convolutional Networks on Graphs" <https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02901>`_
    paper: overlays a regular grid of user-defined size over a point cloud
    and clusters all the points within the same voxel.

    Args:
        pos: Node positions, of shape ``[N, D]``.
        size: Size of a voxel (in each dimension, or the same for all).
        batch: Graph of each node, of shape ``[N]``. Nodes of different graphs
            are never in the same voxel. Default: ``None`` (a single graph).
        start: Start coordinates of the grid (in each dimension, or the same
            for all). Default: ``None`` (the minimum of ``pos``).
        end: End coordinates of the grid. Default: ``None`` (the maximum of
            ``pos``).

    Returns:
        The voxel (cluster) id of each node, of shape ``[N]`` (``int64``). Ids
        are not consecutive, see :func:`consecutive_cluster`.

    Example:

    .. code-block:: python

        import mlx.core as mx
        from mlx_graphs.utils import voxel_grid

        pos = mx.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.4, 0.2], [1.5, 0.1], [0.2, 1.7]])
        >>> voxel_grid(pos, size=1.0)
        array([0, 0, 1, 2], dtype=int64)
    """
    pos = pos.reshape(-1, 1) if pos.ndim == 1 else pos
    if not mx.issubdtype(pos.dtype, mx.floating):
        pos = pos.astype(mx.float32)
    num_points, dim = pos.shape
    if batch is None:
        batch_column = mx.zeros((num_points, 1), dtype=pos.dtype)
    else:
        batch_column = batch.reshape(-1, 1).astype(pos.dtype)
    pos = mx.concatenate([pos, batch_column], axis=1)
    if num_points == 0:
        return mx.zeros((0,), dtype=mx.int64)

    size_ = np.concatenate([_repeat(size, dim, "size"), [1.0]])
    size_arr = mx.array(size_, dtype=pos.dtype)
    if start is None:
        start_arr = pos.min(axis=0)
    else:
        start_arr = mx.array(
            np.concatenate([_repeat(start, dim, "start"), [0.0]]), dtype=pos.dtype
        )
    if end is None:
        end_arr = pos.max(axis=0)
    else:
        end_arr = mx.concatenate(
            [
                mx.array(_repeat(end, dim, "end"), dtype=pos.dtype),
                batch_column.max(axis=0),
            ]
        )
    # Same operations as PyG's grid_cluster (truncation towards zero).
    pos = pos - start_arr[None, :]
    num_voxels = ((end_arr - start_arr) / size_arr).astype(mx.int64) + 1
    num_voxels = mx.cumprod(num_voxels)
    num_voxels = mx.concatenate([mx.ones((1,), dtype=mx.int64), num_voxels[:-1]])
    voxel = (pos / size_arr[None, :]).astype(mx.int64)
    return (voxel * num_voxels[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

items.title: Coming from PyTorch Geometric
items.text: mlx-graphs follows the design of PyTorch Geometric (PyG): graphs in COO format, a MessagePassing base class, batching by concatenating graphs, and layers with the same names. Porting a PyG model is mostly renaming. This page lists the differences and walks through porting a model and its training loop.

items.title: Names at a glance
items.text:
PyG mlx-graphs Data(x, edge_index, edge_attr, y) GraphData(edge_index, node_features, edge_features, node_labels / graph_labels); data.x, data.edge_attr and data.y also work DataLoader(dataset, batch_size) Dataloader (dataset, batch_size), with shuffle, drop_last, follow_batch, sampler and batch_sampler batch.batch, batch.ptr batch.batch_indices (batch.batch and batch.ptr also work) GCNConv(in_channels, out_channels) GCNConv(node_features_dim, out_features_dim) conv(x, edge_index) conv(edge_index, node_features): edges first global_mean_pool(x, batch) global_mean_pool(node_features, batch_indices) torch_geometric.nn.models.GCN GCN (also GraphSAGE, GIN, GAT, MLP) Planetoid(root, "Cora") PlanetoidDataset("cora") SAGEConv(..., aggr=["mean", "max"]), aggr=SoftmaxAggregation() the same: aggregation names, lists and modules (mlx_graphs.nn.aggr) BatchNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm, PairNorm... the same names (aliases of BatchNormalization, ...) message(self, x_j, x_i) message(self, src_features, dst_features, **kwargs) .to(device) nothing: memory is shared by the CPU and the GPU

The tensors are mx.array instead of torch.Tensor.

items.title: Where PyG features live
items.text:
Beyond layers and datasets, most of PyG's toolbox has a counterpart with the same name:

PyG mlx-graphs torch_geometric.loader: NeighborLoader, LinkNeighborLoader, HGTLoader, ClusterLoader, GraphSAINT, ShaDowKHopSampler, ImbalancedSampler, DynamicBatchSampler... mlx_graphs.loaders, same names. The samplers are built in (no pyg-lib / torch-sparse needed). torch_geometric.nn.to_hetero, to_hetero_with_bases, HeteroConv, HANConv, HGTConv to_hetero(), to_hetero_with_bases() and the same layers, on HeteroGraphData TemporalData, TemporalDataLoader, TGNMemory TemporalData, TemporalDataLoader, TGNMemory (see the TGN tutorial) GPSConv, SGFormer, Polynormer, AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE, AddRandomWalkPE the same names in mlx_graphs.nn and mlx_graphs.transforms torch_geometric.transforms: NormalizeFeatures, ToUndirected, RandomLinkSplit... mlx_graphs.transforms, same names torch_geometric.metrics (link prediction), AUC / AP mlx_graphs.metrics torch_geometric.utils mlx_graphs.utils, mostly the same names

items.title: Converting data
items.text:
from_pyg() converts a PyG Data object to a GraphData, and to_pyg() converts back. x, edge_attr and y are renamed, and every other attribute (masks, positions...) keeps its name:

from torch_geometric.datasets import Planetoid

from mlx_graphs.utils import from_pyg

dataset = Planetoid(root="data/Planetoid", name="Cora")
data = dataset[0]
graph = from_pyg(data)
>>> GraphData(
        edge_index(shape=(2, 10556), int64)
        node_features(shape=(2708, 1433), float32)
        node_labels(shape=(2708,), int64)
        train_mask(shape=(2708,), bool)
        val_mask(shape=(2708,), bool)
        test_mask(shape=(2708,), bool))

A whole PyG dataset converts graph by graph, and the list goes straight into a Dataloader:

from torch_geometric.datasets import TUDataset

from mlx_graphs.loaders import Dataloader

graphs = [from_pyg(data) for data in TUDataset(root="data/TU", name="MUTAG")]
loader = Dataloader(graphs, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

Many datasets are also built in (Datasets), with no PyG needed.

items.title: Porting a model
items.text:
A 2-layer GCN for node classification, in PyG:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv

class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = GCNConv(in_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hidden_dim, out_dim)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        x = F.dropout(x, p=0.5, training=self.training)
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x, edge_index))
        x = F.dropout(x, p=0.5, training=self.training)
        return self.conv2(x, edge_index)

And in mlx-graphs:

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
from mlx_graphs.nn import GCNConv

class GCN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = GCNConv(in_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hidden_dim, out_dim)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=0.5)

    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features):
        h = self.dropout(node_features)
        h = nn.relu(self.conv1(edge_index, h))
        h = self.dropout(h)
        return self.conv2(edge_index, h)

The differences: mlx.nn.Module and __call__ instead of forward, edge_index first in the calls, and dropout as a module (it follows model.train() / model.eval() as in PyTorch).

The ready-made GCN model does the same in one line:

from mlx_graphs.nn import GCN

model = GCN(1433, 64, num_layers=2, out_features_dim=7, dropout=0.5)

items.title: Porting the training loop
items.text:
PyG trains with autograd and an optimizer that holds the parameters:

model = GCN(dataset.num_features, 64, dataset.num_classes)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)

for epoch in range(200):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    out = model(data.x, data.edge_index)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(out[data.train_mask], data.y[data.train_mask])
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

MLX computes gradients with a function transformation, nn.value_and_grad, and evaluates lazily: mx.eval runs the step. Here with the ready-made model on the Cora graph converted above:

import mlx.optimizers as optim
import numpy as np

from mlx_graphs.nn import GCN

model = GCN(graph.num_node_features, 64, num_layers=2, out_features_dim=7, dropout=0.5)
# bias_correction=True: the update rule of torch.optim.Adam
optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=0.01, bias_correction=True)
train = mx.array(np.nonzero(np.array(graph.train_mask))[0])

def loss_fn(model):
    out = model(graph.edge_index, graph.node_features)
    return nn.losses.cross_entropy(
        out[train], graph.node_labels[train], reduction="mean"
    )

loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)
model.train()
for epoch in range(200):
    loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model)
    optimizer.update(model, grads)
    mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state)

model.eval()
pred = model(graph.edge_index, graph.node_features).argmax(axis=1)

Boolean masks are turned into index arrays once (train), since MLX indexes with integer arrays.

Warning

Create MLX's Adam / AdamW with bias_correction=True when porting from PyTorch. MLX's default has no bias correction and takes much larger first steps, which changes how training goes (about 4 points of accuracy for GAT on Cora in our runs).

items.title: Porting a custom layer
items.text:
A PyG layer that weights neighbour features by an edge weight:

from torch_geometric.nn import MessagePassing

class WeightedConv(MessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__(aggr="add")
        self.lin = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index, edge_weight):
        return self.propagate(edge_index, x=self.lin(x), edge_weight=edge_weight)

    def message(self, x_j, edge_weight):
        return edge_weight.view(-1, 1) * x_j

In mlx-graphs, propagate takes the node features and passes extra arguments to message through message_kwargs. x_j and x_i become src_features and dst_features:

from mlx_graphs.nn import Linear, MessagePassing

class WeightedConv(MessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__(aggr="add")
        self.lin = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)

    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features, edge_weights):
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index,
            self.lin(node_features),
            message_kwargs={"edge_weights": edge_weights},
        )

    def message(self, src_features, dst_features, edge_weights=None, **kwargs):
        return edge_weights.reshape(-1, 1) * src_features

This message is a weighted sum of neighbour features, which is what the default message already computes. Dropping the message override and decorating the class with fused_message_passing() aggregates with one sparse x dense matmul on the GPU instead of building the [num_edges, features] array of messages, which is how the built-in layers get their speed (see the Benchmarks):

from mlx_graphs.nn import fused_message_passing

@fused_message_passing
class WeightedConv(MessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__(aggr="add")
        self.lin = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)

    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features, edge_weights):
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index,
            self.lin(node_features),
            message_kwargs={"edge_weights": edge_weights},
        )

items.title: Things to watch for
items.text:
• Self-loops. GCNConv, GATConv and GATv2Conv add self-loops by default, as in PyG. Before this release they didn't: pass add_self_loops=False to reproduce older mlx-graphs results.
  • No lazy sizes. MLX layers need their input sizes when they are built: there is no in_channels=-1. to_hetero() takes the input size of each node type with input_dims (e.g. data.num_node_features).
  • Lazy evaluation. MLX builds a graph of operations and runs it when a value is needed. Call mx.eval on the parameters and optimizer state at the end of each training step, and .item() to read a loss.
  • Optimizer. bias_correction=True for Adam / AdamW, as above.
  • Unused parameters. MLX returns a zero gradient for a parameter that doesn't contribute to the loss, where PyTorch leaves its .grad at None and the optimizer skips it. With weight decay or an L2 term, such parameters then shrink at every step. To keep part of a model unused for a while (e.g. a warm-up), freeze() it and call optimizer.init(...) after unfreezing.
  • Index dtypes. The built-in datasets and loaders use int32 indices (edge_index, batch, the n_id of sampled subgraphs...), where PyG uses int64. from_pyg() keeps PyG's dtypes; both work.
  • Memory with varying shapes. MLX caches buffers by size. With batches of graphs of different sizes, cap the cache with mx.set_cache_limit(...) to keep memory bounded.
  • Compilation. Most layers work under mx.compile. Layers that need the number of nodes per graph on the host (the LSTM, sort and set transformer aggregations, TopKPooling / SAGPooling, and GPSConv / SGFormer / Polynormer unless given a precomputed layout) work with nn.value_and_grad but not inside mx.compile.
  • Initialization. Layers are initialized as in PyG (Glorot for GCN and GAT, PyTorch's default Linear initialization for GraphSAGE and GraphConv), so a ported model starts from the same distribution.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
mlx-graphs is available on PyPI. To install it, run

pip install mlx-graphs

It requires a Mac with Apple Silicon and Python 3.10 or later. MLX and mlx-cluster, which provides the sparse GPU kernels of the fused message passing, are installed with it, together with NumPy, requests, fsspec and tqdm.

items.title: Build from source
items.text:
To build and install mlx-graphs from source, start by cloning the GitHub repository

git clone git@github.com:mlx-graphs/mlx-graphs.git && cd mlx-graphs

Then build and install it with pip (we suggest using a separate virtual environment)

pip install -e .

items.title: Installing test, dev, benchmarks, docs dependencies
items.text:
To install the extra dependencies for testing, development, benchmarks and building the documentation, you can run any of the following

pip install -e '.[test]'        # pytest, scipy, networkx, PyTorch, PyG, pandas, scikit-learn
pip install -e '.[dev]'         # pre-commit
pip install -e '.[benchmarks]'  # scipy, matplotlib, ogb, PyTorch, PyG
pip install -e '.[docs]'        # this documentation site (Zensical)

For dev purposes you may want to install the current version of mlx via pip install "mlx @ git+https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx.git".

items.title: Building the documentation
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical. The API reference is generated from the docstrings by static analysis, so MLX does not need to be importable:

pip install -e '.[docs]'
python docs/scripts/gen.py   # API pages, notebooks, changelog, benchmark sections
zensical serve                    # live preview on http://localhost:8000/mlx-graphs/
zensical build --strict --clean   # static site in site/

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: Train a graph neural network on your Mac's GPU in a few lines, then see how graphs, mini-batches and layers work in mlx-graphs. Install it first: pip install mlx-graphs.

items.title: Train a GCN on Cora
items.text:
Node classification on the Cora citation graph (2,708 papers, 7 topics) with a 2-layer GCN, full batch:

import time

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim

from mlx_graphs.datasets import PlanetoidDataset
from mlx_graphs.nn import GCN
from mlx_graphs.transforms import NormalizeFeatures
from mlx_graphs.utils import mask_to_index

mx.random.seed(0)
graph = NormalizeFeatures()(PlanetoidDataset("cora")[0])  # downloaded on first use
train, test = mask_to_index(graph.train_mask), mask_to_index(graph.test_mask)

model = GCN(graph.num_node_features, 64, num_layers=2, out_features_dim=7, dropout=0.5)
# bias_correction=True: the same update rule as torch.optim.Adam
optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=0.01, bias_correction=True)


def loss_fn(model):
    logits = model(graph.edge_index, graph.node_features)
    return nn.losses.cross_entropy(logits[train], graph.node_labels[train], reduction="mean")


loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)
start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(200):
    loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model)
    optimizer.update(model, grads)
    mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state)  # MLX is lazy: run the step
ms_per_epoch = (time.perf_counter() - start) / 200 * 1e3

model.eval()
predictions = model(graph.edge_index, graph.node_features).argmax(axis=1)
accuracy = (predictions[test] == graph.node_labels[test]).mean().item()
print(f"test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}, {ms_per_epoch:.2f} ms per epoch")

On an Apple M5 Pro (the time per epoch varied from 0.9 to 1.4 ms between our runs):

test accuracy: 0.786, 1.06 ms per epoch

The whole graph lives in unified memory, and the message passing of the built-in layers runs as fused sparse kernels on the GPU. The Benchmarks compare training times and accuracy with PyTorch Geometric on the same Macs.

Tip

Create MLX's Adam / AdamW with bias_correction=True. MLX's default (no bias correction) takes much larger first steps than PyTorch's Adam, which can cost accuracy (about 4 points for GAT on Cora in our runs).

items.title: Graphs in mlx-graphs
items.text:
A graph is a GraphData: an edge_index of shape [2, num_edges] (sources, then targets) and optional node, edge and graph features and labels. Any other keyword becomes an attribute. Several graphs batch into one GraphDataBatch, a single disconnected graph whose batch_indices give each node's graph:

import mlx.core as mx

from mlx_graphs.data import GraphData, batch

graph = GraphData(
    edge_index=mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3, 0]]),  # [2, num_edges]: sources, targets
    node_features=mx.random.normal((4, 8)),  # [num_nodes, num_features]
    node_labels=mx.array([0, 1, 1, 0]),
    timestamps=mx.arange(4),  # any other attribute is kept as is
)
print(graph)

# several graphs as one disconnected graph, for mini-batches of graphs
graphs = batch([graph, graph, graph])
print(graphs.num_graphs, graphs.num_nodes, graphs.batch_indices)
print(graphs[1])

GraphData(
    edge_index(shape=(2, 4), int32)
    node_features(shape=(4, 8), float32)
    node_labels(shape=(4,), int32)
    timestamps(shape=(4,), int32))
3 12 array([0, 0, 0, ..., 2, 2, 2], dtype=int32)
GraphData(
    edge_index(shape=(2, 4), int32)
    node_features(shape=(4, 8), float32)
    node_labels(shape=(4,), int32)
    timestamps(shape=(4,), int32))

The GraphData reference lists all its arguments and methods. Graph utilities (self-loops, subgraphs, conversions to and from PyG, NetworkX and SciPy...) are in mlx_graphs.utils.

items.title: Classify molecules: MUTAG
items.text:
Graph classification on MUTAG (188 molecules, mutagenic or not): a Dataloader batches the graphs, a GIN embeds the atoms, global_mean_pool averages them per molecule and a linear layer classifies:

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim

from mlx_graphs.datasets import TUDataset
from mlx_graphs.loaders import Dataloader
from mlx_graphs.nn import GIN, Linear, global_mean_pool

mx.random.seed(0)
dataset = TUDataset("MUTAG").shuffle()  # 188 molecules, 2 classes
train_loader = Dataloader(dataset[:150], batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
test_loader = Dataloader(dataset[150:], batch_size=64)


class Classifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden, num_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.gin = GIN(in_dim, hidden, num_layers=3)
        self.head = Linear(hidden, num_classes)

    def __call__(self, batch):
        h = self.gin(batch.edge_index, batch.node_features)
        return self.head(global_mean_pool(h, batch.batch_indices))  # one row per graph


model = Classifier(dataset.num_node_features, 64, dataset.num_graph_classes)
optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=0.01, bias_correction=True)
loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(
    model, lambda m, b: nn.losses.cross_entropy(m(b), b.graph_labels, reduction="mean")
)

for epoch in range(50):
    for batch in train_loader:
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model, batch)
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state)

correct = sum((model(b).argmax(axis=1) == b.graph_labels).sum().item() for b in test_loader)
print(f"test accuracy: {correct / len(dataset[150:]):.3f}")

test accuracy: 0.816

The 38 test molecules are few, and GPU reductions are not bitwise deterministic, so the accuracy moves a little between runs (0.816 to 0.868 in ours). The graph classification tutorial goes through the same task step by step.

items.title: A layer of your own
items.text:
A layer is a MessagePassing subclass that calls propagate. This one adds the mean of each node's neighbors to the node itself; @fused_message_passing aggregates with one sparse-dense matrix product on the GPU instead of building a message per edge:

import mlx.core as mx

from mlx_graphs.nn import Linear, MessagePassing, fused_message_passing


@fused_message_passing  # aggregate with one sparse-dense matmul on the GPU
class MeanConv(MessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, in_dim: int, out_dim: int):
        super().__init__(aggr="mean")
        self.root = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)
        self.neighbors = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)

    def __call__(self, edge_index: mx.array, node_features: mx.array) -> mx.array:
        aggregated = self.propagate(edge_index, node_features)  # mean of the neighbors
        return self.root(node_features) + self.neighbors(aggregated)


conv = MeanConv(8, 16)
edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3, 0]])
print(conv(edge_index, mx.random.normal((4, 8))).shape)

(4, 16)

Writing your own layers covers messages, aggregations, attention and testing a layer against PyG; Custom GPU kernels shows how to fuse an operation of your own in Metal.

items.title: Custom GPU kernels
items.text:
This guide is for you if you wrote a layer and one of its operations on edges is slow. It shows how to write that operation as a Metal kernel with mx.fast.metal_kernel, give it gradients with mx.custom_function, and plug it into a MessagePassing layer with a fallback. The worked example is a real fused graph operation; all the code on this page comes from docs/snippets/edge_dot_kernel.py, which runs its checks and its benchmark with python docs/snippets/edge_dot_kernel.py. The test suite runs the same checks (tests/docs/test_edge_dot_kernel.py).

The API used here is the one of MLX 0.32. mlx-graphs ships two such kernels, which are longer versions of the same recipe: gatv2_edge_scores.py (GATv2's attention logits) and csr_softmax_spmm.py (softmax over each node's edges fused with the weighted sum).

items.title: When a custom kernel is worth it
items.text:
A message passing layer written with MLX operations gathers the features of both ends of every edge, computes one message per edge, then scatters the messages to their destinations:

  • the gathers build arrays of shape [num_edges, features], written to and read back from memory, often several of them; on a graph with 2 million edges and 64 features, each one is 512 MB in float32;
  • the scatter adds the messages of all edges into the rows of their destinations, with atomic additions on the GPU, which collide on high-degree nodes;
  • the backward pass does the same in reverse.

Two cases are already covered without a kernel of your own:

  • The message is a weighted sum of neighbor features (edge_weight * x_j, mean, sum): decorate the layer with @fused_message_passing, which aggregates with one sparse-dense matrix product and never builds the message array. See Writing your own layers.
  • The attention of GAT, GATv2 and TransformerConv: the built-in layers already use the two kernels above.

Write a kernel when the expensive part is something else, typically a per-edge quantity computed from the features of both ends (a score, a distance, a gate) that the layer needs before its weighted sum. The kernel computes it directly from the node features, so the [num_edges, features] intermediates never exist.

items.title: The example: a per-edge dot product
items.text:
Dot-product attention (TransformerConv, graph transformers) scores every edge (src, dst) with

\[ \text{score}_e = \langle q_{\text{dst}(e)},\; k_{\text{src}(e)} \rangle . \]

The reference implementation is two gathers and a reduction:

def edge_dot_reference(q: mx.array, k: mx.array, edge_index: mx.array) -> mx.array:
    """score[e] = <q[dst[e]], k[src[e]]>, with MLX operations."""
    src, dst = edge_index[0], edge_index[1]
    return (q[dst] * k[src]).sum(axis=-1)  # two [num_edges, channels] gathers

It is correct on any device and differentiable by MLX, so it serves as the fallback and as the ground truth for the tests.

items.title: The Metal kernels
items.text:
mx.fast.metal_kernel takes the body of a Metal function; MLX generates the signature from input_names and output_names, and gives each input x a x_shape array (and x_strides, x_ndim when the body uses them). Inside the body, thread_position_in_grid, thread_index_in_simdgroup and the other Metal attributes are available.

The forward kernel gives each edge one SIMD group of 32 threads: each thread multiplies a strided slice of the channels, and simd_sum adds the 32 partial sums. The backward kernel computes grad_q[dst] += g * k[src] and grad_k[src] += g * q[dst] for every edge. Several edges share a node, so it adds with atomic_fetch_add_explicit, which requires atomic_outputs=True:

SIMD_WIDTH = 32  # threads of an Apple GPU SIMD group
THREADGROUP = (256, 1, 1)

FORWARD = """
    // One SIMD group per edge: each lane sums a strided slice of the channels.
    const uint edge = thread_position_in_grid.x / 32;
    const uint lane = thread_index_in_simdgroup;
    const uint num_edges = edge_index_shape[1];
    const uint channels = q_shape[1];
    const ulong src = edge_index[edge];
    const ulong dst = edge_index[num_edges + edge];
    float acc = 0.0f;
    for (uint c = lane; c < channels; c += 32) {
        acc += q[dst * channels + c] * k[src * channels + c];
    }
    acc = simd_sum(acc);  // reduce the 32 partial sums
    if (lane == 0) {
        score[edge] = acc;
    }
"""

BACKWARD = """
    // d score / d q[dst] = k[src] and d score / d k[src] = q[dst], scaled by
    // the incoming gradient. Several edges share a node: add atomically.
    const uint edge = thread_position_in_grid.x / 32;
    const uint lane = thread_index_in_simdgroup;
    const uint num_edges = edge_index_shape[1];
    const uint channels = q_shape[1];
    const ulong src = edge_index[edge];
    const ulong dst = edge_index[num_edges + edge];
    const float g = cotangent[edge];
    for (uint c = lane; c < channels; c += 32) {
        atomic_fetch_add_explicit(
            &grad_q[dst * channels + c], g * k[src * channels + c],
            memory_order_relaxed);
        atomic_fetch_add_explicit(
            &grad_k[src * channels + c], g * q[dst * channels + c],
            memory_order_relaxed);
    }
"""


@lru_cache(maxsize=1)  # build (and compile) each kernel once
def _kernels():
    forward = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
        name="edge_dot",
        input_names=["q", "k", "edge_index"],
        output_names=["score"],
        source=FORWARD,
        ensure_row_contiguous=True,
    )
    backward = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
        name="edge_dot_backward",
        input_names=["q", "k", "edge_index", "cotangent"],
        output_names=["grad_q", "grad_k"],
        source=BACKWARD,
        ensure_row_contiguous=True,
        atomic_outputs=True,  # outputs are `device atomic<float>*`
    )
    return forward, backward

metal_kernel returns a callable. Every time you make one, MLX creates a new Metal library, which it may compile: build each kernel once (lru_cache here) and call it many times.

items.title: Gradients with mx.custom_function
items.text:
MLX cannot differentiate through a Metal kernel. Wrap the forward call in mx.custom_function and define its vector-Jacobian product with the backward kernel. The VJP receives the inputs (primals), the cotangent of the output and the output itself, and returns one gradient per input:

@mx.custom_function
def _edge_dot_metal(q, k, edge_index):
    forward, _ = _kernels()
    num_edges = edge_index.shape[1]
    return forward(
        inputs=[q, k, edge_index],
        grid=(num_edges * SIMD_WIDTH, 1, 1),  # total threads, not threadgroups
        threadgroup=THREADGROUP,
        output_shapes=[(num_edges,)],
        output_dtypes=[mx.float32],
    )[0]


@_edge_dot_metal.vjp
def _edge_dot_metal_vjp(primals, cotangent, output):
    q, k, edge_index = primals
    _, backward = _kernels()
    num_edges = edge_index.shape[1]
    grad_q, grad_k = backward(
        inputs=[q, k, edge_index, cotangent],
        grid=(num_edges * SIMD_WIDTH, 1, 1),
        threadgroup=THREADGROUP,
        output_shapes=[q.shape, k.shape],
        output_dtypes=[mx.float32, mx.float32],
        init_value=0,  # the atomic adds accumulate into zeros
    )
    # No gradient for the integer edge index.
    return grad_q, grad_k, mx.zeros_like(edge_index)

Things to know about the kernel call:

  • grid is the total number of threads along each axis (Metal's dispatchThreads), not the number of threadgroups: here num_edges * 32.
  • output_shapes and output_dtypes are required; outputs are not initialized unless you pass init_value, which the backward kernel needs because it accumulates.
  • template passes compile-time constants ([("CHANNELS", 64)]); each new value compiles a new specialization. The example reads the sizes from q_shape instead.

The gradient of the backward kernel itself (second-order gradients) is not defined here; the repository's GATv2 kernel shows how to delegate it to the reference with mx.vjp.

items.title: Plugging it into a layer
items.text:
Dispatch to the kernel only when it applies, and use the reference otherwise: on the CPU device, without Metal, for empty graphs, other dtypes or sizes the grid cannot hold:

def edge_dot(q: mx.array, k: mx.array, edge_index: mx.array) -> mx.array:
    """The Metal kernel when it applies, the MLX reference otherwise."""
    if (
        edge_index.ndim == 2
        and 0 < edge_index.shape[1] <= (2**31 - 1) // SIMD_WIDTH
        and edge_index.dtype == mx.int32
        and q.dtype == k.dtype == mx.float32
        and q.ndim == k.ndim == 2
        and q.shape[1] == k.shape[1]
        and mx.default_device().type == mx.gpu
        and mx.metal.is_available()
    ):
        return _edge_dot_metal(q, k, edge_index)
    return edge_dot_reference(q, k, edge_index)

A layer then calls edge_dot like any MLX operation, normalizes the scores over each node's incoming edges with softmax, and lets propagate do the weighted sum:

class DotAttentionConv(MessagePassing):
    """Single-head dot-product graph attention, scored with `edge_dot`."""

    def __init__(self, in_dim: int, out_dim: int):
        super().__init__(aggr="add")
        self.query = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)
        self.key = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)
        self.value = Linear(in_dim, out_dim)
        self.scale = 1 / math.sqrt(out_dim)

    def __call__(self, edge_index: mx.array, node_features: mx.array) -> mx.array:
        q = self.query(node_features)
        k = self.key(node_features)
        v = self.value(node_features)
        scores = edge_dot(q, k, edge_index) * self.scale
        # softmax over the incoming edges of each destination node
        weights = softmax(scores, edge_index[1], num_nodes=node_features.shape[0])
        # the default message is edge_weights * source features
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index, v, message_kwargs={"edge_weights": weights[:, None]}
        )

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Compare values and gradients with the reference, with a random cotangent (a plain .sum() would hide errors that cancel out), on random graphs of a few sizes, on nodes without edges and on an empty graph:

def random_graph(num_nodes, num_edges, channels, seed=0):
    mx.random.seed(seed)
    edge_index = mx.random.randint(0, num_nodes, (2, num_edges)).astype(mx.int32)
    q = mx.random.normal((num_nodes, channels))
    k = mx.random.normal((num_nodes, channels))
    return q, k, edge_index


def check(q, k, edge_index, atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4):
    """Values and gradients of the kernel against the reference."""
    weights = mx.random.normal((edge_index.shape[1],))  # a non-trivial cotangent

    def loss(fn):
        return lambda q, k: (fn(q, k, edge_index) * weights).sum()

    value, grads = mx.value_and_grad(loss(edge_dot), argnums=(0, 1))(q, k)
    ref_value, ref_grads = mx.value_and_grad(loss(edge_dot_reference), argnums=(0, 1))(
        q, k
    )
    assert mx.allclose(
        edge_dot(q, k, edge_index),
        edge_dot_reference(q, k, edge_index),
        atol=atol,
        rtol=rtol,
    )
    assert mx.allclose(value, ref_value, atol=atol, rtol=rtol)
    for grad, ref_grad in zip(grads, ref_grads):
        assert mx.allclose(grad, ref_grad, atol=atol, rtol=rtol)


def run_tests():
    for num_nodes, num_edges, channels in [
        (50, 300, 16),
        (1000, 20000, 64),
        (7, 5, 100),
    ]:
        check(*random_graph(num_nodes, num_edges, channels))
    # isolated nodes: edges only between the first 10 of 100 nodes
    q, k, _ = random_graph(100, 1, 32)
    edge_index = mx.random.randint(0, 10, (2, 500)).astype(mx.int32)
    check(q, k, edge_index)
    # an empty graph falls back to the reference, which returns no scores
    q, k, _ = random_graph(10, 1, 8)
    empty = mx.zeros((2, 0), dtype=mx.int32)
    assert edge_dot(q, k, empty).shape == (0,)
    # the layer runs and is differentiable
    layer = DotAttentionConv(16, 32)
    x = mx.random.normal((50, 16))
    edge_index = mx.random.randint(0, 50, (2, 400)).astype(mx.int32)
    out = layer(edge_index, x)
    grads = nn.value_and_grad(layer, lambda m: m(edge_index, x).sum())(layer)[1]
    mx.eval(out, grads)
    assert out.shape == (50, 32)
    print("kernel matches the reference: values and gradients (atol=rtol=1e-4)")

The tolerance is 1e-4: the kernel adds the channels in a different order than MLX, and the atomic additions of the backward kernel run in an order that changes from run to run, so results differ in the last bits and are not bitwise deterministic.

items.title: Benchmarking
items.text:
MLX evaluates lazily: time mx.eval(...), after a few warm-up calls that compile the kernel:

def timeit(fn, *args, warmup=5, iters=20):
    for _ in range(warmup):  # compiles the kernel, warms the caches
        mx.eval(fn(*args))
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters):
        mx.eval(fn(*args))  # MLX is lazy: evaluate to time the work
    return (time.perf_counter() - start) / iters * 1e3  # ms


def benchmark(num_nodes=100_000, num_edges=2_000_000, channels=64):
    q, k, edge_index = random_graph(num_nodes, num_edges, channels)
    mx.eval(q, k, edge_index)

    def forward_backward(fn):
        grad = mx.grad(lambda q, k: fn(q, k, edge_index).sum(), argnums=(0, 1))
        return lambda q, k: grad(q, k)

    print(f"{num_nodes:,} nodes, {num_edges:,} edges, {channels} channels")
    for name, fn in [
        ("forward", lambda f: lambda q, k: f(q, k, edge_index)),
        ("forward + backward", forward_backward),
    ]:
        kernel = timeit(fn(edge_dot), q, k)
        reference = timeit(fn(edge_dot_reference), q, k)
        print(
            f"  {name:<20} kernel {kernel:6.2f} ms  reference {reference:6.2f} ms"
            f"  speedup {reference / kernel:4.1f}x"
        )

On an Apple M5 Pro (MLX 0.32.4), python docs/snippets/edge_dot_kernel.py prints:

MLX 0.32.4, Metal available: True, Apple M5 Pro
kernel matches the reference: values and gradients (atol=rtol=1e-4)
100,000 nodes, 2,000,000 edges, 64 channels
  forward              kernel   2.72 ms  reference  15.46 ms  speedup  5.7x
  forward + backward   kernel  10.39 ms  reference  24.79 ms  speedup  2.4x
10,000 nodes, 100,000 edges, 64 channels
  forward              kernel   0.26 ms  reference   0.86 ms  speedup  3.3x
  forward + backward   kernel   0.41 ms  reference   1.20 ms  speedup  2.9x

Times vary between runs: over our runs on this machine, the forward speedup on 2 million edges was 5.5x to 5.7x and the forward + backward one 2.4x to 2.8x.

How to read it:

  • The forward pass gains the most: the reference writes and reads two [2M, 64] arrays (1 GB), the kernel only reads the node features.
  • With the backward pass the gain is smaller: both versions scatter-add into the node gradients, and the kernel's atomic additions collide on the same rows as the reference's.
  • On small graphs, launch and Python overhead dominate both versions; measure at the sizes you train on.

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
• Index dtypes: the kernel reads int32 indices. Check the dtype in the dispatch (or cast once outside the training loop); a Metal kernel reinterprets the bytes it is given, so int64 indices would be read as garbage. Compute offsets in ulong (src * channels overflows 32 bits past 2^31 elements).
  • Sorted or CSR layouts: kernels that walk the edges of each node (like csr_softmax_spmm) need the edges sorted by destination with a row pointer; convert once and cache it, as the fused message passing does.
  • Threadgroup sizes: a threadgroup holds at most 1024 threads; keep it a multiple of the SIMD width (32), and make sure every lane of a SIMD group reaches simd_sum (no early return for part of a group).
  • Atomics: only for 32-bit types; they make floating-point sums non-deterministic. Reduce in registers or threadgroup memory first when many threads write the same address (the GATv2 kernel reduces each threadgroup's share before writing).
  • Contiguity: with ensure_row_contiguous=True (the default) MLX copies strided inputs before the call, and the body can index them as flat row-major arrays. With False, use x_strides and elem_to_loc.
  • Caching: build the kernel objects once (lru_cache) instead of in every call; with template, each new value is a new specialization to compile, so keep their number small.
  • Importable without a GPU: documentation tools and some tests import modules with mlx replaced by a mock. Build kernels lazily, inside functions, and avoid annotations evaluated at import time on MLX types, such as mx.array | None: that one broke the import of csr_softmax_spmm under a mock until it was written Optional[mx.array] (#214).

items.title: Heavier kernels
items.text: mx.fast.metal_kernel suits element-wise and per-edge work written in one Metal function. For kernels that need several passes, shared buffers or their own memory planning (sparse matrix products, random walks, graph partitioning), write an MLX C++ extension: mlx-cluster, which provides the SpMM of the fused message passing and the random walks of Node2Vec and MetaPath2Vec, is one, built on MLX's custom extensions.

items.title: Datasets
items.text:
MLX-graphs provides several built-in datasets for graph machine learning tasks.

Note

Datasets are automatically downloaded to .mlx_graphs_data/ in the current working directory upon first use. You can specify a custom directory by passing base_dir to the dataset constructor.
