items.title: Using Datasets
items.text:
Loading a dataset is straightforward:

from mlx_graphs.datasets import KarateClubDataset, PlanetoidDataset

# Simple built-in dataset
dataset = KarateClubDataset()
graph = dataset[0]
print(f"Nodes: {graph.num_nodes}, Edges: {graph.num_edges}")

# Citation network dataset
cora = PlanetoidDataset(name="cora")
print(cora[0])

items.title: Add your own dataset
items.text:
Subclass Dataset and implement two methods: download, which fetches the raw files into self.raw_path, and process, which turns them into a list of GraphData in self.graphs. The first instantiation runs both and saves the processed graphs under base_dir (.mlx_graphs_data/ by default); later ones load them. Indexing, slicing, shuffle, the num_* properties, transforms and the Dataloader then work as for the built-in datasets.

A made-up dataset, generated instead of downloaded: is a graph a cycle or a path?

import mlx.core as mx
import numpy as np

from mlx_graphs.data import GraphData
from mlx_graphs.datasets import Dataset
from mlx_graphs.loaders import Dataloader


class CyclesOrPaths(Dataset):
    """Graph classification: is the graph a cycle (label 1) or a path (label 0)?"""

    def __init__(self, num_graphs: int = 200, base_dir=None):
        self.num_graphs_to_make = num_graphs
        super().__init__(name="cycles_or_paths", base_dir=base_dir)

    def download(self):
        pass  # nothing to download: the graphs are generated in process()

    def process(self):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
        self.graphs = []
        for i in range(self.num_graphs_to_make):
            n = int(rng.integers(5, 20))
            src = np.arange(n - 1)
            if i % 2:  # close the path into a cycle
                src = np.arange(n)
            dst = (src + 1) % n
            edges = np.concatenate([np.stack([src, dst]), np.stack([dst, src])], axis=1)
            self.graphs.append(
                GraphData(
                    edge_index=mx.array(edges, dtype=mx.int32),
                    node_features=mx.ones((n, 1)),
                    graph_labels=mx.array([i % 2]),
                )
            )


dataset = CyclesOrPaths()  # processed once, then loaded from .mlx_graphs_data/
print(dataset)
print(dataset.num_graphs, dataset.num_graph_classes, dataset[0])
loader = Dataloader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
print(next(iter(loader)).num_graphs)

cycles_or_paths(num_graphs=200)
200 2 GraphData(
    edge_index(shape=(2, 32), int32)
    node_features(shape=(17, 1), float32)
    graph_labels(shape=(1,), int32))
32

For a dataset that is downloaded, call download in download (and check_sha1 or extract_archive as needed), and read the files of self.raw_path in process. The built-in datasets, in mlx_graphs/datasets, are examples. For a dataset of heterogeneous graphs, subclass HeteroDataset.

items.title: Computing Dataset Statistics
items.text:
To compute statistics for any dataset, use the included utility script:

# Stats for all available datasets
python examples/compute_dataset_stats.py

# Stats for a specific dataset
python examples/compute_dataset_stats.py --dataset karate_club

# Output as markdown table (for this page, or issues)
python examples/compute_dataset_stats.py --format markdown

# Output as RST table
python examples/compute_dataset_stats.py --format rst

items.title: Large graphs: stores and temporal sampling
items.text: Mini-batch training with NeighborLoader only needs, at every step, the features of the sampled nodes. This page shows how to keep the features out of memory with a feature store, and how to sample neighborhoods that respect time.

items.title: Large datasets
items.text:
Reddit (233K nodes, 115M edges), Reddit2, Flickr, Yelp, AmazonProducts (1.6M nodes, 264M edges) and PPI follow PyG's files, processing and splits. The single-graph datasets are stored as safetensors after the first processing, and load in seconds:

from mlx_graphs.datasets import Reddit
from mlx_graphs.loaders import NeighborLoader

data = Reddit()[0]
loader = NeighborLoader(
    data, num_neighbors=[25, 10], input_nodes=data.train_mask,
    batch_size=1024, shuffle=True,
)

The Datasets guide lists their sizes.

items.title: Feature and graph stores
items.text:
A FeatureStore holds named arrays (node features, labels, timestamps, ...) and returns the rows asked for; a GraphStore holds the edges and converts them to the CSC layout used by the samplers. Like PyG's remote backend, a (feature_store, graph_store) pair can replace the graph in NeighborLoader: the sampler reads the graph store, and only the rows of the sampled nodes (and edges) are gathered from the feature store. Arrays named x, y and edge_attr become the node_features, node_labels and edge_features of the mini-batch; other arrays keep their name.

MemmapFeatureStore stores every array in a .npy file and reads rows with positional reads, so the features can be larger than the memory. Write them in chunks with create_tensor:

import numpy as np
from mlx_graphs.data import MemmapFeatureStore, InMemoryGraphStore
from mlx_graphs.loaders import NeighborLoader

feature_store = MemmapFeatureStore("features/")
x = feature_store.create_tensor("x", (num_nodes, 1024), "float32")
for start in range(0, num_nodes, 100_000):
    x[start : start + 100_000] = load_feature_chunk(start)
x.flush()
del x
feature_store["y"] = labels

graph_store = InMemoryGraphStore()
graph_store.put_edge_index(edge_index, layout="coo", size=(num_nodes, num_nodes))

loader = NeighborLoader(
    (feature_store, graph_store), num_neighbors=[10, 5], batch_size=1024
)
for batch in loader:
    out = model(batch.edge_index, batch.node_features)

An existing graph converts with InMemoryFeatureStore.from_data(data) / MemmapFeatureStore.from_data(data, root) and InMemoryGraphStore.from_data(data). MemmapGraphStore keeps the edges (e.g. already in CSC) in .npy files, to reopen a large graph without sorting its edges again. The stores API page lists all of them.

benchmarks/quality/feature_store_memory.py trains nothing but iterates a NeighborLoader over a 6.1 GB features file (250 MB of features per mini-batch): the process peaks under 3 GB of resident memory, the size of a few mini-batches rather than of the file.

items.title: Temporal sampling
items.text:
With time_attr, NeighborLoader only samples the neighbors whose timestamp is not later than the time of their seed, as in PyG:

# node-level time: a neighbor's time is its node's
data.time = node_timestamps  # [num_nodes]
loader = NeighborLoader(
    data, num_neighbors=[10, 5], input_nodes=seeds, batch_size=256,
    time_attr="time", temporal_strategy="last",
)

# edge-level time: the time of the edge; seed times are then required
data.time = edge_timestamps  # [num_edges]
loader = NeighborLoader(
    data, num_neighbors=[10, 5], input_nodes=seeds, input_time=seed_times,
    time_attr="time",
)
  • temporal_strategy="uniform" samples uniformly among the valid neighbors, "last" keeps the most recent ones (then the mini-batches are the same as PyG's with pyg-lib).
  • Every seed gets its own subgraph (disjoint=True): a node sampled for two seeds appears twice, and batch.batch gives the seed of every node.
  • LinkNeighborLoader takes time_attr and edge_label_time: both ends of a supervision edge (and its negatives) are sampled at the time of the edge.

Temporal sampling runs on the host, with numpy: the neighbors of every node are sorted by time once, and each hop is a vectorized binary search and sampling step over the whole frontier.

The validation page compares training on these datasets, and the temporal sampler, with PyG.

items.title: Creating message passing layers
items.text: Every graph layer of mlx-graphs is a subclass of MessagePassing, the counterpart of PyG's MessagePassing. A layer computes one message per edge, aggregates the messages that reach each node and updates the node embeddings. This page shows how to write such a layer, how to choose its aggregation, how to write attention layers, how to make a layer fast, and how to check it against PyG.

items.title: The MessagePassing contract
items.text:
A layer chooses its aggregation in __init__ and calls self.propagate in __call__. propagate(edge_index, node_features, message_kwargs=None, aggregate_kwargs=None, update_kwargs=None) runs three methods, and each one can be overridden:

Method What it receives and returns message(src_features, dst_features, **message_kwargs) The features of the two ends of every edge: src_features = node_features[edge_index[0]] (PyG's x_j) and dst_features = node_features[edge_index[1]] (PyG's x_i), plus the entries of message_kwargs. Returns one message per edge, [num_edges, ...]. By default, the source features, multiplied by edge_weights if that keyword is given. aggregate(messages, indices, **aggregate_kwargs) The messages and their destination nodes (indices = edge_index[1]). Returns one row per destination node. By default, it reduces the messages with the layer's aggregation. update_nodes(aggregated, **update_kwargs) The aggregated messages, plus the entries of update_kwargs. Returns the output of the layer. By default, the aggregated messages unchanged.

Messages flow from edge_index[0] (the source) to edge_index[1] (the destination), as with PyG's default flow="source_to_target". An undirected graph lists every edge in both directions. Nodes without incoming edges get zeros with the "add", "mean", "max" and "min" aggregations.

propagate also sets self.num_nodes to the number of destination nodes, read from the shape of the features. The default aggregate uses it as the size of its output, so the output always has one row per node, even for nodes without edges.

Edges first

The built-in layers take the graph first: conv(edge_index, node_features, ...), where PyG writes conv(x, edge_index). propagate takes its arguments in the same order. Write your own __call__ the same way, so that your layers work in the models and wrappers that call layers like this (e.g. to_hetero()).

The smallest layer passes the features through propagate with the default message:

import mlx.core as mx

from mlx_graphs.nn import MessagePassing

class NeighborAggr(MessagePassing):
    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features):
        return self.propagate(edge_index, node_features)

# edges 0 -> 1, 1 -> 2, 2 -> 1 and 3 -> 1; node 0 has no incoming edge
edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 1, 1]])
x = mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])

print(NeighborAggr(aggr="mean")(edge_index, x))

array([[0],
       [2.66667],
       [2],
       [0]], dtype=float32)

Node 1 receives the features of nodes 0, 2 and 3, and averages them.

Bipartite graphs

node_features can also be a (src_features, dst_features) tuple, for messages between two sets of nodes (e.g. author -> paper in a heterogeneous graph). edge_index[0] then indexes src_features, edge_index[1] indexes dst_features, and the output has one row per destination node:

authors = mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
papers = mx.zeros((2, 1))
writes = mx.array([[0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1]])  # author -> paper

print(NeighborAggr(aggr="mean")(writes, (authors, papers)))

array([[1.5],
       [3]], dtype=float32)

items.title: A layer with edge features, step by step
items.text:
This section builds a layer that uses the features of both ends of an edge and the edge's own features:

\[\mathbf{h}_i = \mathbf{W}_r \mathbf{x}_i + \mathrm{mean}_{j \to i} \, \mathrm{ReLU} \left( \mathbf{W}_s \mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{W}_d \mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{W}_e \mathbf{e}_{j i} \right)\]

1. Decide what goes where. The sum inside the ReLU is the message of edge \(j \to i\). The mean is the aggregation. Adding the root term \(\mathbf{W}_r \mathbf{x}_i\) is the update.

2. Project the nodes once, not every edge. The linear maps act on one node at a time, so they can be applied to the [num_nodes, features] arrays before propagate gathers them per edge. That computes num_nodes projections instead of num_edges, which is how GATConv and SAGEConv work. The projected source and destination features go to propagate as a (src, dst) tuple, the projected edge features through message_kwargs and the root term through update_kwargs.

3. Write the layer.

import mlx.nn as nn

from mlx_graphs.nn import Linear

class EdgeFeatureConv(MessagePassing):
    # update_nodes adds a root term of size out_features_dim, so a list of
    # aggregations whose outputs are concatenated cannot work (see below)
    supports_concat_aggr = False

    def __init__(self, node_features_dim, edge_features_dim, out_features_dim, **kwargs):
        kwargs.setdefault("aggr", "mean")
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.lin_src = Linear(node_features_dim, out_features_dim)
        self.lin_dst = Linear(node_features_dim, out_features_dim, bias=False)
        self.lin_edge = Linear(edge_features_dim, out_features_dim, bias=False)
        self.lin_root = Linear(node_features_dim, out_features_dim, bias=False)

    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features, edge_features):
        if isinstance(node_features, tuple):  # bipartite (src, dst)
            src, dst = node_features
        else:
            src = dst = node_features
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index,
            (self.lin_src(src), self.lin_dst(dst)),
            message_kwargs={"edge_features": self.lin_edge(edge_features)},
            update_kwargs={"root": self.lin_root(dst)},
        )

    def message(self, src_features, dst_features, edge_features=None, **kwargs):
        return nn.relu(src_features + dst_features + edge_features)

    def update_nodes(self, aggregated, root=None, **kwargs):
        return aggregated + root

message and update_nodes take their extra arguments by name, as given in message_kwargs and update_kwargs. Keep a **kwargs in their signature: propagate passes every entry of the dictionaries.

4. Run it. A small graph with a duplicate edge, a self-loop and an isolated node (node 5), which are the cases where layers usually go wrong:

mx.random.seed(0)
edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1, 4, 4, 3, 2]])
x = mx.random.normal((6, 8))
edge_features = mx.random.normal((edge_index.shape[1], 3))

conv = EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16)
out = conv(edge_index, x, edge_features)
print(out.shape)

(6, 16)

5. Check it against the formula, written with scatter():

from mlx_graphs.utils import scatter

src, dst = edge_index
messages = nn.relu(
    conv.lin_src(x)[src] + conv.lin_dst(x)[dst] + conv.lin_edge(edge_features)
)
expected = scatter(messages, dst, x.shape[0], "mean") + conv.lin_root(x)
print(mx.allclose(out, expected, atol=1e-5).item())
# node 5 has no incoming edge: only its root term is left
print(mx.allclose(out[5], conv.lin_root(x)[5]).item())

True
True

6. Train it. The layer is an mlx.nn.Module, so its parameters get gradients like any other module's:

from mlx.utils import tree_flatten

def loss_fn(model):
    return model(edge_index, x, edge_features).square().mean()

loss, grads = nn.value_and_grad(conv, loss_fn)(conv)
print([name for name, _ in tree_flatten(grads)])

['lin_src.weight', 'lin_src.bias', 'lin_dst.weight', 'lin_edge.weight', 'lin_root.weight']

7. Use it on a bipartite graph. __call__ already accepts a (src, dst) tuple:

x_src, x_dst = mx.random.normal((4, 8)), mx.random.normal((2, 8))
bipartite = mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 1, 1]])
print(conv(bipartite, (x_src, x_dst), mx.random.normal((4, 3))).shape)

(2, 16)

Because __init__ passes **kwargs to MessagePassing, the aggregation can be changed when building the layer, e.g. EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16, aggr="max").

items.title: Aggregations
items.text:
The aggr argument of MessagePassing.__init__ accepts the same values as PyG's:

aggr What the layer does with it "add" (or "sum"), "mean", "max", "min", "mul", "var", "std", "median" Reduces with scatter(). The first four can run on the fused kernels (see Speed). Any other name: "softmax", "powermean", "lstm", "set_transformer"... Builds the aggregation module of that name with aggregation_resolver(), stored in self.aggr_module. As in PyG, "softmax" is SoftmaxAggregation, which gives one output per node. A name with aggr_kwargs Builds the aggregation module of that name with these arguments (even for "mean" or "max"). An Aggregation instance Uses it as self.aggr_module. Its parameters (e.g. a learnable temperature) are trained with the layer. A list of names and/or aggregations Combines them with MultiAggregation: concatenated along the last axis by default, or combined element-wise with aggr_kwargs={"mode": "sum"} (also "mean", "max", "min", "logsumexp", "std", "var", or "proj", a linear layer after the concatenation).

With the NeighborAggr layer of the first section:

from mlx_graphs.nn.aggr import SoftmaxAggregation

edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 1, 1]])
x = mx.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])

print(NeighborAggr(aggr="max")(edge_index, x)[1])
print(NeighborAggr(aggr=["mean", "max"])(edge_index, x)[1])
print(NeighborAggr(aggr=["mean", "max"], aggr_kwargs={"mode": "sum"})(edge_index, x)[1])

conv = NeighborAggr(aggr=SoftmaxAggregation(learn=True))
print(conv.aggr_module)
print([name for name, _ in tree_flatten(conv.trainable_parameters())])

array([4], dtype=float32)
array([2.66667, 4], dtype=float32)
array([6.66667], dtype=float32)
SoftmaxAggregation(learn=True)
['aggr_module.t']

supports_concat_aggr

A list of aggregations concatenates their outputs, so the aggregated features are len(aggr) times wider. Most layers project or combine the aggregated features with arrays sized for one aggregation, and would fail with a shape error, or for multi-head attention return wrong rows. Such layers set the class attribute supports_concat_aggr = False, as EdgeFeatureConv does above: MessagePassing.__init__ then refuses a concatenating list with a clear error, and still accepts a list combined with aggr_kwargs={"mode": ...}:

try:
    EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16, aggr=["mean", "max"])
except ValueError as error:
    print(str(error).split(":")[0])

conv = EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16, aggr=["mean", "max"], aggr_kwargs={"mode": "mean"})
print(conv.aggr_module)

EdgeFeatureConv does not support a list of aggregations whose outputs are concatenated
MultiAggregation(mode=mean
  (aggrs.0): MeanAggregation()
  (aggrs.1): MaxAggregation()
)

The default is True, for layers whose output is the aggregation itself (such as NeighborAggr). A layer can also support concatenation by sizing its next projection with self.aggr_module.get_out_features_dim(dim), which is what SAGEConv does ("aggr_module" in self tells whether the layer has an aggregation module).

aggregation_resolver

aggregation_resolver() turns a name, a list or a module into an Aggregation, as PyG's function of the same name. Names are case-insensitive and can be short names or class names, and PyG's in_channels / out_channels are accepted for node_features_dim / out_features_dim:

from mlx_graphs.nn.aggr import aggregation_resolver

print(aggregation_resolver("SoftmaxAggregation", learn=True))
print(aggregation_resolver("lstm", in_channels=8, out_channels=8))
print(aggregation_resolver(["mean", "std"], mode="cat"))

SoftmaxAggregation(learn=True)
LSTMAggregation(
  (lstm): LSTM(input_dims=8, hidden_size=8, bias=True)
)
MultiAggregation(mode=cat
  (aggrs.0): MeanAggregation()
  (aggrs.1): StdAggregation(semi_grad=False)
)

Aggregations also work on their own, e.g. as a readout over the nodes of each graph of a batch: aggr(x, index, dim_size) reduces the rows of x that share an index:

from mlx_graphs.nn.aggr import SumAggregation

print(SumAggregation()(x, mx.array([0, 0, 1, 1]), dim_size=2))

array([[3],
       [7]], dtype=float32)

items.title: Attention layers
items.text:
An attention layer weighs each message by a coefficient that is normalized over the incoming edges of the destination node. That normalization needs the scores of all the incoming edges of a node at once, so it can't be done inside message, which sees one edge at a time. Compute the scores before propagate, normalize them with scatter(scores, dst, num_nodes, "softmax") (or softmax(), its PyG-named version), and pass the coefficients to propagate as edge_weights. Unlike the other reductions of scatter, "softmax" returns one value per edge.

This is how GATConv works. Its scores are a sum of a term of the source node and a term of the destination node, so they are computed per node and only gathered per edge as [num_edges, heads] scalars. A simplified GAT layer (no self-loops, dropout or bias):

from mlx_graphs.nn import fused_message_passing
from mlx_graphs.nn.linear import glorot

@fused_message_passing
class SimpleGATConv(MessagePassing):
    supports_concat_aggr = False

    def __init__(self, node_features_dim, out_features_dim, heads=1, negative_slope=0.2):
        super().__init__(aggr="add")
        self.heads, self.out_features_dim = heads, out_features_dim
        self.negative_slope = negative_slope
        self.lin = Linear(node_features_dim, heads * out_features_dim, bias=False)
        self.att_src = glorot((1, heads, out_features_dim))
        self.att_dst = glorot((1, heads, out_features_dim))

    def scores(self, edge_index, node_features):
        """Attention coefficients [num_edges, heads] and projected features."""
        H, C = self.heads, self.out_features_dim
        h = self.lin(node_features).reshape(-1, H, C)  # [num_nodes, H, C]
        src, dst = edge_index
        a_src = (h * self.att_src).sum(-1)  # [num_nodes, H]
        a_dst = (h * self.att_dst).sum(-1)
        logits = nn.leaky_relu(a_src[src] + a_dst[dst], self.negative_slope)
        return scatter(logits, dst, node_features.shape[0], "softmax"), h

    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features):
        alpha, h = self.scores(edge_index, node_features)
        # one weight per edge and head: aggregated as one SpMM per head
        out = self.propagate(edge_index, h, message_kwargs={"edge_weights": alpha})
        return out.reshape(node_features.shape[0], -1)  # concatenate the heads

mx.random.seed(0)
edge_index = mx.array([[0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 2], [1, 0, 2, 1, 4, 4, 3, 2]])
x = mx.random.normal((6, 8))

conv = SimpleGATConv(8, 16, heads=4)
print(conv(edge_index, x).shape)

alpha, _ = conv.scores(edge_index, x)
# the coefficients of the incoming edges of each node sum to 1
print(scatter(alpha, edge_index[1], 6, "add")[:, 0])

(6, 64)
array([1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0], dtype=float32)

The default message multiplies features of shape [num_edges, heads, channels] by edge_weights of shape [num_edges, heads], one weight per head, and so does the fused kernel. Node 5 has no incoming edge: its coefficients sum to 0 and its output is 0.

softmax() gives the same coefficients:

from mlx_graphs.utils import softmax

H, C = conv.heads, conv.out_features_dim
h = conv.lin(x).reshape(-1, H, C)
src, dst = edge_index
logits = nn.leaky_relu(
    (h * conv.att_src).sum(-1)[src] + (h * conv.att_dst).sum(-1)[dst], 0.2
)
print(mx.allclose(softmax(logits, dst, num_nodes=6), alpha).item())

True

Two details of GATConv are worth copying. Edges can be excluded by setting their logits to -inf before the softmax, and dropout is applied to the coefficients (nn.Dropout on alpha), after the softmax.

items.title: Speed
items.text:
Fused message passing

Gather-scatter, the default path of propagate, builds a [num_edges, features] array of messages and reduces it. On large graphs, that array costs more time and memory than the rest of the layer. When the messages are a weighted sum of neighbour features, the class decorator fused_message_passing() replaces message + aggregate by a single sparse x dense matmul (SpMM) from mlx-cluster (message_and_aggregate), and the message array is never built. The built-in GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, GAT and GATv2 layers, among others, use it.

The decorator only enables the fused path. propagate decides at every call, and falls back to gather-scatter, with the same result, when:

  • mlx_cluster is not installed, or fused message passing is turned off (set_fused_message_passing(), fused_message_passing_mode());
  • aggr is not "add", "mean", "max" or "min", e.g. a list or an aggregation module ("max" and "min" also need a recent mlx-cluster);
  • an entry of message_kwargs other than edge_weights, or of aggregate_kwargs, is not None (e.g. edge_features): the messages are then no longer a weighted sum of neighbour features;
  • the source features are not floating point or have fewer than two dimensions, or edge_weights is neither one scalar per edge nor [num_edges, heads] for [num_nodes, heads, channels] features;
  • the layer subclasses a decorated layer and overrides message() or aggregate() without also overriding message_and_aggregate().

The two paths give the same output, which fused_message_passing_mode() makes easy to check:

from mlx_graphs.nn import fused_message_passing_mode, is_fused_message_passing_enabled

@fused_message_passing
class WeightedSum(MessagePassing):
    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features, edge_weights=None):
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index, node_features, message_kwargs={"edge_weights": edge_weights}
        )

conv = WeightedSum(aggr="add")
weights = mx.random.uniform(shape=(edge_index.shape[1],))
print(is_fused_message_passing_enabled())

fused = conv(edge_index, x, weights)
with fused_message_passing_mode(False):
    reference = conv(edge_index, x, weights)
print(mx.allclose(fused, reference, atol=1e-5).item())

True
True

allow_message_override

The fused kernel ignores message and aggregate, so decorating a class that overrides them raises an error when the class is defined:

try:

    @fused_message_passing
    class Doubled(MessagePassing):
        def message(self, src_features, dst_features, **kwargs):
            return 2 * src_features

except TypeError as error:
    print(error)

Doubled overrides message(), which the fused SpMM kernel would ignore. Implement message_and_aggregate(), or pass allow_message_override=True if the override reduces to the default when only edge_weights are given.

Layers whose messages are not a weighted sum of neighbour features, such as EdgeFeatureConv or EdgeConv (an MLP per edge), have no fused path and are left undecorated. Some layers override message only for an optional input, and fall back to the default message without it. They are decorated with allow_message_override=True: the fused path runs when the optional input is None and gather-scatter runs otherwise. This is how GINConv handles its optional edge features:

@fused_message_passing(allow_message_override=True)
class MaybeEdgeConv(MessagePassing):
    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features, edge_features=None):
        return self.propagate(
            edge_index, node_features, message_kwargs={"edge_features": edge_features}
        )

    def message(self, src_features, dst_features, edge_features=None, **kwargs):
        if edge_features is None:  # the default message: fused
            return super().message(src_features, dst_features, **kwargs)
        return nn.relu(src_features + edge_features)  # gather-scatter

conv = MaybeEdgeConv()
print(conv(edge_index, x).shape)
print(conv(edge_index, x, mx.random.normal((edge_index.shape[1], 8))).shape)

(6, 8)
(6, 8)

A layer can also provide its own fused implementation by overriding message_and_aggregate(edge_index, node_features, edge_weights=None, **kwargs).

format

@fused_message_passing(format=...) picks the kernel:

  • "coo" works on edge_index as it is.
  • "csr" converts the graph to CSR once and uses a faster, deterministic kernel without atomics. The conversion (and its transpose, for the backward pass) is cached per edge_index array, in a cache of 16 graphs.
  • "auto" (the default) starts with "coo" and switches to "csr" when the conversion pays off: right away for graphs with at least a million edges, and after a few calls with the same edge_index array otherwise (e.g. full-batch training). Mini-batches seen once stay on COO.

set_fused_message_passing() (True, format="csr") overrides the format of every layer.

clear_csr_cache

Cached conversions are found by the identity of the edge_index array, not by its content. Modifying an edge_index in place between calls leaves a stale conversion in the cache. Build a new array instead, or call clear_csr_cache():

from mlx_graphs.nn import clear_csr_cache

@fused_message_passing(format="csr")
class CSRSum(MessagePassing):
    def __call__(self, edge_index, node_features):
        return self.propagate(edge_index, node_features)

conv = CSRSum()
graph = mx.array([[0, 1], [1, 2]])
features = mx.array([[1.0], [10.0], [100.0]])
print(conv(graph, features)[:, 0])

graph[0, 0] = 2  # in place: the edge 0 -> 1 becomes 2 -> 1
print(conv(graph, features)[:, 0])  # stale: still the old graph

clear_csr_cache()
print(conv(graph, features)[:, 0])

array([0, 1, 10], dtype=float32)
array([0, 1, 10], dtype=float32)
array([0, 100, 10], dtype=float32)

Staying compatible with mx.compile

mx.compile traces a function once and replays the trace. While tracing, arrays have no values, so anything that reads a value on the host fails: .item(), float(array), np.array(array), or a Python if on an array. Shapes are known, so sizes read from shapes are fine.

The usual culprit is a number of nodes computed as index.max() + 1. degree(), softmax() and the aggregation modules do that (with .item()) when they are not given a size. Pass the size you already know: num_nodes to degree and softmax, out_size to scatter (whose default is the number of values, not of nodes) and dim_size to an aggregation. propagate and the default aggregate already use self.num_nodes, read from the shape of the features.

from mlx_graphs.utils import degree

dst = edge_index[1]
try:
    mx.compile(lambda index: degree(index))(dst)
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

print(mx.compile(lambda index: degree(index, 6))(dst))

[eval] Attempting to eval an array during function transformations like compile or vmap is not allowed.
array([1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 0], dtype=float32)

The layers of this page follow these rules and compile:

conv = EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16)
edge_features = mx.random.normal((edge_index.shape[1], 3))
compiled = mx.compile(lambda e, h, f: conv(e, h, f))
eager = conv(edge_index, x, edge_features)
print(mx.allclose(compiled(edge_index, x, edge_features), eager, atol=1e-5).item())

gat = SimpleGATConv(8, 16, heads=4)
compiled = mx.compile(lambda e, h: gat(e, h))
print(mx.allclose(compiled(edge_index, x), gat(edge_index, x), atol=1e-5).item())

True
True

The CSR conversion of the fused kernels also reads the graph on the host. When edge_index is an input of the compiled function, fused layers (format="auto" or "csr") fall back to the COO kernel. To keep the CSR kernel under mx.compile, call the layer once eagerly, which caches the conversion, and let the compiled function capture that same edge_index array instead of taking it as an input:

conv = CSRSum()
graph = mx.array([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4, 0]])
features = mx.random.normal((5, 4))

eager = conv(graph, features)  # converts and caches graph
compiled = mx.compile(lambda h: conv(graph, h))
print(mx.allclose(compiled(features), eager).item())

True

Layers that need the sizes of the graphs of a batch on the host (the LSTM, GRU, sort and set transformer aggregations, TopKPooling / SAGPooling, and GPSConv / SGFormer / Polynormer without a precomputed layout) work with nn.value_and_grad but not inside mx.compile.

items.title: Testing a layer against PyG
items.text:
Most layers of mlx-graphs have a test that builds the same layer in PyG, copies PyG's weights into the mlx-graphs layer and compares the outputs (and, for many of them, the gradients) on the same random graph. They are in tests/nn/conv/test_*.py. For example test_gat_conv.py compares the output of GATConv and the gradients with respect to the node and edge features, and test_gine_conv.py compares GINEConv on homogeneous and bipartite graphs. tests/pyg_copy.py has helpers to convert a torch state_dict to mlx-graphs names (torch_state) and load it with shape checks (load_torch). The tests need torch and torch_geometric (pip install -e '.[test]').

The pattern, for EdgeFeatureConv:

  1. Write the same layer in PyG.
  2. Copy the weights. torch.nn.Linear and mlx.nn.Linear store their weights with the same [out_features, in_features] shape.
  3. Run both on a graph with duplicate edges, self-loops and isolated nodes.
  4. Compare the outputs and the input gradients.
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch_geometric.nn import MessagePassing as PyGMessagePassing

class PyGEdgeFeatureConv(PyGMessagePassing):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, edge_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__(aggr="mean")
        self.lin_src = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim)
        self.lin_dst = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim, bias=False)
        self.lin_edge = torch.nn.Linear(edge_dim, out_dim, bias=False)
        self.lin_root = torch.nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index, edge_attr):
        out = self.propagate(
            edge_index,
            h_src=self.lin_src(x),
            h_dst=self.lin_dst(x),
            edge_attr=self.lin_edge(edge_attr),
        )
        return out + self.lin_root(x)

    def message(self, h_src_j, h_dst_i, edge_attr):
        return torch.relu(h_src_j + h_dst_i + edge_attr)

# a random graph with duplicate edges, self-loops and isolated nodes
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
edges = rng.integers(0, 25, (2, 100))
edges = np.concatenate([edges, edges[:, :10], [[0, 1], [0, 1]]], axis=1)
x_np = rng.normal(size=(30, 8)).astype(np.float32)
e_np = rng.normal(size=(edges.shape[1], 3)).astype(np.float32)

torch.manual_seed(0)
ref = PyGEdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16)
conv = EdgeFeatureConv(8, 3, 16)
for name in ("lin_src", "lin_dst", "lin_edge", "lin_root"):
    for param, value in getattr(ref, name).named_parameters():
        setattr(getattr(conv, name), param, mx.array(value.detach().numpy()))

x_torch = torch.tensor(x_np, requires_grad=True)
expected = ref(x_torch, torch.tensor(edges), torch.tensor(e_np))
expected.square().sum().backward()

def loss_fn(features):
    return conv(mx.array(edges), features, mx.array(e_np)).square().sum()

out = conv(mx.array(edges), mx.array(x_np), mx.array(e_np))
grad = mx.grad(loss_fn)(mx.array(x_np))

# MLX's float32 GPU matmul is accurate to ~1e-3 relative: a wrong formula
# is off by O(1), so a loose tolerance still catches it
print(np.allclose(np.array(out), expected.detach().numpy(), rtol=2e-2, atol=2e-2))
grad_error = np.linalg.norm(np.array(grad) - x_torch.grad.numpy())
print(grad_error <= 2e-2 * np.linalg.norm(x_torch.grad.numpy()))

True
True

A few things make these tests catch bugs:

  • Edge cases in the graph. Duplicate edges, self-loops and nodes without incoming edges are where aggregations and normalizations differ. test_zero_edges.py also runs the layers that project per-edge arrays on graphs without edges.
  • Gradients. A forward pass can match while the backward pass doesn't (e.g. infinite derivatives of norms at zero, or the gradient of max among tied messages). Compare gradients with respect to the inputs, and check that every parameter gets a finite gradient.
  • Tolerances. MLX's float32 matmul on the GPU has a relative error of about 1e-3, where torch on the CPU has about 1e-7. The tests use a tolerance of 2e-2, which a wrong formula exceeds by far.
  • Both paths. For a layer decorated with @fused_message_passing, compare the fused and gather-scatter outputs with fused_message_passing_mode() (see tests/nn/test_fused_message_passing.py).

See Validation for the layer-level, sampler and training checks against PyG.

items.title: Graph neural networks for cybersecurity
items.text:
View on GitHub Download notebook

Goal: Security data is full of graphs: system calls between processes and files, money flows between wallets, network flows between hosts, function calls inside a program. This tutorial trains recent GNN architectures with mlx-graphs on four public security datasets, from self-supervised anomaly detection to node, edge and graph classification:

Task Graph Predict Dataset Models 1 Host intrusion detection processes, files and sockets linked by system calls anomalous nodes, without labels DARPA TC E3 CADETS Velox, Orthrus 2 Anti-money laundering Bitcoin transactions linked by payments node Elliptic MLP, GCN, GraphSAGE, GATv2, Graph Transformer, BWGNN 3 Network intrusion detection hosts linked by NetFlow records edge NF-UNSW-NB15-v3 MLP, E-GraphSAGE 4 Malware classification Android function call graphs graph MalNet-Tiny GIN, GraphGPS

Along the way we write three layers that mlx-graphs does not ship (a beta-wavelet filter, an edge-feature message passing layer and a linear global attention) and look at the pitfalls that make security benchmarks look easier than they are: data snooping, time drift, shortcut features and class imbalance.

Concepts: Self-supervised anomaly detection, Temporal neighbor sampling, Node, edge and graph classification, Custom MessagePassing layers, Custom Dataset, Temporal splits, Class imbalance

Requirements: besides mlx-graphs, this notebook uses pip install pandas pyarrow scikit-learn matplotlib gensim. The datasets take about 2.2 GB of downloads, including 1.9 GB for CADETS, which you download by hand (see section 1). Running the whole notebook takes about 45 minutes on an M5 Pro; lower NUM_SEEDS below to make sections 2 to 4 faster.

import os
import time
from math import comb

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, precision_score, recall_score

from mlx_graphs.data import GraphData
from mlx_graphs.loaders import Dataloader
from mlx_graphs.nn import Linear, MessagePassing, TransformerConv

# Each model is trained with NUM_SEEDS seeds and we report the mean and standard
# deviation: on these datasets, one run is not enough to rank two models.
NUM_SEEDS = 3

# MLX keeps freed buffers in a cache for reuse. Batches of graphs all have
# different shapes, so we cap that cache to keep the memory footprint small.
mx.set_cache_limit(1 << 30)


def mean_std(values):
    return f"{np.mean(values):.3f} ± {np.std(values):.3f}"

items.title: 1. Host intrusion detection on provenance graphs (self-supervised anomaly detection)
items.text:
An operating system can record every action of every process: which files a process reads and writes, which programs it executes, which network connections it opens. Linked together, these records form a provenance graph, where nodes are processes, files and network sockets, and edges are timestamped system events between them. An attack leaves a trace in this graph: a compromised web server that downloads and runs a payload adds new paths between processes, files and remote hosts.

Provenance-based intrusion detection systems (PIDSs) learn what normal activity looks like from a few days of benign provenance graphs, then flag the nodes that behave unusually. In this section, we build two recent PIDSs with mlx-graphs and evaluate them on the attacks of the DARPA Transparent Computing CADETS dataset:

  • Orthrus (Jiang et al., USENIX Security 2025) embeds every node with a graph attention network (TransformerConv) over its most recent neighbors, and is trained to predict the type of each event from the embeddings of its two nodes. Events whose type the model cannot predict are anomalous.
  • Velox (Bilot et al., USENIX Security 2025) keeps the same objective but replaces the graph neural network with a single linear layer. Bilot et al. show that this much simpler model is competitive with the state of the art, and trains in a fraction of the time.

We follow the preprocessing, hyperparameters and evaluation of PIDSMaker, the framework released with the second paper, and its configurations without data snooping (orthrus_non_snooped and velox): the node features are learned from the training days only, and the detection threshold is set on a validation day without attacks.

import io
import json
import re
import tarfile
import urllib.request
import zipfile
import zlib
from array import array
from collections import defaultdict
from contextlib import redirect_stderr
from pathlib import Path

from gensim.models import Word2Vec

from mlx_graphs.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from mlx_graphs.nn.models.tgn import LastNeighborLoader

DATA_DIR = Path(".mlx_graphs_data/darpa_tc_e3_cadets")
SEED = 0
EPOCHS = 12
BATCH_SIZE = 1024  # edges per mini-batch
WINDOW_NS = 15 * 60 * 10**9  # 15-minute time windows
EMB_DIM = 256  # word2vec dimension
# CADETS E3 hyperparameters of PIDSMaker (docs/tuned_systems.md). For Orthrus,
# we keep the learning rate of its `orthrus_non_snooped` configuration (1e-4):
# with the tuned 1e-3, training sometimes diverged in our runs.
CONFIGS = {
    "Velox": dict(dim=256, lr=1e-4, dropout=0.3),
    "Orthrus": dict(dim=256, lr=1e-4, dropout=0.3),
}

items.title: The dataset
items.text:
In April 2018, the third engagement of the DARPA Transparent Computing program recorded two weeks of activity on several hosts while a red team attacked them. CADETS is a FreeBSD web server, instrumented with DTrace. Its records follow DARPA's Common Data Model (CDM18): Subject records are processes, FileObject and NetFlowObject records are files and network flows, and Event records are system calls of a process on an object, with a timestamp in nanoseconds.

The red team attacked the Nginx web server of CADETS on April 6, 11, 12 and 13: it exploited a backdoor in Nginx, downloaded payloads such as /tmp/main and ran them. We use the node-level ground truth of Orthrus, distributed with PIDSMaker, which lists the malicious processes, files and netflows of each attack. As in PIDSMaker, we evaluate on the attacks of April 6, 12 and 13.

The records are published on Google Drive as three .tar.gz archives of JSON lines (1.9 GB in total). Google Drive limits the number of downloads per day, so download them by hand:

  1. open the CADETS folder of the DARPA release,
  2. select the three JSON archives, ta1-cadets-e3-official.json.tar.gz, ta1-cadets-e3-official-1.json.tar.gz and ta1-cadets-e3-official-2.json.tar.gz (not the .bin ones),
  3. click Download: Google Drive packs them into a single drive-download-....zip,
  4. set CADETS_ARCHIVE below to the path of that zip.

The notebook reads the records directly from the zip, without extracting anything. The ground truth is downloaded from the PIDSMaker repository.

# Path of the zip downloaded from Google Drive: change it to yours
CADETS_ARCHIVE = Path(
    "~/Downloads/drive-download-20261121T130000Z-1-001.zip"
).expanduser()

GT_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ubc-provenance/PIDSMaker/main/"
    "Ground_Truth/orthrus/E3-CADETS/{}"
)
ATTACKS = {
    "Apr 6": "node_Nginx_Backdoor_06.csv",
    "Apr 12": "node_Nginx_Backdoor_12.csv",
    "Apr 13": "node_Nginx_Backdoor_13.csv",
}

with zipfile.ZipFile(CADETS_ARCHIVE) as z:
    ARCHIVES = sorted(n for n in z.namelist() if n.endswith(".json.tar.gz"))
assert len(ARCHIVES) == 3, f"expected the 3 CADETS JSON archives, found {ARCHIVES}"
print("\n".join(ARCHIVES))

for csv in ATTACKS.values():
    path = DATA_DIR / "ground_truth" / csv
    if not path.exists():
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(GT_URL.format(csv), path)

ta1-cadets-e3-official-1.json.tar.gz
ta1-cadets-e3-official-2.json.tar.gz
ta1-cadets-e3-official.json.tar.gz

items.title: From audit records to a provenance graph
items.text:
We stream the JSON records out of the zip and its archives, without extracting them on disk, and keep:

  • nodes: processes (Subject), files (FileObject, except Unix sockets, which Orthrus treats as netflows) and netflows (NetFlowObject). In CADETS, the name of a process and the path of a file are not in their own records but in the events that use them (the exec property and the predicateObjectPath field), so we collect them from the events, as Orthrus does. A netflow is named by its remote address and port.
  • edges: the events of the 10 types used by Orthrus, from the process (subject) to the object (predicateObject). For the events through which information flows from the object to the process (EXECUTE, OPEN, READ, RECVFROM, RECVMSG), the edge is reversed.

Parsing the 44 million records takes about 3 minutes, so we cache the result.

CDM = "com.bbn.tc.schema.avro.cdm18."
EDGE_TYPES = [
    "EVENT_CONNECT",
    "EVENT_EXECUTE",
    "EVENT_OPEN",
    "EVENT_READ",
    "EVENT_RECVFROM",
    "EVENT_RECVMSG",
    "EVENT_SENDMSG",
    "EVENT_SENDTO",
    "EVENT_WRITE",
    "EVENT_CLONE",
]
EDGE_TYPE_ID = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(EDGE_TYPES)}
REVERSED = {
    "EVENT_EXECUTE",
    "EVENT_OPEN",
    "EVENT_READ",
    "EVENT_RECVFROM",
    "EVENT_RECVMSG",
}
NODE_TYPES = ["process", "file", "netflow"]
PROCESS, FILE, NETFLOW = 0, 1, 2


def iter_records(zip_path):
    # Yields the JSON lines of the three archives, streamed out of the zip.
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as z:
        for archive in ARCHIVES:
            with z.open(archive) as f, tarfile.open(fileobj=f, mode="r|gz") as tar:
                for member in tar:
                    if member.isfile():
                        yield from tar.extractfile(member)


def parse_cadets(zip_path):
    uuid_to_id = {}

    def uid(uuid):
        return uuid_to_id.setdefault(uuid, len(uuid_to_id))

    node_type, netflow_name, exec_of, path_of = {}, {}, {}, {}
    src, dst, subject = array("q"), array("q"), array("q")
    etype, ts = array("b"), array("q")
    for line in iter_records(zip_path):
        kind = line[11 : line.index(b'"', 11)].decode().removeprefix(CDM)
        if kind not in ("Event", "Subject", "FileObject", "NetFlowObject"):
            continue
        d = json.loads(line)["datum"][CDM + kind]
        if kind == "Subject":
            node_type[uid(d["uuid"])] = PROCESS
        elif kind == "FileObject":
            i = uid(d["uuid"])
            if d["type"] == "FILE_OBJECT_UNIX_SOCKET":
                node_type[i], netflow_name[i] = NETFLOW, "unix socket"
            else:
                node_type[i] = FILE
        elif kind == "NetFlowObject":
            i = uid(d["uuid"])
            node_type[i] = NETFLOW
            netflow_name[i] = f"{d['remoteAddress']}:{d['remotePort']}"
        else:  # Event
            if d["subject"] is None or d["predicateObject"] is None:
                continue
            s = uid(d["subject"][CDM + "UUID"])
            o = uid(d["predicateObject"][CDM + "UUID"])
            exe = ((d["properties"] or {}).get("map") or {}).get("exec")
            if exe:
                exec_of[s] = exe
            path = d["predicateObjectPath"]
            if path is not None and path["string"] != "<unknown>":
                path_of[o] = path["string"]
            t = EDGE_TYPE_ID.get(d["type"])
            if t is None:
                continue
            subject.append(s)
            if d["type"] in REVERSED:
                s, o = o, s
            src.append(s)
            dst.append(o)
            etype.append(t)
            ts.append(d["timestampNanos"])

    types = np.full(len(uuid_to_id), -1, dtype=np.int8)  # -1: not a node
    types[list(node_type)] = list(node_type.values())
    names = [""] * len(uuid_to_id)
    for i, t in node_type.items():
        names[i] = (exec_of, path_of, netflow_name)[t].get(i) or ""
    arrays = dict(src=src, dst=dst, subject=subject, edge_type=etype, t=ts)
    arrays = {k: np.frombuffer(v, dtype=v.typecode).copy() for k, v in arrays.items()}
    return arrays, types, list(uuid_to_id), names


CACHE = DATA_DIR / "processed"
if not (CACHE / "events.npz").exists():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    arrays, types, uuids, names = parse_cadets(CADETS_ARCHIVE)
    print(f"Parsed in {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s")
    CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    np.savez(CACHE / "events.npz", node_type=types, **arrays)
    (CACHE / "nodes.json").write_text(json.dumps({"uuid": uuids, "name": names}))
    del arrays, types, uuids, names

events = dict(np.load(CACHE / "events.npz"))
objects = json.loads((CACHE / "nodes.json").read_text())
print(f"{len(objects['uuid']):,} objects, {events['t'].size:,} events")

2,741,785 objects, 18,893,277 events

items.title: Splits, time windows and edge fusion
items.text:
PIDSMaker splits CADETS by day, in the US/Eastern time zone of the engagement. The days without attacks are used for training (April 2 to 5 and 7 to 9) and validation (April 10), and the four days with attacks for testing.

A process often repeats the same system call on the same object, e.g. hundreds of READs of one file. Like Orthrus, we cut the stream into 15-minute windows and, inside each window, fuse the consecutive events of the same type between the same two nodes into the first one. This divides the number of edges by more than 3 without changing the structure of the graph.

SPLITS = {
    "train": [
        "2018-04-02",
        "2018-04-03",
        "2018-04-04",
        "2018-04-05",
        "2018-04-07",
        "2018-04-08",
        "2018-04-09",
    ],
    "val": ["2018-04-10"],
    "test": ["2018-04-06", "2018-04-11", "2018-04-12", "2018-04-13"],
}
TRAIN, VAL, TEST = 0, 1, 2

node_type = events["node_type"]
src, dst, etype, t, subject = (
    events[k] for k in ("src", "dst", "edge_type", "t", "subject")
)

# Keep the events of a process on a process, a file or a netflow
obj = np.where(subject == src, dst, src)
keep = (node_type[subject] == PROCESS) & (node_type[obj] >= 0)

# Day of every event in the US/Eastern time zone
day = pd.to_datetime(t, utc=True).tz_convert("US/Eastern").tz_localize(None)
day = day.to_numpy().astype("datetime64[D]")
split = np.full(t.size, -1, dtype=np.int8)
for k, dates in enumerate(SPLITS.values()):
    split[np.isin(day, np.array(dates, dtype="datetime64[D]"))] = k
keep &= split >= 0
src, dst, etype, t, split = (a[keep] for a in (src, dst, etype, t, split))
del events, day, subject, obj, keep
print(f"{t.size:,} events between processes, files and netflows")

# Edge fusion inside 15-minute windows
window = (t - t.min()) // WINDOW_NS
order = np.lexsort((t, dst, src, window))  # by window, edge, then time
w, s, d, e = window[order], src[order], dst[order], etype[order]
first = np.ones(order.size, dtype=bool)
first[1:] = (
    (w[1:] != w[:-1]) | (s[1:] != s[:-1]) | (d[1:] != d[:-1]) | (e[1:] != e[:-1])
)
kept = order[first]
kept = kept[np.argsort(t[kept], kind="stable")]  # back to time order
src, dst, etype, t, split, window = (
    a[kept] for a in (src, dst, etype, t, split, window)
)
del w, s, d, e, order, first, kept
print(f"{t.size:,} edges after fusion")

# Relabel the nodes 0..num_nodes-1
used, inverse = np.unique(np.concatenate([src, dst]), return_inverse=True)
src, dst = inverse[: src.size], inverse[src.size :]
num_nodes = used.size
ntype = node_type[used].astype(np.int64)
name = [objects["name"][i] for i in used]
node_of_uuid = {objects["uuid"][i]: k for k, i in enumerate(used)}

print(
    f"{num_nodes:,} nodes: "
    + ", ".join(
        f"{np.sum(ntype == k):,} {n}es"
        if n == "process"
        else f"{np.sum(ntype == k):,} {n}s"
        for k, n in enumerate(NODE_TYPES)
    )
)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "days": [len(v) for v in SPLITS.values()],
        "edges": [int(np.sum(split == k)) for k in range(3)],
    },
    index=list(SPLITS),
)

18,699,410 events between processes, files and netflows

5,688,677 edges after fusion

643,486 nodes: 209,587 processes, 233,699 files, 200,200 netflows
days edges train 7 3229340 val 1 501962 test 4 1957375

items.title: Node features
items.text:
The name of a node says a lot about it: /usr/local/sbin/nginx is not /tmp/main, and 81.49.200.166:80 is not a local DNS server. Orthrus turns these names into vectors with word2vec. A name is split into tokens (/, usr, /, local, ... for a path, the bytes of an address separated by . and : for a netflow), word2vec learns a vector for every token from the names of the training nodes, and a node is embedded as the weighted mean of its token vectors, with weights that decrease along the name. Tokens never seen in training, which only appear in the test days, get a zero vector. The node type is appended as a one-hot vector.

def tokenize(text, kind):
    if kind == NETFLOW:
        return text.replace(":", " : ").replace(".", " . ").split()
    return re.sub(r"\\+", "/", text).replace("/", " / ").split()


tokens = [tokenize(n, k) for n, k in zip(name, ntype)]

# Corpus: the distinct names of the nodes seen during training
train_nodes = np.unique(np.concatenate([src[split == TRAIN], dst[split == TRAIN]]))
corpus = list({name[i]: tokens[i] for i in train_nodes if tokens[i]}.values())

# gensim 4.4 declares the BLAS dot product with `except -1`, so every dot product
# equal to -1.0 prints "Exception ignored in ... our_dot_float" to sys.stderr.
# The value is correct: we hide these messages while training.
start = time.perf_counter()
with redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):
    w2v = Word2Vec(
        corpus,
        vector_size=EMB_DIM,
        window=5,
        min_count=1,
        sg=1,  # skip-gram
        negative=5,
        alpha=0.025,
        epochs=50,
        workers=1,
        seed=SEED,
        hashfxn=lambda s: zlib.crc32(s.encode()),  # reproducible initialization
    )
print(
    f"word2vec: {len(corpus):,} names, {len(w2v.wv):,} tokens, "
    f"trained in {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s"
)


def embed(toks, decline=0.3):
    # Weighted mean of the token vectors, as in Orthrus.
    if not toks:
        return np.zeros(EMB_DIM)
    n = len(toks)
    step = -decline / n
    weights = 1 / n - 0.5 * (n - 1) * step + step * np.arange(n)
    vecs = np.stack([w2v.wv[w] if w in w2v.wv else np.zeros(EMB_DIM) for w in toks])
    v = (weights[:, None] * vecs).mean(axis=0)
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) + 1e-12)


features = np.zeros((num_nodes, EMB_DIM + len(NODE_TYPES)), dtype=np.float32)
for i, tk in enumerate(tokens):
    features[i, :EMB_DIM] = embed(tk)
features[np.arange(num_nodes), EMB_DIM + ntype] = 1.0  # one-hot node type
X = mx.array(features)
del features, tokens, corpus, objects  # free host memory
print(X.shape)

Each ground-truth file lists the UUIDs of the malicious nodes of one attack. A few of them never appear in an edge we keep, and cannot be detected.

attack_nodes = {}
for attack, csv in ATTACKS.items():
    uuids = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "ground_truth" / csv, header=None)[0]
    attack_nodes[attack] = {node_of_uuid[u] for u in uuids if u in node_of_uuid}
    print(

        f"{len(attack_nodes[attack])} in the graph"
    )
malicious = set().union(*attack_nodes.values())

items.title: Two detectors with the same objective
items.text:
Both systems are self-supervised: they never see an attack during training. They learn to predict the type of every event (READ, WRITE, CONNECT, ...) from its two nodes. On benign activity, an event's type is predictable: nginx reads its configuration files and sends to remote clients. The cross-entropy of an event is its anomaly score, and an event the model cannot explain gets a high score.

The two systems share the decoder, an MLP on the concatenation of the projected source and destination embeddings, and differ in the encoder:

  • Velox embeds a node by a single linear layer of its features. The embedding of a node does not depend on the graph at all.
  • Orthrus embeds a node by two TransformerConv layers (8 heads, then 1) over its recent neighborhood. A LastNeighborLoader keeps the 20 most recent neighbors of every node, and each edge carries the one-hot type of the event as edge features. The embedding of a node therefore depends on what it did recently.
NUM_TYPES = len(EDGE_TYPES)
EDGE_ONE_HOT = mx.eye(NUM_TYPES)


class EdgeTypeDecoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin_src = nn.Linear(dim, 2 * dim)
        self.lin_dst = nn.Linear(dim, 2 * dim)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(4 * dim, 2 * dim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(2 * dim, NUM_TYPES)
        )

    def __call__(self, h_src, h_dst):
        return self.mlp(
            mx.concatenate([self.lin_src(h_src), self.lin_dst(h_dst)], axis=-1)
        )


class Velox(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, dim, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Linear(in_dim, dim)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.decoder = EdgeTypeDecoder(dim)

    def __call__(self, batch_src, batch_dst):
        h_src = self.dropout(self.encoder(X[batch_src]))
        h_dst = self.dropout(self.encoder(X[batch_dst]))
        return self.decoder(h_src, h_dst)


class Orthrus(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, dim, dropout, proj_dim=100, heads=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Linear(in_dim, proj_dim)
        self.conv1 = TransformerConv(
            proj_dim, dim, heads=heads, dropout=dropout, edge_features_dim=NUM_TYPES
        )
        self.conv2 = TransformerConv(
            heads * dim,
            dim,
            heads=1,
            concat=False,
            dropout=dropout,
            edge_features_dim=NUM_TYPES,
        )
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.decoder = EdgeTypeDecoder(dim)

    def __call__(self, n_id, edge_index, edge_types, batch_src, batch_dst):
        # n_id: the batch nodes and their recent neighbors; batch_src/dst: local ids
        e = EDGE_ONE_HOT[edge_types]
        h = self.proj(X[n_id])
        h = self.dropout(nn.relu(self.conv1(edge_index, h, e)))
        h = self.conv2(edge_index, h, e)
        return self.decoder(h[batch_src], h[batch_dst])

items.title: Mini-batches and neighborhoods
items.text:
The edges are processed in time order, in mini-batches of 1,024 edges that do not cross a 15-minute window. For Orthrus, Neighborhood asks the LastNeighborLoader for the recent neighbors of the batch's nodes, and maps the batch's edges to the local indexing of that subgraph. The batch's own edges are inserted into the loader only after the batch is processed, so the model never sees the type of an event before predicting it.

ETYPE = mx.array(etype.astype(np.int32))


def batches(mask):
    # Chronological batches of BATCH_SIZE edges that do not cross a 15-min window.
    idx = np.flatnonzero(mask)
    out = []
    for chunk in np.split(idx, np.flatnonzero(np.diff(window[idx])) + 1):
        out.extend(np.split(chunk, np.arange(BATCH_SIZE, chunk.size, BATCH_SIZE)))
    return out


class Neighborhood:
    # Recent neighborhood of the batches of a stream of edges.

    def __init__(self, stream):
        self.loader = LastNeighborLoader(num_nodes, size=20)
        self.stream = stream  # edge id of the i-th edge inserted in the loader
        self.assoc = np.zeros(num_nodes, dtype=np.int64)

    def __call__(self, b):
        n_id, edge_index, e_id = self.loader(
            np.unique(np.concatenate([src[b], dst[b]]))
        )
        self.assoc[np.array(n_id)] = np.arange(n_id.size)
        edge_types = ETYPE[mx.array(self.stream[np.array(e_id)].astype(np.int32))]

        def local(nodes):
            return mx.array(self.assoc[nodes].astype(np.int32))

        return n_id, edge_index, edge_types, local(src[b]), local(dst[b])

    def insert(self, b):
        self.loader.insert(src[b], dst[b])


def inputs(model, neighborhood, b):
    if isinstance(model, Orthrus):
        return neighborhood(b)
    return mx.array(src[b].astype(np.int32)), mx.array(dst[b].astype(np.int32))


def loss_fn(model, x, y):
    return nn.losses.cross_entropy(model(*x), y, reduction="mean")


def train_epoch(model, optimizer, train_batches):
    model.train()
    neighborhood = Neighborhood(np.concatenate(train_batches))
    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)
    total = 0.0
    for b in train_batches:
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(
            model, inputs(model, neighborhood, b), ETYPE[mx.array(b)]
        )
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state, loss)
        neighborhood.insert(b)
        total += loss.item() * b.size
    return total / sum(b.size for b in train_batches)


def edge_scores(model, all_batches):
    # Anomaly score (cross-entropy) of every edge, replaying the whole stream.
    model.eval()
    neighborhood = Neighborhood(np.concatenate(all_batches))
    scores = np.zeros(t.size, dtype=np.float32)
    for b in all_batches:
        logits = model(*inputs(model, neighborhood, b))
        loss = nn.losses.cross_entropy(logits, ETYPE[mx.array(b)], reduction="none")
        scores[b] = np.array(loss)
        neighborhood.insert(b)
    return scores


train_batches = batches(split == TRAIN)
all_batches = batches(np.ones(t.size, dtype=bool))
print(f"{len(train_batches):,} training batches, {len(all_batches):,} batches in total")

3,440 training batches, 6,051 batches in total

items.title: Training
items.text:
We train each model for 12 epochs with Adam, and time every epoch. After training, the whole stream (training, validation and test days, in time order) is replayed once to score every edge.

def run(name, seed=SEED):
    cfg = CONFIGS[name]
    mx.random.seed(seed)
    model = {"Velox": Velox, "Orthrus": Orthrus}[name](
        X.shape[1], cfg["dim"], cfg["dropout"]
    )
    optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=cfg["lr"], bias_correction=True)
    epoch_s = []
    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        loss = train_epoch(model, optimizer, train_batches)
        epoch_s.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
        print(f"{name} epoch {epoch:02d}  loss {loss:.4f}  {epoch_s[-1]:.1f} s")
    start = time.perf_counter()
    scores = edge_scores(model, all_batches)
    return dict(scores=scores, epoch_s=epoch_s, score_s=time.perf_counter() - start)


runs = {"Velox": run("Velox")}

items.title: Detection
items.text:
A node's anomaly score is the highest score of its test edges, as a source or a destination. The threshold is the highest edge score of the validation day: on a day without attacks, nothing should be flagged. The test nodes above the threshold are the alerts.

Besides the counts of true and false positives, we report the metrics of Bilot et al.:

  • precision and MCC of the alerts,
  • attacks detected: the number of attacks with at least one true positive. A security analyst who receives an alert on one malicious node can then trace the rest of the attack.
  • ADP (attack detection precision): the area under the curve of the percentage of attacks detected against the precision, when the threshold goes down the ranking. It is 1 when, for each attack, a malicious node is ranked above all benign nodes.

We also report the ROC AUC and the average precision of the node scores, which do not depend on the threshold.

test = split == TEST
test_nodes = np.unique(np.concatenate([src[test], dst[test]]))
y_true = np.isin(test_nodes, list(malicious))


def node_scores(scores):
    out = np.zeros(num_nodes, dtype=np.float32)
    np.maximum.at(out, src[test], scores[test])
    np.maximum.at(out, dst[test], scores[test])
    return out[test_nodes]


def adp(node_score):
    # Area under (precision, % of attacks detected) along the ranking.
    best = defaultdict(float, {0.0: 0.0})
    tp = fp = 0
    found = set()
    for k in np.argsort(-node_score, kind="stable"):
        node = test_nodes[k]
        if y_true[k]:
            tp += 1
            found |= {a for a, nodes in attack_nodes.items() if node in nodes}
        else:
            fp += 1
        precision = tp / (tp + fp)
        best[precision] = max(best[precision], len(found) / len(attack_nodes))
    xs = sorted(best)
    return float(np.trapezoid([best[x] for x in xs], xs))


def evaluate(scores):
    threshold = scores[split == VAL].max()
    node_score = node_scores(scores)
    y_pred = node_score > threshold
    tp, fp = int(np.sum(y_true & y_pred)), int(np.sum(~y_true & y_pred))
    fn, tn = int(np.sum(y_true & ~y_pred)), int(np.sum(~y_true & ~y_pred))
    denom = np.sqrt(float(tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn))
    flagged = set(test_nodes[y_pred])
    detected = sum(bool(nodes & flagged) for nodes in attack_nodes.values())
    return {
        "threshold": round(float(threshold), 2),
        "TP": tp,
        "FP": fp,
        "FN": fn,
        "precision": round(tp / max(tp + fp, 1), 3),
        "MCC": round((tp * tn - fp * fn) / denom if denom else 0.0, 3),
        "attacks detected": f"{detected}/{len(attack_nodes)}",
        "ADP": round(adp(node_score), 3),
        "ROC AUC": round(roc_auc_score(y_true, node_score), 3),
        "AP": round(average_precision_score(y_true, node_score), 3),
    }


print(f"{test_nodes.size:,} test nodes, {y_true.sum()} malicious")
results = pd.DataFrame({name: evaluate(r["scores"]) for name, r in runs.items()}).T
results

        f"threshold {threshold:.1f}",
        (order.size, threshold),
        xytext=(0, 4),
        textcoords="offset points",
        ha="right",
        va="bottom",
        color=INK,

    )
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_title(model, loc="left", color=INK)
    ax.set_xlabel("rank of the test node (log scale)", color=MUTED)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)

    for side in ("left", "bottom"):

axes[0].set_ylabel("node anomaly score", color=MUTED)

Both detectors find the three attacks. Velox raises 62 alerts, 39 of them on malicious nodes (precision 0.63), and ranks the April 12 attack first: the files /tmp/main and /tmp/test that the red team wrote, and the processes that ran them. The payload of April 6, /tmp/vUgefal, follows in its top 15. Orthrus raises 41 alerts, 24 of them malicious (precision 0.59). It ranks a benign sh shell and /etc/motd first, then nodes of the three attacks, such as the payloads /tmp/pEja72mA and /tmp/vUgefal, in ranks 3 to 8, hence an ADP of 0.75 against 0.965 for Velox. The other false positives near the top are benign processes and objects such as sshd sessions or a Unix socket.

About half of the malicious nodes stay below the threshold (recall 0.57 for Velox, 0.35 for Orthrus): they are nodes that the attacks used but whose events look ordinary. This is less of a problem than it seems. One alert per attack is enough for an analyst to start an investigation, and to trace the rest of the attack in the provenance graph.

These numbers vary from run to run: the order of the floating-point additions on the GPU changes the training of Orthrus slightly, and Bilot et al. report that PIDSs are unstable in general. In another run of this notebook, Orthrus ranked nodes of the three attacks first, with an ADP of 1. To measure the variation, train with several seeds with run(name, seed=...).

Runtime. On an Apple M5 Pro, Velox trains about 10 times faster than Orthrus (5.3 s against 50.4 s per epoch) and scores the whole stream in 3 s instead of 32 s, and its detection is at least as good. Orthrus does much more work per batch: it gathers the 20 latest neighbors of the batch's nodes from the LastNeighborLoader and runs an 8-head attention over them, where Velox multiplies the features of each node by one matrix. This is the finding of Bilot et al.: on these datasets, a model without message passing can match a graph neural network, at a fraction of the cost.
