items.title: Positional and structural encodings
items.text:
The CSL dataset (Circular Skip Links, Murphy et al., 2019) shows why encodings matter. Each of its 150 graphs is a cycle of 41 nodes, in which every node is also linked to the nodes \(s\) steps away, for one of 10 skip lengths \(s\). The class of a graph is its skip length.

csl = GNNBenchmarkDataset("CSL")
csl_labels = np.array([int(g.graph_labels.item()) for g in csl.graphs])
print(csl, csl[0], sep="\n")
print("nodes per graph:", {g.num_nodes for g in csl.graphs})
degrees = {int(d) for g in csl.graphs for d in np.array(degree(g.edge_index[0]))}
print("degrees:", degrees)
print("graphs per class:", np.bincount(csl_labels))

Loading CSL data ... Done
CSL(num_graphs=150)
GraphData(
    edge_index(shape=(2, 164), int32)
    graph_labels(shape=(1,), int32))
nodes per graph: {41}
degrees: {4}
graphs per class: [15 15 15 15 15 15 15 15 15 15]

All the graphs have 41 nodes of degree 4 and no node features. An MPNN starts with the same features on every node, and since all the neighborhoods look the same, every layer computes the same embedding for every node of every graph: it cannot tell the classes apart. (These graphs are indistinguishable by the 1-WL test, which bounds the power of MPNNs.)

mlx-graphs has two transforms that add encodings to the graphs. They compute them on the host with NumPy, once per graph, so they are best used as a pre_transform:

  • AddRandomWalkPE(k) adds the random-walk structural encoding (RWSE): for every node, the probability of being back at the start after \(1, \ldots, k\) steps of a random walk. It describes the neighborhood of a node (cycles, branching) and is the same for nodes with the same surroundings.
  • AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE(k) adds the Laplacian eigenvector positional encoding (LapPE): the \(k\) eigenvectors of the normalized graph Laplacian with the smallest non-trivial eigenvalues. They are the graph's analog of the sine waves of a sequence transformer: they give each node a coordinate.

Let's compute both on CSL.

rwse = AddRandomWalkPE(WALK_LENGTH)
lappe = AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE(k=4, is_undirected=True)
csl_pe = [lappe(rwse(g)) for g in csl.graphs]

first_of_class = [int(np.where(csl_labels == c)[0][0]) for c in range(10)]
rw = np.stack([np.array(csl_pe[i].random_walk_pe) for i in first_of_class])
print("std of the RWSE over the nodes of each graph:", rw.std(axis=1).max().round(6))
signatures = np.unique(rw[:, 0].round(5), axis=0)
print(f"distinct RWSE signatures: {len(signatures)} for 10 classes")
print("return probability after 1-8 steps (node 0, one graph per class):")
print(rw[:, 0, :8].round(3))

std of the RWSE over the nodes of each graph: 0.0
distinct RWSE signatures: 10 for 10 classes
return probability after 1-8 steps (node 0, one graph per class):
[[0.    0.25  0.094 0.141 0.098 0.105 0.09  0.088]
 [0.    0.25  0.    0.172 0.    0.142 0.    0.123]
 [0.    0.25  0.    0.141 0.01  0.098 0.018 0.075]
 [0.    0.25  0.    0.141 0.    0.101 0.    0.082]
 [0.    0.25  0.    0.141 0.    0.098 0.001 0.075]

 [0.    0.25  0.    0.141 0.    0.098 0.004 0.075]

All the nodes of a CSL graph have the same RWSE, because every node has the same surroundings. Across classes, however, the return probabilities differ: the skip length changes the cycles that a walk can close. With RWSE as input features, a model can classify the graphs, which an MPNN without encodings cannot. Several skip lengths only differ after a few steps, which is why the walk length matters: with 20 steps, the 10 classes have 10 distinct signatures.

LapPE, on the other hand, gives every node its own coordinates:

print(np.array(csl_pe[0].laplacian_eigenvector_pe[:5]).round(3))

items.title: Encoders: RWSEEncoder and LapPEEncoder
items.text:
A GPS model projects the encodings to a few channels and concatenates them with the embeddings of the node features. mlx-graphs provides two such projections:

  • RWSEEncoder(pe_dim, out_dim) normalizes the RWSE (batch norm by default) and applies a linear layer. It is the pe_norm + pe_lin of PyG's GPS example.
  • LapPEEncoder(pe_dim, out_dim) does the same for LapPE, with one extra step. An eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}\) is only defined up to its sign: \(-\mathbf{u}\) is just as valid, and the eigensolver picks one at random. So, during training, LapPEEncoder flips the sign of every eigenvector of every graph at random at each call, which teaches the model not to depend on it. In evaluation mode, it does not flip anything.
lap_encoder = LapPEEncoder(pe_dim=4, out_features_dim=PE_DIM)
pe = csl_pe[0].laplacian_eigenvector_pe

for mode in ["train", "eval"]:
    lap_encoder.train(mode == "train")
    same = mx.allclose(lap_encoder(pe), lap_encoder(pe)).item()
    print(f"{mode} mode, two calls give the same output: {same}")

rw_encoder = RWSEEncoder(WALK_LENGTH, PE_DIM)
print("projected RWSE:", rw_encoder(csl_pe[0].random_walk_pe).shape)

train mode, two calls give the same output: False
eval mode, two calls give the same output: True
projected RWSE: (41, 8)

When the encoder receives the batch_indices of a batch, each graph gets its own random signs. In short: use RWSE (AddRandomWalkPE + RWSEEncoder) when the local structure matters, as in molecules; it is cheap and needs no sign handling. Use LapPE (AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE + LapPEEncoder) for a global position of the nodes; it needs an eigendecomposition per graph. They can also be combined. Our Peptides-func model uses RWSE, as PyG's example.

items.title: The GPS model in mlx-graphs
items.text:
The model has four parts:

  • Input embeddings. FeatureEncoder sums one nn.Embedding per categorical feature, as OGB's AtomEncoder and BondEncoder. Atoms are embedded into CHANNELS - PE_DIM channels, and the projected RWSE fill the last PE_DIM channels. Bonds are embedded into CHANNELS channels.
  • GPS layers. Each GPSConv wraps a local GINEConv, which uses the bond embeddings, and adds a 4-head global attention with dropout 0.5 on the attention weights. Batch normalization and the MLP are built in.
  • Readout. global_mean_pool averages the nodes of every graph.
  • Head. A 3-layer MLP gives the logits of the 10 functions.

GPSConv lays out the nodes of each graph into a dense [num_graphs, max_nodes, channels] array for the attention, with a mask for the padding. The optional layout argument is used in the mx.compile section below.

class FeatureEncoder(nn.Module):
    """Sum of one embedding per categorical feature, initialized as
    torch.nn.Embedding (N(0, 1))."""

    def __init__(self, vocab_sizes, dims):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = [nn.Embedding(size, dims) for size in vocab_sizes]
        for embedding in self.embeddings:
            embedding.weight = mx.random.normal(embedding.weight.shape)

    def __call__(self, features):
        return sum(emb(features[:, i]) for i, emb in enumerate(self.embeddings))


class GPS(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, atom_vocab, bond_vocab, attn_type="multihead"):
        super().__init__()
        self.node_emb = FeatureEncoder(atom_vocab, CHANNELS - PE_DIM)
        self.pe_encoder = RWSEEncoder(WALK_LENGTH, PE_DIM)
        self.edge_emb = FeatureEncoder(bond_vocab, CHANNELS)
        if attn_type == "multihead":
            attn_kwargs = {"dropout": ATTN_DROPOUT}
        else:
            attn_kwargs = {"head_channels": CHANNELS // HEADS}
        self.convs = []
        for _ in range(NUM_LAYERS):
            mlp = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS)
            )
            self.convs.append(
                GPSConv(
                    CHANNELS,
                    GINEConv(mlp),
                    heads=HEADS,
                    attn_type=attn_type,
                    attn_kwargs=attn_kwargs,
                )
            )
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS // 2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(CHANNELS // 2, CHANNELS // 4),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(CHANNELS // 4, 10),
        )

    def __call__(
        self, node_features, pe, edge_index, edge_features, batch_indices, num_graphs,
        layout=None,
    ):  # fmt: skip
        x = mx.concatenate([self.node_emb(node_features), self.pe_encoder(pe)], 1)
        edge_features = self.edge_emb(edge_features)
        for conv in self.convs:
            x = conv(edge_index, x, batch_indices, layout, edge_features=edge_features)
        x = global_mean_pool(x, batch_indices, num_graphs)
        return self.mlp(x)


def inputs(batch):
    return (
        batch.node_features,
        batch.random_walk_pe,
        batch.edge_index,
        batch.edge_features,
        batch.batch_indices,
        batch.num_graphs,
    )


def vocab_sizes(attr):
    """Number of categories of every column of a categorical feature."""
    graphs = [g for ds in datasets.values() for g in ds.graphs]
    return (np.max([np.array(getattr(g, attr)).max(0) for g in graphs], 0) + 1).tolist()


atom_vocab, bond_vocab = vocab_sizes("node_features"), vocab_sizes("edge_features")
mlx_model = GPS(atom_vocab, bond_vocab)
mx.eval(mlx_model.parameters())
num_params = sum(v.size for _, v in tree_flatten(mlx_model.trainable_parameters()))
print(f"atom vocabularies {atom_vocab}, bond vocabularies {bond_vocab}")
print(f"{num_params:,} trainable parameters")

atom vocabularies [17, 3, 7, 7, 5, 1, 6, 2, 2], bond vocabularies [4, 1, 2]
173,914 trainable parameters

items.title: Training with mlx-graphs
items.text:
Peptides-func is a multi-label task: each peptide can have several of the 10 functions. The loss is the binary cross-entropy of the 10 logits, and the metric is the average precision (AP) of every function, averaged over the functions, as in OGB and LRGB.

Two details matter when porting PyG training code to MLX:

  • torch.optim.Adam corrects the bias of its moment estimates, which are initialized at zero. mlx.optimizers.Adam does not by default: pass bias_correction=True to get the same update rule. Without it, the first updates are about 3 times larger, as the cell below shows.
  • torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=...) adds an L2 penalty to the gradients. With MLX, we add it to the gradients ourselves.
grad = {"w": mx.array([0.1])}
for bias_correction in [False, True]:
    opt = optim.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3, bias_correction=bias_correction)
    params = {"w": mx.array([1.0])}
    steps = []
    for _ in range(3):
        new = opt.apply_gradients(grad, params)
        steps.append(f"{(params['w'] - new['w']).item():.2e}")
        params = new
    print(f"bias_correction={bias_correction}: first updates {steps}")

bias_correction=False: first updates ['3.16e-03', '4.25e-03', '4.95e-03']
bias_correction=True: first updates ['1.00e-03', '1.00e-03', '1.00e-03']

The training loop computes the loss and its gradients with nn.value_and_grad, adds the L2 penalty, and updates the weights. mx.eval then runs the lazy computation of the step. We time the training and the evaluation (on the validation and test sets) separately. We train for 8 epochs only, to keep the whole notebook under 20 minutes; the GPS paper trains for 200 epochs.

def average_precision(labels, scores):
    """Mean over tasks of the average precision (as OGB / LRGB's eval_ap),
    skipping tasks without both positive and negative labels."""
    aps = []
    for task in range(labels.shape[1]):
        y, s = labels[:, task], scores[:, task]
        if y.min() == y.max():
            continue
        y = y[np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")]
        precision = np.cumsum(y) / np.arange(1, y.size + 1)
        aps.append((precision * y).sum() / y.sum())
    return float(np.mean(aps))


def mlx_loss_fn(model, batch):
    logits = model(*inputs(batch))
    return nn.losses.binary_cross_entropy(
        logits, batch.graph_labels, with_logits=True, reduction="mean"
    )


def mlx_train_epoch(model, optimizer, loader):
    model.train()
    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, mlx_loss_fn)
    total_loss, total_graphs = 0.0, 0
    for batch in loader:
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model, batch)
        grads = tree_map(
            lambda g, p: g + WEIGHT_DECAY * p, grads, model.trainable_parameters()
        )
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state, loss)
        total_loss += loss.item() * batch.num_graphs
        total_graphs += batch.num_graphs
    return total_loss / total_graphs


def mlx_evaluate(model, loader):
    model.eval()
    labels, scores = [], []
    for batch in loader:
        scores.append(np.array(model(*inputs(batch))))
        labels.append(np.array(batch.graph_labels))
    return average_precision(np.concatenate(labels), np.concatenate(scores))


def run_epochs(train_epoch, evaluate):
    history = []
    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        loss = train_epoch()
        train_s = time.perf_counter() - start
        start = time.perf_counter()
        val_ap, test_ap = evaluate()
        eval_s = time.perf_counter() - start
        history.append(
            dict(epoch=epoch, loss=loss, val_ap=val_ap, test_ap=test_ap,
                 train_s=train_s, eval_s=eval_s)
        )  # fmt: skip
        print(
            f"Epoch {epoch:02d}  loss {loss:.4f}  val AP {val_ap:.4f}  "
            f"test AP {test_ap:.4f}  train {train_s:.1f} s  eval {eval_s:.1f} s"
        )
    return history


train_loader = Dataloader(datasets["train"], BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
val_loader = Dataloader(datasets["val"], EVAL_BATCH_SIZE)
test_loader = Dataloader(datasets["test"], EVAL_BATCH_SIZE)
# bias_correction=True gives the update rule of torch.optim.Adam
mlx_optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=LR, bias_correction=True)

mlx_history = run_epochs(
    lambda: mlx_train_epoch(mlx_model, mlx_optimizer, train_loader),
    lambda: (mlx_evaluate(mlx_model, val_loader), mlx_evaluate(mlx_model, test_loader)),
)

PyG's example also halves the learning rate when the validation AP has not improved for 20 epochs (ReduceLROnPlateau). We leave it out, as it cannot trigger in 8 epochs.

Thanks to the cache limit set at the beginning, MLX keeps at most 1 GB of freed buffers for reuse:

print(f"MLX buffer cache: {mx.get_cache_memory() / 1024**3:.2f} GB, "
      f"peak memory: {mx.get_peak_memory() / 1024**3:.2f} GB")  # fmt: skip

MLX buffer cache: 1.00 GB, peak memory: 1.92 GB

items.title: Attention variants: multi-head vs Performer
items.text:
Before comparing with PyG, let's look at two features of GPSConv that matter for speed. GPSConv supports two global attentions, chosen with attn_type:

  • "multihead" (mlx_graphs.nn.attention.MultiheadAttention) is the standard softmax attention. It is exact, but its cost grows with the square of the number of nodes of the largest graph in the batch.
  • "performer" (mlx_graphs.nn.attention.PerformerAttention, Choromanski et al., 2021) approximates the attention with random features, which avoids the \(N \times N\) attention matrix: its cost is linear in the number of nodes. Call redraw_projection_matrix() on the layer to draw new random features from time to time, as PyG's example does.

Let's time one GPSConv layer (attention only, conv=None, in evaluation mode) with each attention, on batches of 8,192 nodes made of graphs of increasing size, and record the peak memory of MLX.

def time_forward(module, *args, repeats=10):
    for _ in range(3):  # warm-up
        mx.eval(module(*args))
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        mx.eval(module(*args))
    return (time.perf_counter() - start) / repeats * 1000


no_edges = mx.zeros((2, 0), dtype=mx.int32)
timings = []
for graph_size in [128, 512, 2048, 4096]:
    num_graphs = 8192 // graph_size
    batch_indices = mx.repeat(mx.arange(num_graphs), graph_size)
    x = mx.random.normal((8192, CHANNELS))
    row = {"nodes per graph": graph_size, "graphs": num_graphs}
    for attn_type, kwargs in [
        ("multihead", {}),
        ("performer", {"head_channels": CHANNELS // HEADS}),
    ]:
        layer = GPSConv(CHANNELS, None, heads=HEADS, attn_type=attn_type,
                        attn_kwargs=kwargs)  # fmt: skip
        layer.eval()
        mx.reset_peak_memory()
        milliseconds = time_forward(layer, no_edges, x, batch_indices)
        row[f"{attn_type} (ms)"] = round(milliseconds, 2)
        row[f"{attn_type} peak (MB)"] = round(mx.get_peak_memory() / 1024**2)
    timings.append(row)
pd.DataFrame(timings).set_index("nodes per graph")
graphs multihead (ms) multihead peak (MB) performer (ms) performer peak (MB) nodes per graph 128 64 2.00 396 1.78 398 512 16 2.82 444 0.92 398 2048 4 9.42 636 0.95 397 4096 2 18.43 892 0.99 397

With the same number of nodes per batch, the multi-head attention gets slower and needs more memory as the graphs grow: its cost is proportional to the sum of the squared graph sizes. The time and peak memory of the Performer stay flat. (The peak memory also counts the arrays that were already allocated, such as the datasets.) For graphs of a few hundred nodes, like the peptides, both are fast, and the exact attention is the usual choice. The Performer pays off for graphs of thousands of nodes, or when the memory of the attention is the bottleneck. Its approximation can cost some accuracy, so compare both on your task.

The Peptides-func model can switch to the Performer with GPS(atom_vocab, bond_vocab, attn_type="performer").

items.title: mx.compile with a precomputed layout
items.text:
To run the dense attention, GPSConv needs to know which nodes belong to which graph, and how large the largest graph is. By default, it computes this layout from batch_indices on the host, in every layer. Reading batch_indices back from the GPU forces MLX to stop and evaluate the pending computation, a GPU synchronization, and it makes the layer impossible to trace with mx.compile, which needs functions of arrays only.

GPSConv (and SGFormer and Polynormer) accept a precomputed layout, a DenseLayout:

  • DenseLayout(batch_indices, num_nodes) computes it on the host, once per batch instead of once per layer;
  • DenseLayout.from_sizes(batch_indices, num_nodes, num_graphs, max_num_nodes) builds it on the device, from the number of graphs and an upper bound of the graph size. There is no synchronization, and it works inside mx.compile.

A larger max_num_nodes only adds padding, which the masked multi-head attention ignores, so the outputs are the same, up to floating-point rounding:

batch = next(iter(Dataloader(datasets["train"], BATCH_SIZE)))
num_nodes, num_graphs = batch.num_nodes, batch.num_graphs
max_num_nodes = int(sizes.max())  # largest peptide of the dataset
layout = DenseLayout.from_sizes(
    batch.batch_indices, num_nodes, num_graphs, max_num_nodes
)
mlx_model.eval()
default_out = mlx_model(*inputs(batch))
layout_out = mlx_model(*inputs(batch), layout=layout)
difference = mx.abs(default_out - layout_out).max().item()
print(f"largest difference between the logits: {difference:.1e}")

largest difference between the logits: 0.0e+00

Now let's compile a full training step: forward, backward, L2 penalty and Adam update. The model, the optimizer state and the random state (for the dropout) are passed to mx.compile as implicit inputs and outputs. We time four versions of the step on the same batch, each with a fresh model: the default layout, a DenseLayout built once per batch on the host, a layout built from sizes on the device, and the same compiled. The bound max_num_nodes is the size of the largest peptide of the dataset, so that this layout is valid for any batch of 32 graphs.

from functools import partial


def make_step(model, optimizer, layout_type, compiled=False):
    def loss_fn(model, x, pe, edge_index, edge_features, batch_indices, labels):
        layout = None  # default: computed on the host by every layer
        if layout_type == "host":  # on the host, once per batch
            layout = DenseLayout(batch_indices, x.shape[0])
        elif layout_type == "sizes":  # on the device, from constant sizes
            layout = DenseLayout.from_sizes(
                batch_indices, x.shape[0], num_graphs, max_num_nodes
            )
        logits = model(x, pe, edge_index, edge_features, batch_indices, num_graphs,
                       layout)  # fmt: skip
        return nn.losses.binary_cross_entropy(logits, labels, with_logits=True)

    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)

    def step(*arrays):
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model, *arrays)
        grads = tree_map(
            lambda g, p: g + WEIGHT_DECAY * p, grads, model.trainable_parameters()
        )
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        return loss

    if compiled:
        state = [model.state, optimizer.state, mx.random.state]
        step = partial(mx.compile, inputs=state, outputs=state)(step)
    return step


arrays = (
    batch.node_features,
    batch.random_walk_pe,
    batch.edge_index,
    batch.edge_features,
    batch.batch_indices,
    batch.graph_labels,
)
step_times = {}
for label, layout_type, compiled in [
    ("default (layout in every layer)", None, False),
    ("DenseLayout once per batch", "host", False),
    ("DenseLayout.from_sizes", "sizes", False),
    ("DenseLayout.from_sizes + mx.compile", "sizes", True),
]:
    mx.random.seed(SEED)
    model = GPS(atom_vocab, bond_vocab)
    optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=LR, bias_correction=True)
    model.train()
    step = make_step(model, optimizer, layout_type, compiled)
    for _ in range(3):  # warm-up (and compilation)
        mx.eval(step(*arrays), model.parameters(), optimizer.state)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(20):
        mx.eval(step(*arrays), model.parameters(), optimizer.state)
    step_times[label] = (time.perf_counter() - start) / 20 * 1000
    print(f"{label:36s} {step_times[label]:6.1f} ms per step")

default (layout in every layer)        78.0 ms per step
DenseLayout once per batch             76.7 ms per step
DenseLayout.from_sizes                 97.6 ms per step
DenseLayout.from_sizes + mx.compile    72.8 ms per step

Building the layout once per batch instead of in every layer changes little here, because the step is dominated by the work on the GPU. The layout from sizes alone is slower: the dense arrays are padded to the largest peptide of the dataset instead of the largest graph of the batch, so the attention does more work. Compiling the step makes it the fastest of the four (see the times printed above): mx.compile fuses the elementwise operations of the step into fewer GPU kernels, and skips the construction of the computation graph at every call.

One caveat: mx.compile traces the function for the shapes it receives. Every batch of Peptides-func has a different number of nodes and edges, so a compiled step would be traced again for almost every batch, which costs more than it saves. To benefit from compilation in a full training loop, pad the batches to a few fixed sizes (buckets), so that the same compiled graphs are reused.

items.title: The same model in PyG
items.text:
The PyG version uses PyG's own GPSConv, GINEConv and global_mean_pool, with the same architecture and hyperparameters. To train both frameworks on exactly the same data, we convert the mlx-graphs graphs, with their RWSE, into PyG Data objects. (PyG's LRGBDataset with the AddRandomWalkPE transform gives the same graphs and encodings.)

PyG runs on the CPU here. PyG's GPSConv relies on many small indexing and scatter operations, for which the CPU is a better choice than the MPS backend.

import torch
from torch.nn import BatchNorm1d, Embedding, Linear, ModuleList, ReLU, Sequential
from torch_geometric.data import Data
from torch_geometric.loader import DataLoader as PyGDataLoader
from torch_geometric.nn import GINEConv as PyGGINEConv
from torch_geometric.nn import GPSConv as PyGGPSConv
from torch_geometric.nn import global_mean_pool as pyg_global_mean_pool

torch.manual_seed(SEED)
# Release the buffers that MLX keeps for reuse, for PyTorch to use them.
mx.clear_cache()


def to_pyg(dataset):
    def tensor(array, dtype):
        return torch.from_numpy(np.array(array)).to(dtype)

    return [
        Data(
            x=tensor(g.node_features, torch.long),
            edge_index=tensor(g.edge_index, torch.long),
            edge_attr=tensor(g.edge_features, torch.long),
            y=tensor(g.graph_labels, torch.float),
            pe=tensor(g.random_walk_pe, torch.float),
        )
        for g in dataset
    ]


pyg_data = {split: to_pyg(dataset) for split, dataset in datasets.items()}
print(pyg_data["train"][0])

Data(x=[338, 9], edge_index=[2, 682], edge_attr=[682, 3], y=[1, 10], pe=[338, 20])

class PyGFeatureEncoder(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_sizes, dims):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = ModuleList([Embedding(v, dims) for v in vocab_sizes])

    def forward(self, features):
        return sum(emb(features[:, i]) for i, emb in enumerate(self.embeddings))


class PyGGPS(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, atom_vocab, bond_vocab):
        super().__init__()
        self.node_emb = PyGFeatureEncoder(atom_vocab, CHANNELS - PE_DIM)
        self.pe_norm = BatchNorm1d(WALK_LENGTH)
        self.pe_lin = Linear(WALK_LENGTH, PE_DIM)
        self.edge_emb = PyGFeatureEncoder(bond_vocab, CHANNELS)
        self.convs = ModuleList()
        for _ in range(NUM_LAYERS):
            mlp = Sequential(
                Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS), ReLU(), Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS)
            )
            conv = PyGGPSConv(
                CHANNELS,
                PyGGINEConv(mlp),
                heads=HEADS,
                attn_type="multihead",
                attn_kwargs={"dropout": ATTN_DROPOUT},
            )
            self.convs.append(conv)
        self.mlp = Sequential(
            Linear(CHANNELS, CHANNELS // 2),
            ReLU(),
            Linear(CHANNELS // 2, CHANNELS // 4),
            ReLU(),
            Linear(CHANNELS // 4, 10),
        )

    def forward(self, x, pe, edge_index, edge_attr, batch):
        x = torch.cat([self.node_emb(x), self.pe_lin(self.pe_norm(pe))], 1)
        edge_attr = self.edge_emb(edge_attr)
        for conv in self.convs:
            x = conv(x, edge_index, batch, edge_attr=edge_attr)
        return self.mlp(pyg_global_mean_pool(x, batch))


pyg_model = PyGGPS(atom_vocab, bond_vocab)
pyg_params = sum(p.numel() for p in pyg_model.parameters())
print(f"{pyg_params:,} trainable parameters (mlx-graphs: {num_params:,})")

173,914 trainable parameters (mlx-graphs: 173,914)

Both models have the same number of trainable parameters. The training loop is the usual PyG one.

pyg_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
    pyg_model.parameters(), lr=LR, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY
)
criterion = torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
pyg_train_loader = PyGDataLoader(pyg_data["train"], BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
pyg_val_loader = PyGDataLoader(pyg_data["val"], EVAL_BATCH_SIZE)
pyg_test_loader = PyGDataLoader(pyg_data["test"], EVAL_BATCH_SIZE)


def pyg_train_epoch():
    pyg_model.train()
    total_loss, total_graphs = 0.0, 0
    for data in pyg_train_loader:
        pyg_optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = pyg_model(data.x, data.pe, data.edge_index, data.edge_attr, data.batch)
        loss = criterion(out, data.y)
        loss.backward()
        pyg_optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item() * data.num_graphs
        total_graphs += data.num_graphs
    return total_loss / total_graphs


@torch.no_grad()
def pyg_evaluate(loader):
    pyg_model.eval()
    labels, scores = [], []
    for data in loader:
        out = pyg_model(data.x, data.pe, data.edge_index, data.edge_attr, data.batch)
        scores.append(out.numpy())
        labels.append(data.y.numpy())
    return average_precision(np.concatenate(labels), np.concatenate(scores))

Accuracy. After 8 epochs, both models are early in their training: the test AP is still rising, and it jumps from one epoch to the next, as does the validation AP used to select the model. The two frameworks end in the same range, and the gap between them is of the order of these fluctuations. The mlx-graphs run is also not exactly reproducible on the GPU, so two runs with the same seed differ slightly. Comparing final accuracies would need a much longer training: the GPS paper trains for 200 epochs. For an exact check, benchmarks/gps_peptides/grad_parity.py in the mlx-graphs repository copies the weights of the PyG model into the mlx-graphs model, and finds the same loss and the same gradients, up to the precision of GPU matrix products.

Runtime. These timings were measured on an Apple M5 Pro, with mlx-graphs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU (6 threads). mlx-graphs is faster than PyG at both training and evaluation (see the speedups printed above). Timings vary from run to run and from machine to machine, so run the notebook on your own machine to compare.

items.title: Scalable graph transformers: SGFormer and Polynormer
items.text:
GPS attends over all the nodes of each graph, which suits many small graphs. For node classification on one large graph, quadratic attention is out of reach, and mlx-graphs provides two models with linear global attention, as PyG:

  • SGFormer (Wu et al., 2023) adds a single linear attention branch (SGFormerAttention) to a GCN branch, and combines them with a weight graph_weight.
  • Polynormer (Deng et al., 2024) stacks local layers (GCN, or GAT with local_attn=True) and global linear attention layers (PolynormerAttention) that build polynomial functions of the input features. It is trained in two phases: the local layers first, then the global layers, enabled with model._global = True.

Both take (edge_index, node_features) and return log-probabilities per node. We train them on Cora (2,708 papers, 7 classes, 140 training labels), with a GCN as a baseline, and report the test accuracy at the epoch of the best validation accuracy.

cora = PlanetoidDataset("cora")[0]
labels = cora.node_labels
split_idx = {
    name: mx.array(np.where(np.array(getattr(cora, f"{name}_mask")))[0])
    for name in ["train", "val", "test"]
}


def accuracy(model, split):
    pred = model(cora.edge_index, cora.node_features).argmax(-1)
    return (pred[split_idx[split]] == labels[split_idx[split]]).mean().item()


def train_node_classifier(model, epochs=200, warmup=None, lr=0.01, wd=5e-4):
    optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=lr, bias_correction=True)
    idx = split_idx["train"]

    def loss_fn(model):
        # SGFormer and Polynormer return log-probabilities, the GCN logits:
        # log_softmax gives log-probabilities in both cases
        log_probs = nn.log_softmax(model(cora.edge_index, cora.node_features)[idx])
        return -mx.take_along_axis(log_probs, labels[idx, None], 1).mean()

    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)
    global_part = []
    if warmup is not None:  # Polynormer: train the local layers first
        global_part = [*model.global_attn, model.ln, model.pred_global]
        for module in global_part:
            module.freeze()
    best_val, best_test, start = 0.0, 0.0, time.perf_counter()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        if epoch == warmup:  # then enable the global attention
            model._global = True
            for module in global_part:
                module.unfreeze()
            optimizer.init(model.trainable_parameters())
        model.train()
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model)
        grads = tree_map(lambda g, p: g + wd * p, grads, model.trainable_parameters())
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state)
        model.eval()
        val_acc = accuracy(model, "val")
        if val_acc > best_val:
            best_val, best_test = val_acc, accuracy(model, "test")
    return dict(val_acc=round(best_val, 3), test_acc=round(best_test, 3),
                seconds=round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1))  # fmt: skip


num_features, num_classes = cora.node_features.shape[1], 7
results = {}
mx.random.seed(SEED)
gcn = GCN(num_features, 64, 2, num_classes, dropout=0.5)
results["GCN"] = train_node_classifier(gcn)
mx.random.seed(SEED)
results["SGFormer"] = train_node_classifier(SGFormer(num_features, 64, num_classes))
mx.random.seed(SEED)
polynormer = Polynormer(num_features, 64, num_classes, local_layers=3, global_layers=2)
results["Polynormer"] = train_node_classifier(polynormer, warmup=100)
pd.DataFrame(results).T

Loading cora data ... Done
val_acc test_acc seconds GCN 0.794 0.801 0.3 SGFormer 0.656 0.655 1.3 Polynormer 0.742 0.753 1.3

On Cora, the GCN baseline is the most accurate of the three. Cora is a small citation graph with only 140 labels, in which linked papers usually share their class: the neighbors carry most of the signal, and the global attention mostly adds parameters that can overfit. (PyG's SGFormer and Polynormer reach similar accuracies with these settings.) The two models are designed for large graphs, such as ogbn-arxiv or ogbn-products, on which their linear attention scales to millions of nodes, since it never builds an \(N \times N\) matrix; the code above runs on them unchanged.

As a rule of thumb, use GPSConv for datasets of many small graphs, SGFormer for a simple scalable baseline on a large graph, and Polynormer for a more expressive model on a large graph, at the cost of a two-phase training.

The Polynormer warm-up shows a difference between MLX and PyTorch to keep in mind. During the warm-up, the global layers are not used. PyTorch leaves their .grad at None, and torch.optim.Adam skips them. MLX returns zero gradients for them instead, and an L2 penalty added to the gradients would then let Adam shrink them toward zero at every step, as if they were trained to vanish. So we freeze() them during the warm-up, then unfreeze() them and initialize their optimizer state with optimizer.init(...).

items.title: Practical tips
items.text:
• Adam. Use optim.Adam(..., bias_correction=True) to get the update rule of torch.optim.Adam, and add weight_decay * p to the gradients for its L2 penalty.
  • Unused parameters. MLX gives zero gradients to parameters that do not take part in the loss, where PyTorch skips them. Freeze such parameters if a penalty or a momentum could move them.
  • Buffer cache. Batches of graphs have different shapes, so MLX can rarely reuse its freed buffers, and its cache can grow to many GB. Bound it with mx.set_cache_limit(...) (1 GB here), and release it with mx.clear_cache() before another framework runs in the same process.
  • Encodings. Compute the PE/SE once, as a pre_transform of the dataset: they are computed on the host with NumPy and saved with the processed graphs.
  • Layouts and compilation. Build a DenseLayout once per batch instead of once per layer, and use DenseLayout.from_sizes(...) to compile a step with mx.compile, with padded batch sizes.
  • Attention. Keep attn_type="multihead" for graphs of up to a few thousand nodes, and switch to "performer", SGFormer or Polynormer beyond.

items.title: Going further
items.text:
• examples/graph_gps_peptides.py is a command-line version of the GPS part of this tutorial, with the learning rate schedule of PyG's example. Train it for more epochs: the GPS paper trains for 200 epochs, with a tuned configuration.
  • Peptides-struct uses the same graphs with 11 regression targets: load it with LRGBDataset("peptides-struct") and replace the loss with the mean absolute error.
  • Add LapPE to the model: Compose([AddRandomWalkPE(20), AddLaplacianEigenvectorPE(8)]) as the pre_transform, and a LapPEEncoder next to the RWSEEncoder, called with the batch_indices.
  • Replace the local GINEConv with another layer (e.g. GATConv), or pass conv=None for a pure transformer. GPSConv also supports other normalizations (norm="layer_norm", "graph_norm", ...).

items.title: Heterogeneous graphs with to_hetero: mlx-graphs vs PyG
items.text:
View on GitHub Download notebook

Many real graphs connect different kinds of entities. A bibliography links authors to the papers they write, papers to the terms they use and to the conferences where they appear. Such a graph is heterogeneous: every node has a node type (author, paper, ...), every edge an edge type written as a (source type, relation, destination type) triple, and each node type has its own features, with its own size. A homogeneous GNN layer has a single weight matrix for all nodes, so it cannot use them directly.

mlx-graphs offers the same tools as PyTorch Geometric (PyG) for such graphs:

Tool What it is for HeteroGraphData stores a heterogeneous graph, with dicts keyed by node type and by edge type to_hetero turns a homogeneous model (GraphSAGE, GAT, or your own in the PyG style) into a heterogeneous one, with one copy of every layer per node type and per edge type to_hetero_with_bases the same with a basis decomposition, which keeps the parameter count low when there are many edge types HeteroConv, HeteroDictLinear, HGTConv, HANConv heterogeneous layers to write a model by hand NeighborLoader, HGTLoader mini-batches of sampled subgraphs, for graphs too large for full-batch training

This tutorial goes through them on the DBLP bibliography, where the task is to classify authors into four research areas. Its backbone is to_hetero: we convert a GraphSAGE and a GAT, train them with mlx-graphs, train the same models with PyG on the same data, and compare their test accuracy and time per epoch. The other tools follow, each with a short demo.

The PyG part needs a few extra dependencies:

pip install torch torch_geometric pandas matplotlib

import time
import warnings

import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from mlx.utils import tree_flatten

from mlx_graphs.datasets import DBLP
from mlx_graphs.loaders import HGTLoader, NeighborLoader
from mlx_graphs.nn import (
    GATConv,
    GraphSAGE,
    HANConv,
    HeteroConv,
    HeteroDictLinear,
    HGTConv,
    SAGEConv,
    to_hetero,
    to_hetero_with_bases,
)

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
# PyG uses torch.jit.script, which recent PyTorch versions flag as deprecated

# Hyperparameters, shared by mlx-graphs and PyG

HEADS = 8  # GAT attention heads

LR = 0.005
WEIGHT_DECAY = 0.001
EPOCHS = 100  # full-batch epochs
SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
MINI_BATCH_EPOCHS = 50

items.title: 1. HeteroGraphData in a nutshell
items.text:
Before loading DBLP, let us build a tiny graph by hand: 3 authors with 2 features each, 4 papers with 3 features each, a writes relation from authors to papers and a cites relation between papers. Every attribute that depends on the type is a dict: node_features_dict is keyed by node type, edge_index_dict by edge type, and each edge index holds the local ids of the nodes within their own type.

toy = HeteroGraphData(
    edge_index_dict={
        ("author", "writes", "paper"): mx.array([[0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 1, 3]]),
        ("paper", "cites", "paper"): mx.array([[1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 2]]),
    },
    node_features_dict={
        "author": mx.random.normal((3, 2)),
        "paper": mx.random.normal((4, 3)),
    },
)
print(toy)
print("node types:", toy.node_types)
print("edge types:", toy.edge_types)
print("nodes:", toy.num_nodes, "| features:", toy.num_node_features)

HeteroGraphData(
node_features(
  'author': (shape=(3, 2), float32),
  'paper': (shape=(4, 3), float32),
)
 edge_index(
  'author -> writes -> paper':(shape=(2, 4), int32),
  'paper -> cites -> paper':(shape=(2, 3), int32),
)
 edge_labels_index_dict(

node types: ['author', 'paper']
edge types: [('author', 'writes', 'paper'), ('paper', 'cites', 'paper')]
nodes: {'author': 3, 'paper': 4} | features: {'author': 2, 'paper': 3}

metadata() returns the pair (node_types, edge_types). It describes the schema of the graph, and it is what to_hetero and the heterogeneous layers need to create their per-type weights.

toy.metadata()

(['author', 'paper'], [('author', 'writes', 'paper'), ('paper', 'cites', 'paper')])

Reverse edges. Message passing sends information along the edges, from source to destination. Here, no edge points to an author, so a GNN could never update the author representations. The usual fix is to add a reverse edge type for every relation between two different node types (PyG's ToUndirected transform on a HeteroData does this). Flipping the two rows of an edge index is all it takes:

def add_reverse_edges(data):
    for (src, rel, dst), edge_index in list(data.edge_index_dict.items()):
        if src != dst:
            data.edge_index_dict[(dst, f"rev_{rel}", src)] = edge_index[::-1]
    return data


toy = add_reverse_edges(toy)
toy.edge_types

[('author', 'writes', 'paper'), ('paper', 'cites', 'paper'), ('paper', 'rev_writes', 'author')]

Back to a homogeneous graph. to_homogeneous() stacks the nodes of all types (in the order of node_types) and offsets the edges accordingly, as PyG's HeteroData.to_homogeneous(). The features of the different types are zero-padded to the widest one, and two vectors record where everything came from: node_type holds the index of each node's type in node_types, and edge_type the index of each edge's type in edge_types. This is the input format of relational layers that take the edge type as an argument, such as RGCNConv.

homo = toy.to_homogeneous()
print(homo)
print("node_type:", homo.node_type.tolist())
print("edge_type:", homo.edge_type.tolist())
print("edge_index:", homo.edge_index.tolist())

GraphData(
    edge_index(shape=(2, 11), int32)
    node_features(shape=(7, 3), float32)
    node_type(shape=(7,), int32)
    edge_type(shape=(11,), int32))

edge_type: [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2]
edge_index: [[0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 3, 4, 4, 6], [3, 4, 4, 6, 3, 3, 5, 0, 0, 1, 2]]

items.title: 2. The DBLP dataset
items.text:
DBLP (as prepared for the MAGNN paper) has four node types: 4,057 authors, 14,328 papers, 7,723 terms and 20 conferences. Authors are described by a bag of words of their paper keywords (334 features), papers by a bag of words of their title (4,231 features) and terms by word embeddings (50 features). Conferences have no features. Every author is labeled with one of four research areas (database, data mining, artificial intelligence, information retrieval). The split is that of MAGNN: 400 authors for training, 400 for validation, and the remaining 3,257 for testing.

Conferences have no features. As in PyG's DBLP examples, we give each of them a single constant feature, so that every node type has an input. We also prepare the labels and the split masks of the authors.

items.title: 3. From a homogeneous model to a heterogeneous one with to_hetero
items.text:
to_hetero takes an ordinary GNN, written for a homogeneous graph, and the metadata of the heterogeneous graph. It returns a model in which:

  • every message passing layer has one copy per edge type: the copy for paper -> author computes the messages that papers send to authors, with its own weights;
  • every other module (Linear, normalizations, MLPs, ...) has one copy per node type;
  • the outputs of all edge types that point to the same node type are combined with aggr (a sum by default).

We start with mlx-graphs' built-in GraphSAGE. The (HIDDEN, HIDDEN) tuple asks for separate weights for the source and the destination nodes of every layer, which bipartite edge types such as author -> paper need. It is the counterpart of PyG's GraphSAGE((-1, -1), ...).

sage = GraphSAGE(
    (HIDDEN, HIDDEN),
    HIDDEN,
    num_layers=2,
    out_features_dim=NUM_CLASSES,
    dropout=DROPOUT,
)
hetero_sage = to_hetero(
    sage, data.metadata(), aggr="sum", input_dims=data.num_node_features
)
hetero_sage

ToHeteroModel(node_types=['author', 'paper', 'term', 'conference'], edge_types=[('author', 'to', 'paper'), ('paper', 'to', 'author'), ('paper', 'to', 'term'), ('paper', 'to', 'conference'), ('term', 'to', 'paper'), ('conference', 'to', 'paper')], aggr='sum')

Why input_dims? In PyG, layers created with an input size of -1 are lazy: they find their input size during the first forward pass, so each per-type copy adapts to the features it receives. MLX has no lazy layers, so we tell to_hetero the number of features of every node type instead. During the conversion, it runs the model once on a tiny graph to find the layers that read the input features, and rebuilds their copies for the right sizes: the first layer's copy for paper -> author reads 4,231 paper features on the source side and 334 author features on the destination side. The input size given to the homogeneous model does not matter. (The other option is to project every node type to a common size first, e.g. with HeteroDictLinear, and convert a model built for that size without input_dims.)

The converted model is called like the original one, with dicts in place of arrays, and returns a dict of outputs keyed by node type:

out = hetero_sage(data.edge_index_dict, data.node_features_dict)
{node_type: value.shape for node_type, value in out.items()}

{'author': (4057, 4), 'paper': (14328, 4), 'term': (7723, 4), 'conference': (20, 4)}

The converted parameters. The copies are stored under the name of their type, as in PyG: author__to__paper for the edge type ("author", "to", "paper"). Here are the parameters of the first layer (module.convs.0): the full name of the first one is module.convs.0.author__to__paper.neigh_proj.weight. Every copy has its own input sizes, and the paper features make the copies whose source is a paper (and the root weights of papers) the largest.

def count_parameters(model):
    return sum(v.size for _, v in tree_flatten(model.trainable_parameters()))


prefix = "module.convs.0."
first_layer = [
    {
        "copy": name[len(prefix) :].split(".", 1)[0],
        "parameter": name[len(prefix) :].split(".", 1)[1],
        "shape": value.shape,
    }
    for name, value in tree_flatten(hetero_sage.trainable_parameters())
    if name.startswith(prefix)
]
print(f"homogeneous GraphSAGE: {count_parameters(sage):,} parameters")
print(f"to_hetero(GraphSAGE): {count_parameters(hetero_sage):,} parameters")
pd.DataFrame(first_layer)

A copy can also be reached by its type, with module_for:

hetero_sage.module.convs[0].module_for(("paper", "to", "author"))

SAGEConv(
  (neigh_proj): Linear(input_dims=4231, output_dims=64, bias=False)
  (self_proj): Linear(input_dims=334, output_dims=64, bias=True)
)

A GAT. to_hetero also converts models written by hand, as long as they are written in the PyG style. Here is a two-layer GAT. It matches PyG's GAT model, which also applies dropout to the attention coefficients. Two details matter for heterogeneous graphs: GATConv adds self-loops by default, which makes no sense when the source and destination nodes have different types, so we disable them (as PyG's examples do; to_hetero raises an error otherwise), and the (HIDDEN, HIDDEN) tuples again give separate source and destination projections.

class GAT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden, out, heads, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = GATConv(
            (hidden, hidden),
            hidden // heads,
            heads=heads,
            dropout=dropout,
            add_self_loops=False,
        )
        self.conv2 = GATConv(
            (hidden, hidden),
            out,
            heads=heads,
            concat=False,
            dropout=dropout,
            add_self_loops=False,
        )
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def __call__(self, edge_index, x):
        x = self.dropout(nn.relu(self.conv1(edge_index, x)))
        return self.conv2(edge_index, x)


hetero_gat = to_hetero(
    GAT(HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, HEADS, DROPOUT),
    data.metadata(),
    input_dims=data.num_node_features,
)
print(f"to_hetero(GAT): {count_parameters(hetero_gat):,} parameters")

to_hetero(GAT): 1,700,120 parameters

What to_hetero cannot convert. The converted model runs the original __call__ on arrays that hold the rows of all node types one after the other, and the per-type copies split them again. Row-wise operations (activations, dropout, residual connections, concatenating features) therefore work as written, but operations that mix or select rows do not: x[:n], x.mean(axis=0), global pooling or sorting would act on all node types at once. Do them on the output dicts instead. Every node type must also be the destination of at least one edge type (add reverse edges), GCNConv and layers that add self-loops cannot be used on bipartite edge types, and the model must not add or drop edges in its __call__. The docstring of to_hetero lists every case.

items.title: 4. Training with mlx-graphs
items.text:
DBLP is small enough for full-batch training: every epoch runs the model on the whole graph and computes the cross-entropy on the 400 training authors. We use AdamW, with bias_correction=True for the update rule of torch.optim.AdamW. After every epoch, we evaluate on the validation and test authors and keep the test accuracy of the epoch with the best validation accuracy. We time the training step only (forward, backward and optimizer update), and report the median over the epochs.

train_full_batch takes a forward function that returns the author logits, so that we can reuse it for the other models of this tutorial.

def accuracy(logits, mask):
    correct = (logits.argmax(-1) == labels).astype(mx.float32)
    return ((correct * mask).sum() / mask.sum()).item()


def train_full_batch(model, forward, epochs=EPOCHS):
    optimizer = optim.AdamW(LR, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY, bias_correction=True)

    def loss_fn(model):
        losses = nn.losses.cross_entropy(forward(model), labels)
        return (losses * masks["train"]).sum() / masks["train"].sum()

    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)
    best_val, test_at_best, times = -1.0, 0.0, []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        start = time.perf_counter()
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model)
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state, loss)
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)

        model.eval()
        logits = forward(model)
        val_acc, test_acc = (
            accuracy(logits, masks["val"]),
            accuracy(logits, masks["test"]),
        )
        if val_acc > best_val:
            best_val, test_at_best = val_acc, test_acc
    return {
        "val_acc": best_val,
        "test_acc": test_at_best,
        "epoch_s": float(np.median(times[1:])),
    }


def hetero_forward(model):
    return model(data.edge_index_dict, data.node_features_dict)[TARGET]

Each model is trained three times, with different random seeds. A fresh model is converted for every run.

MLX_MODELS = {
    "GraphSAGE": lambda: GraphSAGE(
        (HIDDEN, HIDDEN),
        HIDDEN,
        num_layers=2,
        out_features_dim=NUM_CLASSES,
        dropout=DROPOUT,
    ),
    "GAT": lambda: GAT(HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, HEADS, DROPOUT),
}

mlx_runs = []
for name, make_model in MLX_MODELS.items():
    for seed in SEEDS:
        mx.random.seed(seed)
        model = to_hetero(
            make_model(), data.metadata(), input_dims=data.num_node_features
        )
        result = train_full_batch(model, hetero_forward)
        mlx_runs.append(
            {"framework": "mlx-graphs", "model": name, "seed": seed, **result}
        )
        print(
            f"mlx-graphs {name:<9} seed {seed}: val {result['val_acc']:.4f}  "
            f"test {result['test_acc']:.4f}  {1000 * result['epoch_s']:.1f} ms/epoch"
        )

mlx-graphs GraphSAGE seed 0: val 0.8100  test 0.8311  20.2 ms/epoch
mlx-graphs GraphSAGE seed 1: val 0.8200  test 0.8296  20.2 ms/epoch
mlx-graphs GraphSAGE seed 2: val 0.8175  test 0.8413  20.3 ms/epoch
mlx-graphs GAT       seed 0: val 0.8250  test 0.8351  38.6 ms/epoch
mlx-graphs GAT       seed 1: val 0.8425  test 0.8339  38.7 ms/epoch
mlx-graphs GAT       seed 2: val 0.8300  test 0.8354  38.8 ms/epoch

Combining edge types. In DBLP, papers receive messages from three edge types (from authors, terms and conferences), while authors, terms and conferences each receive messages from papers only. aggr sets how to_hetero combines the messages of several edge types: "sum" (the default), "mean", "max", "min" or "mul". It changes the paper representations, and through them the second layer's author representations. One run of each:

aggr_rows = []
for aggr in ["sum", "mean", "max"]:
    mx.random.seed(0)
    model = to_hetero(
        MLX_MODELS["GraphSAGE"](),
        data.metadata(),
        aggr=aggr,
        input_dims=data.num_node_features,
    )
    result = train_full_batch(model, hetero_forward)
    aggr_rows.append({"aggr": aggr, "test accuracy": round(result["test_acc"], 4)})
pd.DataFrame(aggr_rows).set_index("aggr")
test accuracy aggr sum 0.8311 mean 0.8256 max 0.8274

items.title: 5. The same models in PyG
items.text:
For a like-for-like comparison, we build a PyG HeteroData from the arrays of the mlx-graphs graph: both frameworks then train on exactly the same features, edges and splits. (In a PyG-only project, torch_geometric.datasets.DBLP provides the same dataset.)

The models are PyG's GraphSAGE((-1, -1), ...) and the same two-layer GAT, converted with PyG's to_hetero, and trained with the same hyperparameters, optimizer and model selection. PyG runs on the CPU.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.data import HeteroData
from torch_geometric.nn import GATConv as PyGGATConv
from torch_geometric.nn import GraphSAGE as PyGGraphSAGE
from torch_geometric.nn import to_hetero as pyg_to_hetero

pyg_data = HeteroData()
for node_type, x in data.node_features_dict.items():
    pyg_data[node_type].x = torch.from_numpy(np.array(x))
for edge_type, edge_index in data.edge_index_dict.items():
    pyg_data[edge_type].edge_index = torch.from_numpy(np.array(edge_index)).long()
pyg_data[TARGET].y = torch.from_numpy(np.array(labels)).long()
for split, mask in masks.items():
    pyg_data[TARGET][f"{split}_mask"] = torch.from_numpy(np.array(mask)).bool()
print(pyg_data)

HeteroData(
  author={
    x=[4057, 334],
    y=[4057],
    train_mask=[4057],
    val_mask=[4057],
    test_mask=[4057],
  },
  paper={ x=[14328, 4231] },
  term={ x=[7723, 50] },
  conference={ x=[20, 1] },
  (author, to, paper)={ edge_index=[2, 19645] },
  (paper, to, author)={ edge_index=[2, 19645] },
  (paper, to, term)={ edge_index=[2, 85810] },
  (paper, to, conference)={ edge_index=[2, 14328] },
  (term, to, paper)={ edge_index=[2, 85810] },
  (conference, to, paper)={ edge_index=[2, 14328] }
)

class PyGGAT(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden, out, heads, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = PyGGATConv(
            (-1, -1),
            hidden // heads,
            heads=heads,
            dropout=dropout,
            add_self_loops=False,
        )
        self.conv2 = PyGGATConv(
            (-1, -1),
            out,
            heads=heads,
            concat=False,
            dropout=dropout,
            add_self_loops=False,
        )
        self.dropout = torch.nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        x = self.dropout(self.conv1(x, edge_index).relu())
        return self.conv2(x, edge_index)


PYG_MODELS = {
    "GraphSAGE": lambda: PyGGraphSAGE(
        (-1, -1), HIDDEN, num_layers=2, out_channels=NUM_CLASSES, dropout=DROPOUT
    ),
    "GAT": lambda: PyGGAT(HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, HEADS, DROPOUT),
}


def pyg_train_full_batch(model, epochs=EPOCHS):
    x_dict, edge_index_dict = pyg_data.x_dict, pyg_data.edge_index_dict
    y, author = pyg_data[TARGET].y, pyg_data[TARGET]
    with torch.no_grad():  # initializes the lazy (-1) layers
        model(x_dict, edge_index_dict)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY)

    best_val, test_at_best, times = -1.0, 0.0, []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        start = time.perf_counter()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = model(x_dict, edge_index_dict)[TARGET]
        loss = F.cross_entropy(out[author.train_mask], y[author.train_mask])
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            pred = model(x_dict, edge_index_dict)[TARGET].argmax(-1)
        val_acc = (pred[author.val_mask] == y[author.val_mask]).float().mean().item()
        test_acc = (pred[author.test_mask] == y[author.test_mask]).float().mean().item()
        if val_acc > best_val:
            best_val, test_at_best = val_acc, test_acc
    return {
        "val_acc": best_val,
        "test_acc": test_at_best,
        "epoch_s": float(np.median(times[1:])),
    }

Before training with PyG, we release the memory that MLX keeps in its cache, since both frameworks share the same unified memory.

del model, hetero_sage, hetero_gat, out
mx.clear_cache()
print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__}, {torch.get_num_threads()} CPU threads")

pyg_runs = []
for name, make_model in PYG_MODELS.items():
    for seed in SEEDS:
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        model = pyg_to_hetero(make_model(), pyg_data.metadata(), aggr="sum")
        result = pyg_train_full_batch(model)
        pyg_runs.append({"framework": "PyG", "model": name, "seed": seed, **result})
        print(
            f"PyG {name:<9} seed {seed}: val {result['val_acc']:.4f}  "
            f"test {result['test_acc']:.4f}  {1000 * result['epoch_s']:.1f} ms/epoch"
        )
del model

The table gives the mean and standard deviation of the test accuracy over the three seeds, and the median time of a training epoch over all epochs of the three runs (the median is less sensitive than the mean to an epoch slowed down by other programs).

Accuracy. With the same data, architecture, optimizer and model selection, the two frameworks reach the same test accuracy, around 0.83 for both models. The differences between mlx-graphs and PyG are of the same size as the differences between seeds (see the standard deviations in the table): DBLP has only 400 training authors, so the random initialization and dropout matter more than the framework.

Runtime. These timings were measured on an Apple M5 Pro, with mlx-graphs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU (with the number of threads printed above). An mlx-graphs training epoch is several times faster than a PyG one for both models; the speedups printed above give the exact factors of this run. Timings vary from run to run and from machine to machine, so run the notebook on your own machine to compare.

items.title: 7. Fewer parameters with to_hetero_with_bases
items.text:
to_hetero creates one copy of every message passing layer per edge type, so the number of parameters grows with the number of relations. On graphs with many relations (knowledge graphs have hundreds), this means many parameters and a risk of overfitting the rare relations. The basis decomposition of R-GCN shares the work: to_hetero_with_bases keeps num_bases copies of every layer, runs them on the whole graph at once, and learns for every edge type one coefficient per basis that scales its messages. The number of parameters then depends on num_bases, not on the number of edge types.

All node types must have the same input size, since the copies are shared by all node types. in_channels={"node_features": HIDDEN} adds a bias-free linear projection per node type of the node_features argument to HIDDEN features (PyG's LinearAlign), and input_dims gives the input sizes of these projections. to_hetero_with_bases also needs layers that do not add self-loops.

mx.random.seed(0)
bases_sage = to_hetero_with_bases(
    MLX_MODELS["GraphSAGE"](),
    data.metadata(),
    num_bases=3,
    in_channels={"node_features": HIDDEN},
    input_dims=data.num_node_features,
)
mx.random.seed(0)
plain_sage = to_hetero(
    MLX_MODELS["GraphSAGE"](), data.metadata(), input_dims=data.num_node_features
)
n_plain, n_bases = count_parameters(plain_sage), count_parameters(bases_sage)
n_align = sum(v.size for _, v in tree_flatten(bases_sage.align))
print(f"to_hetero(GraphSAGE):            {n_plain:>9,} parameters")
print(f"to_hetero_with_bases(GraphSAGE): {n_bases:>9,} parameters")
print(f"  of which input projections:    {n_align:>9,}")
print(f"  of which message passing:      {n_bases - n_align:>9,}")

to_hetero(GraphSAGE):            1,677,464 parameters
to_hetero_with_bases(GraphSAGE):   321,776 parameters
  of which input projections:      295,424
  of which message passing:         26,352

Most parameters of both models are in the input weights for the 4,231 paper features. The to_hetero model has six of them in its first layer, one for every edge type whose source is a paper and one for the root weight of every edge type whose destination is a paper, while the basis model projects the paper features once. With six edge types, DBLP is a small case: the gap grows with the number of relations. The edge-type coefficients are visible in the parameters:

first_bases = bases_sage.module.convs[0]
first_bases.convs[0].edge_type_weight

array([[0.783287, 0.765768, 0.203009, 0.0670601, -0.17145, -0.903623]], dtype=float32)

mx.random.seed(0)
bases_result = train_full_batch(bases_sage, hetero_forward)
print(
    f"to_hetero_with_bases(GraphSAGE): test {bases_result['test_acc']:.4f}  "
    f"{1000 * bases_result['epoch_s']:.1f} ms/epoch"
)
del plain_sage

to_hetero_with_bases(GraphSAGE): test 0.8001  21.6 ms/epoch

The basis model does different work per epoch: it runs three copies of each layer on the whole graph, and the scaling of the messages by edge type bypasses the fused sparse kernels of mlx-graphs, but it projects the 4,231 paper features once instead of six times. The overview table of section 10 compares its accuracy and epoch time with the other models. The basis decomposition is mainly a tool against too many parameters, when a graph has many relations.

items.title: 8. Native heterogeneous layers
items.text:
to_hetero turns a homogeneous design into a heterogeneous one. mlx-graphs also has layers that are heterogeneous by design, which take x_dict and edge_index_dict directly, as in PyG:

  • HeteroDictLinear applies one linear layer per node type: it maps node types of different sizes to a common size.
  • HeteroConv wraps one homogeneous layer per edge type, chosen by you (the layer may differ between edge types), and combines the results per destination node type. It is the explicit form of what to_hetero builds automatically.
  • HGTConv is the Heterogeneous Graph Transformer layer (Hu et al., 2020): attention over the neighbors of all edge types, with per-type keys, queries, values and per-relation attention matrices.
  • HANConv is the Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network layer (Wang et al., 2019): a GAT per edge type, then a semantic attention that weighs the edge types.

The three models below start with HeteroDictLinear to project every node type to HIDDEN features, apply two heterogeneous layers, and classify the authors with a linear layer.

class HeteroSAGE(nn.Module):
    """HeteroDictLinear, then two HeteroConv layers with one SAGEConv per
    edge type."""

    def __init__(self, input_dims, edge_types, hidden, out, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = HeteroDictLinear(input_dims, hidden)
        self.convs = [
            HeteroConv({et: SAGEConv(hidden, hidden) for et in edge_types}, aggr="sum")
            for _ in range(2)
        ]
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.lin = nn.Linear(hidden, out)

    def __call__(self, x_dict, edge_index_dict):
        h = {t: nn.relu(x) for t, x in self.proj(x_dict).items()}
        for conv in self.convs:
            h = conv(h, edge_index_dict)
            h = {t: self.dropout(nn.relu(x)) for t, x in h.items()}
        return self.lin(h[TARGET])


class HGT(nn.Module):
    """HeteroDictLinear, then two HGTConv layers (as PyG's hgt_dblp.py)."""

    def __init__(self, input_dims, metadata, hidden, out, heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = HeteroDictLinear(input_dims, hidden)
        self.convs = [HGTConv(hidden, hidden, metadata, heads=heads) for _ in range(2)]
        self.lin = nn.Linear(hidden, out)

    def __call__(self, x_dict, edge_index_dict):
        h = {t: nn.relu(x) for t, x in self.proj(x_dict).items()}
        for conv in self.convs:
            h = conv(h, edge_index_dict)
        return self.lin(h[TARGET])


class HAN(nn.Module):
    """Two HANConv layers (each projects its inputs per node type)."""

    def __init__(self, input_dims, metadata, hidden, out, heads, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = HANConv(input_dims, hidden, metadata, heads=heads, dropout=dropout)
        self.conv2 = HANConv(hidden, hidden, metadata, heads=heads, dropout=dropout)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.lin = nn.Linear(hidden, out)

    def __call__(self, x_dict, edge_index_dict):
        h = self.conv1(x_dict, edge_index_dict)
        h = {t: self.dropout(x) for t, x in h.items()}
        h = self.conv2(h, edge_index_dict)
        return self.lin(h[TARGET])


NATIVE_MODELS = {
    "HeteroConv(SAGEConv)": lambda: HeteroSAGE(
        data.num_node_features, data.edge_types, HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, DROPOUT
    ),
    "HGTConv": lambda: HGT(
        data.num_node_features, data.metadata(), HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, heads=2
    ),
    "HANConv": lambda: HAN(
        data.num_node_features, data.metadata(), HIDDEN, NUM_CLASSES, HEADS, DROPOUT
    ),
}


def native_forward(model):
    return model(data.node_features_dict, data.edge_index_dict)


native_runs = []
for name, make_model in NATIVE_MODELS.items():
    mx.random.seed(0)
    model = make_model()
    result = train_full_batch(model, native_forward)
    native_runs.append({"model": name, "parameters": count_parameters(model), **result})
    print(
        f"{name:<21} {count_parameters(model):>9,} parameters  "
        f"test {result['test_acc']:.4f}  {1000 * result['epoch_s']:.1f} ms/epoch"
    )

HeteroConv(SAGEConv)    395,012 parameters  test 0.8096  7.9 ms/epoch
HGTConv                 478,244 parameters  test 0.7636  19.3 ms/epoch
HANConv                 322,564 parameters  test 0.8096  13.2 ms/epoch

Projecting the features first makes these models much smaller than the to_hetero ones, whose first layer reads the raw features once per edge type. HANConv was designed for metapath graphs, where an edge connects two authors that share a paper (author-paper-author) or a conference: here we apply it to the raw relations to show its API, without building metapaths. Its node-level attention has no root weight, so an author only sees its own features through two hops.

HANConv can also return its semantic attention weights, which tell how much each edge type contributes to a node type. Papers receive messages from authors, terms and conferences:

han = model  # the last model trained above
han.eval()
_, semantic = han.conv1(
    data.node_features_dict,
    data.edge_index_dict,
    return_semantic_attention_weights=True,
)
incoming = [et for et in data.edge_types if et[-1] == "paper"]
dict(zip([f"{src} -> paper" for src, _, _ in incoming], semantic["paper"].tolist()))

{'author -> paper': 0.999995231628418, 'term -> paper': 1.6165221268238383e-06, 'conference -> paper': 3.0664973564853426e-06}

The weights sum to one over the incoming edge types, and show which relations the trained model relies on to build the paper representations.

items.title: 9. Mini-batch training with NeighborLoader and HGTLoader
items.text:
Full-batch training needs the whole graph and all its intermediate activations in memory. On large graphs, mini-batches of sampled subgraphs are the way out: every batch holds a set of seed nodes (here, training authors) and a sample of their multi-hop neighborhood, just large enough to compute the seeds' representations. mlx-graphs has the two heterogeneous samplers of PyG:

  • NeighborLoader samples a fixed number of neighbors per node, per edge type and per hop (num_neighbors=[10, 10]: 10 neighbors per edge type at each of the 2 hops), as in GraphSAGE.
  • HGTLoader samples a fixed budget of nodes per node type at each hop (num_samples), favoring nodes connected to many already sampled nodes. It keeps the size of the batches under control even around very high-degree nodes, and was introduced with HGT for ogbn-mag-sized graphs.

Both sample on the host, outside the GPU, and return a HeteroGraphData per batch. PyG's versions of these loaders need the optional pyg-lib (or torch-sparse) package, which is not installed here, so this section is mlx-graphs only.

np.random.seed(0)  # the samplers draw with NumPy
neighbor_loader = NeighborLoader(
    data,
    num_neighbors=[10, 10],
    input_nodes=(TARGET, data.author_train_mask),
    batch_size=128,
    shuffle=True,
)
hgt_loader = HGTLoader(
    data,
    num_samples=[256, 256],
    input_nodes=(TARGET, data.author_train_mask),
    batch_size=128,
    shuffle=True,
)

batch = next(iter(neighbor_loader))
print(batch)

HeteroGraphData(
node_features(
  'author': (shape=(317, 334), float32),
  'paper': (shape=(515, 4231), float32),
  'term': (shape=(1217, 50), float32),
  'conference': (shape=(19, 1), float32),
)
 edge_index(
  'author -> to -> paper':(shape=(2, 868), int64),
  'paper -> to -> author':(shape=(2, 517), int64),
  'paper -> to -> term':(shape=(2, 0), int64),
  'paper -> to -> conference':(shape=(2, 0), int64),
  'term -> to -> paper':(shape=(2, 3173), int64),
  'conference -> to -> paper':(shape=(2, 515), int64),
)
 edge_labels_index_dict(
)
 edge_labels_dict(

node_labels_dict(
  'author': (shape=(317,),int64),
)
batch_size=128
input_type=author
n_id_dict(
  'author': (shape=(317,),int32),
  'paper': (shape=(515,),int32),
  'term': (shape=(1217,),int32),
  'conference': (shape=(19,),int32),
)
e_id_dict(
  '('author', 'to', 'paper')': (shape=(868,),int32),
  '('paper', 'to', 'author')': (shape=(517,),int32),
  '('paper', 'to', 'term')': (shape=(0,),int32),
  '('paper', 'to', 'conference')': (shape=(0,),int32),
  '('term', 'to', 'paper')': (shape=(3173,),int32),
  '('conference', 'to', 'paper')': (shape=(515,),int32),
)
num_sampled_nodes_dict(
  'author': [128, 0, 189],
  'paper': [0, 515, 0],
  'term': [0, 0, 1217],
  'conference': [0, 0, 19],
)
num_sampled_edges_dict(
  '('author', 'to', 'paper')': [0, 868],
  '('paper', 'to', 'author')': [517, 0],
  '('paper', 'to', 'term')': [0, 0],

  '('conference', 'to', 'paper')': [0, 515],

  'author': 317,

  'conference': 19,

author_train_mask(shape=(317,), bool)

author_test_mask(shape=(317,), bool)
