items.title: Comparison with full-batch PyG
items.text:
As a reference, the same 3-layer GraphSAGE trained full-batch in PyG, on the same graph and for the same number of epochs as the full-batch mlx-graphs run. PyG runs on the CPU here. As PyG recommends for full-batch training on large graphs, the graph is passed as a sparse adjacency matrix (to_torch_csr_tensor): SAGEConv then aggregates with a sparse matrix product instead of building one message per edge, which is also what mlx-graphs' fused kernel does. With a plain edge_index, PyG keeps a [num_edges, features] array per layer for the backward pass, several GB on this graph.

PyG's own mini-batch loaders could not run here: its NeighborLoader needs pyg-lib or torch_sparse, ClusterData needs torch_sparse (for METIS), and the GraphSAINT samplers need torch_sparse. These compiled extensions are not installed in this environment, so PyG is only a full-batch reference. The mlx-graphs loaders have no such dependency: their samplers are built in. (The mlx-graphs test suite and benchmarks check them against PyG's pure-Python classes and the papers' definitions.)

import torch  # noqa: E402
import torch.nn.functional as F  # noqa: E402
from torch_geometric.nn import SAGEConv as PyGSAGEConv  # noqa: E402
from torch_geometric.utils import to_torch_csr_tensor  # noqa: E402

mx.clear_cache()  # give the memory cached by MLX back before running PyG

torch.manual_seed(SEED)


class PyGSAGE(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, out_dim, num_layers, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        dims = [in_dim] + [hidden_dim] * (num_layers - 1) + [out_dim]
        self.convs = torch.nn.ModuleList(
            PyGSAGEConv(i, o) for i, o in zip(dims[:-1], dims[1:])
        )
        self.dropout = dropout

    def forward(self, x, adj_t):
        for i, conv in enumerate(self.convs):
            x = conv(x, adj_t)
            if i < len(self.convs) - 1:
                x = F.dropout(F.relu(x), self.dropout, self.training)
        return x


x = torch.from_numpy(np.array(data.node_features))
edge_index = torch.from_numpy(np.array(data.edge_index).astype(np.int64))
# rows are destination nodes, so the source -> destination order is flipped
adj_t = to_torch_csr_tensor(edge_index.flip(0), size=(x.shape[0], x.shape[0]))
y = torch.from_numpy(np.array(data.node_labels).astype(np.int64))
pyg_train, pyg_val, pyg_test = (
    torch.from_numpy(np.array(i).astype(np.int64))
    for i in (train_idx, val_idx, test_idx)
)
pyg_model = PyGSAGE(x.shape[1], HIDDEN, num_classes, NUM_LAYERS, DROPOUT)
pyg_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(pyg_model.parameters(), lr=LR)


def pyg_epoch():
    pyg_model.train()
    pyg_optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = F.cross_entropy(pyg_model(x, adj_t)[pyg_train], y[pyg_train])
    loss.backward()
    pyg_optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()


@torch.no_grad()
def pyg_evaluate():
    pyg_model.eval()
    pred = pyg_model(x, adj_t).argmax(dim=1)
    return [float((pred[i] == y[i]).float().mean()) for i in (pyg_val, pyg_test)]


print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__}, {torch.get_num_threads()} CPU threads")
pyg_history, pyg_times = [], []
for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS["full"] + 1):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    loss = pyg_epoch()
    pyg_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    if epoch % 10 == 0 or epoch == EPOCHS["full"]:
        val, test = pyg_evaluate()
        record = dict(epoch=epoch, train_s=sum(pyg_times), val=val, test=test)
        pyg_history.append(record)
        print(
            f"{'PyG':<14} epoch {epoch:3d}  loss {loss:.4f}  val {val:.4f}  "
            f"test {test:.4f}  ({pyg_times[-1]:.2f} s)"
        )
results["full-batch (PyG)"] = dict(
    name="full-batch (PyG)", history=pyg_history, epoch_times=pyg_times
)

items.title: Conclusions
items.text:
These timings come from an Apple M5 Pro, with mlx-graphs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU. They vary from run to run, so run the notebook on your own machine to compare.

  • Full batch, when the graph fits. ogbn-arxiv fits comfortably in a Mac's memory, and full-batch training has the cheapest epochs: one gradient step over the whole graph, computed with mlx-graphs' fused sparse kernels. The printed line above compares it with PyG's full-batch epoch on the same model.
  • NeighborLoader needs the fewest epochs. Each epoch makes one update per mini-batch, about 90 here instead of one, so it reaches the best accuracy in a handful of epochs. Its epochs are the most expensive: every batch samples a new subgraph and builds new arrays. Use it when the graph, or the activations of the full graph, don't fit in memory, and for layer-wise inference on graphs too large to embed in one pass.
  • ClusterGCN has the cheapest mini-batch epochs after a one-off partitioning, because its batches are fixed groups of clusters. The edges between clusters that are not batched together are dropped, which costs a little accuracy.
  • GraphSAINT sits in between. It samples random-walk subgraphs and corrects their bias with node and edge normalizations computed once before training.
  • Accuracy. Each method ran once, from one seed, for a few epochs, so differences of one or two points are within run-to-run variation. With the same weights, mlx-graphs' GraphSAGE gives PyG's loss and gradients on this graph (see also Validation against PyG).

For graphs that don't fit in memory at all, start with NeighborLoader, and use ClusterLoader when epochs must be cheap.

items.title: Going further
items.text:
• Link prediction. LinkNeighborLoader samples the neighborhoods of the two endpoints of a batch of edges, and adds negative edges (neg_sampling_ratio, or NegativeSampling for more control) with their labels in edge_label_index and edge_label. See the link prediction tutorial.
  • Heterogeneous graphs. NeighborLoader also takes a HeteroGraphData, with input_nodes=("author", mask) and a fan-out per edge type, and HGTLoader samples a budget of nodes per node type, as in the HGT paper. See the heterogeneous graphs tutorial and examples/to_hetero_dblp.py.
  • Temporal graphs. TemporalDataLoader iterates over a stream of timestamped events in chronological mini-batches, with negative destinations: see the Temporal Graph Networks tutorial.

items.title: Node2Vec: node embeddings from random walks
items.text:
View on GitHub Download notebook

Node2Vec (Grover and Leskovec, 2016) learns a vector for every node of a graph without using any node features: two nodes get similar vectors when they often appear close to each other on random walks. It works in two steps.

  1. Biased random walks. From every node, we sample a few walks of fixed length. After a step t -> v, the next node x is a neighbor of v, chosen with an unnormalized weight of 1/p if x is t itself (going back), 1 if x is also a neighbor of t (staying close to t), and 1/q otherwise (moving away). The return parameter p therefore controls how often a walk steps back, and the in-out parameter q interpolates between a breadth-first exploration of the neighborhood (q > 1, BFS-like) and a depth-first one that moves away from the start (q < 1, DFS-like). With p = q = 1 the walks are uniform, as in DeepWalk.
  2. Skip-gram with negative sampling. Nodes that appear within a few steps of each other on a walk are trained to have a large dot product, and random pairs of nodes (the negative samples) a small one. This is the word2vec objective, with walks as sentences and nodes as words.

In this tutorial, we train Node2Vec with mlx-graphs on the Cora citation graph, and evaluate the embeddings on node classification and link prediction. We then look at the effect of p and q, at sampling the walks on the GPU or the CPU, and we finally compare mlx-graphs with PyTorch Geometric (PyG).

Requirements. mlx-graphs samples the walks with the mlx_cluster package (version 0.1.2 or later, which requires mlx>=0.32). The evaluation uses scikit-learn, and the comparison with PyG needs PyTorch and PyG:

pip install mlx_cluster scikit-learn pandas matplotlib torch torch_geometric

import time

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim
import numpy as np

from mlx_graphs.algorithms import Node2Vec
from mlx_graphs.datasets import PlanetoidDataset

SEED = 0
mx.random.seed(SEED)
np.random.seed(SEED)  # the Node2Vec dataloader shuffles the nodes with NumPy

items.title: The dataset
items.text:
We use Cora, from the Planetoid collection of citation networks: 2,708 scientific papers, linked by 10,556 directed edges (5,278 citations, stored in both directions). Each paper belongs to one of 7 topics. Node2Vec only uses the edges: the bag-of-words node features and the labels are used below to evaluate the embeddings, never to train them.

dataset = PlanetoidDataset("Cora")
graph = dataset[0]
num_nodes = graph.num_nodes
print(graph)

labels = np.array(graph.node_labels)
train_mask, test_mask = np.array(graph.train_mask), np.array(graph.test_mask)
print(f"{num_nodes} nodes, {graph.num_edges} edges, {labels.max() + 1} classes")
print(f"mean degree {graph.num_edges / num_nodes:.2f}")
print(f"{train_mask.sum()} training nodes, {test_mask.sum()} test nodes")

Loading cora data ... Done

items.title: The model
items.text:
Node2Vec holds one embedding per node, the graph in CSR format for the walks, and the sampling and loss functions. Its main hyperparameters are:

  • embedding_dim: the size of each embedding vector.
  • walk_length: the number of nodes in each random walk.
  • context_size: the size of the sliding window over a walk. Each walk of walk_length nodes is cut into walk_length - context_size + 1 windows of context_size nodes, and the first node of each window is trained to be close to the other nodes of the window. Cutting long walks into windows reuses every sampled walk many times.
  • walks_per_node: the number of walks started from each node.
  • num_negative_samples: the number of negative (random) windows per positive window.
  • p and q: the return and in-out parameters of the walks (see above).
  • use_gpu: whether to sample the walks on the GPU or on the CPU.

We use the values of PyG's Node2Vec example, with uniform walks for now.

EMBEDDING_DIM = 128
WALK_LENGTH = 20
CONTEXT_SIZE = 10
WALKS_PER_NODE = 10
NUM_NEGATIVE_SAMPLES = 1
BATCH_SIZE = 128
LEARNING_RATE = 0.01
NUM_EPOCHS = 10


def make_model(p=1.0, q=1.0, edge_index=graph.edge_index, use_gpu=True, **kwargs):
    config = dict(
        embedding_dim=EMBEDDING_DIM,
        walk_length=WALK_LENGTH,
        context_size=CONTEXT_SIZE,
        walks_per_node=WALKS_PER_NODE,
        num_negative_samples=NUM_NEGATIVE_SAMPLES,
    )
    config.update(kwargs)
    return Node2Vec(
        edge_index=edge_index, num_nodes=num_nodes, p=p, q=q, use_gpu=use_gpu, **config
    )


model = make_model()
model

Node2Vec(
  (embedding): Embedding(2708, 128)
)

items.title: What a batch of walks looks like
items.text:
pos_sample samples walks_per_node walks from each node of a batch and cuts them into windows. Here we start from node 0 only: the 10 walks of 20 nodes give 10 x 11 = 110 windows of 10 nodes. The windows are grouped by position (the first window of every walk, then the second window of every walk, and so on), so rows 0, 10, 20, ... are the successive windows of the first walk. Each one starts one step further along the walk.

windows = model.pos_sample(mx.array([0]))
print("positive windows:", windows.shape)
print(windows[::WALKS_PER_NODE])

positive windows: (110, 10)
array([[0, 2582, 1166, ..., 633, 0, 633],
       [2582, 1166, 2582, ..., 0, 633, 1866],
       [1166, 2582, 1166, ..., 633, 1866, 633],
       ...,
       [0, 633, 1866, ..., 1701, 1857, 1701],
       [633, 1866, 633, ..., 1857, 1701, 729],
       [1866, 633, 1866, ..., 1701, 729, 2534]], dtype=int64)

Every step of a walk follows an edge of the graph. The negative windows from neg_sample have the same shape, but after the start node the nodes are drawn uniformly at random:

negatives = model.neg_sample(mx.array([0]))
print("negative windows:", negatives.shape)
print(negatives[:3])

negative windows: (110, 10)
array([[0, 1502, 2502, ..., 841, 187, 1915],
       [0, 213, 1266, ..., 1695, 1606, 2132],
       [0, 154, 554, ..., 1873, 2121, 1552]], dtype=int32)

model.dataloader(batch_size) shuffles the nodes and yields one (positive, negative) pair of window arrays per batch of start nodes:

pos, neg = next(model.dataloader(batch_size=BATCH_SIZE))
print(
    f"one batch of {BATCH_SIZE} start nodes: positive {pos.shape}, negative {neg.shape}"
)

one batch of 128 start nodes: positive (14080, 10), negative (14080, 10)

items.title: Training
items.text:
model.loss(pos, neg) is the skip-gram loss: for each window, it takes the embedding z_u of the first node and the embeddings z_v of the other nodes, and averages -log(sigmoid(z_u . z_v)) over the positive windows and -log(1 - sigmoid(z_u . z_v)) over the negative ones. We minimize it with Adam. One epoch samples new walks from every node.

bias_correction=True gives the update rule of torch.optim.Adam, which we use in the comparison with PyG below.

def train(model, num_epochs=NUM_EPOCHS, verbose=False):
    """Trains the model and returns the seconds and the mean loss of each epoch."""
    optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE, bias_correction=True)
    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, model.loss)
    epoch_times, losses = [], []
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        start, total, num_batches = time.perf_counter(), 0.0, 0
        for pos, neg in model.dataloader(batch_size=BATCH_SIZE):
            loss, grads = loss_and_grad(pos, neg)
            optimizer.update(model, grads)
            mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state, loss)
            total, num_batches = total + loss.item(), num_batches + 1
        epoch_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
        losses.append(total / num_batches)
        if verbose:
            print(
                f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d}  loss {losses[-1]:.4f}  {epoch_times[-1]:.2f} s"
            )
    return epoch_times, losses


epoch_times, losses = train(model, verbose=True)

items.title: Evaluating the embeddings
items.text:
A common way to evaluate node embeddings is to train a linear classifier on top of them. We fit a logistic regression on the embeddings of Cora's 140 training nodes, and measure its accuracy on the 1,000 test nodes. As a reference, the same classifier on the bag-of-words features of the papers, which Node2Vec never sees, is also shown.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression


def test_accuracy(features):
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
    clf.fit(features[train_mask], labels[train_mask])
    return clf.score(features[test_mask], labels[test_mask])


embeddings = np.array(model.embedding.weight)
print(f"Node2Vec embeddings: test accuracy {test_accuracy(embeddings):.3f}")
features = np.array(graph.node_features)
print(f"bag-of-words features: test accuracy {test_accuracy(features):.3f}")

Node2Vec embeddings: test accuracy 0.703
bag-of-words features: test accuracy 0.576

Node2Vec learns the topics of the papers from the citation graph alone. The accuracy of a single run changes by about a point from one seed to the next, so we use several seeds when comparing settings below.

items.title: A 2-D view of the embeddings
items.text:
t-SNE projects the 128-dimensional embeddings onto a plane while keeping close points close. Each panel shows all nodes in gray, and the nodes of one class in blue. If the embeddings capture the topics, the nodes of a class form a few dense groups instead of being spread over the whole plane.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

INK, MUTED, GRID, SURFACE = "#1f1f1e", "#6b6a64", "#e6e5e0", "#d9d8d2"
MLX_COLOR, PYG_COLOR = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"

projection = TSNE(n_components=2, init="pca", random_state=SEED).fit_transform(
    embeddings
)

num_classes = labels.max() + 1
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(12, 6.2))
for c, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for side in ax.spines.values():
        side.set_color(GRID)
    if c == num_classes:
        ax.set_visible(False)
        continue
    ax.scatter(*projection.T, s=3, color=SURFACE, linewidths=0)
    members = labels == c
    ax.scatter(*projection[members].T, s=4, color=MLX_COLOR, linewidths=0)
    ax.set_title(
        f"class {c} ({members.sum()} nodes)", loc="left", color=INK, fontsize=10
    )
fig.suptitle(
    "t-SNE of the Node2Vec embeddings, one panel per class",
    x=0.01,
    ha="left",
    color=INK,
)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

items.title: Link prediction
items.text:
The embeddings can also predict missing edges. RandomLinkSplit hides 10% of the citations (the test edges) and samples as many unconnected node pairs (the negative edges). We train a new model on the remaining graph, score each pair by the dot product of its two embeddings (the quantity the skip-gram loss pushes up for nodes close on the walks), and measure the ROC AUC with mlx_graphs.metrics. We don't tune anything here, so the validation split is not used.

from mlx_graphs.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from mlx_graphs.transforms import RandomLinkSplit

mx.random.seed(SEED)
np.random.seed(SEED)
split = RandomLinkSplit(num_val=0.05, num_test=0.1, is_undirected=True)
train_graph, _, test_graph = split(graph)
print(f"training graph: {train_graph.num_edges} edges")
print(f"test pairs: {test_graph.edge_label_index.shape[1]} (half of them are edges)")

link_model = make_model(edge_index=train_graph.edge_index)
train(link_model)

z = link_model.embedding.weight
src, dst = test_graph.edge_label_index
scores = (z[src] * z[dst]).sum(axis=-1)
auc = roc_auc_score(test_graph.edge_label, scores)
ap = average_precision_score(test_graph.edge_label, scores)
print(f"test ROC AUC {auc:.3f}, average precision {ap:.3f}")

training graph: 8976 edges
test pairs: 1054 (half of them are edges)
test ROC AUC 0.894, average precision 0.928

items.title: The effect of p and q
items.text:
We now compare three kinds of walks, changing only q:

  • uniform (p = 1, q = 1): every neighbor is equally likely.
  • BFS-like (p = 1, q = 4): moving away from the previous node is 4 times less likely, so walks stay in the neighborhood of their start.
  • DFS-like (p = 1, q = 0.25): moving away is 4 times more likely, so walks travel further.

To see the difference, we sample one walk of 20 nodes from every node and measure the number of distinct nodes it visits, how often it steps straight back to the node it came from, and the shortest-path distance (in hops) between its first and last nodes.

from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path

WALK_SETTINGS = {
    "uniform (p=1, q=1)": (1.0, 1.0),
    "BFS-like (p=1, q=4)": (1.0, 4.0),
    "DFS-like (p=1, q=0.25)": (1.0, 0.25),
}

src_np, dst_np = np.array(graph.edge_index)
adjacency = csr_matrix((np.ones(src_np.size), (src_np, dst_np)), shape=(num_nodes,) * 2)
hops = shortest_path(adjacency, unweighted=True)


def sample_walks(p, q, walks_per_node=1):
    """Full walks of WALK_LENGTH nodes, rebuilt from the windows of pos_sample."""
    model = make_model(p, q, walks_per_node=walks_per_node, context_size=WALK_LENGTH)
    return np.array(model.pos_sample(mx.arange(num_nodes)))


walk_stats = {}
for name, (p, q) in WALK_SETTINGS.items():
    mx.random.seed(SEED)
    walks = sample_walks(p, q)
    walk_stats[name] = {
        "distinct nodes": np.mean([len(set(w)) for w in walks]),
        "steps back (%)": 100 * np.mean(walks[:, 2:] == walks[:, :-2]),
        "hops start to end": np.mean(hops[walks[:, 0], walks[:, -1]]),
    }
    print(f"{name:<23}", walks[0])

uniform (p=1, q=1)      [   0 1862 2582 1862  926 1862 1701 1052 1701   13 1701 1334 1950 1947
  310 1272 1945  310 1272 1945]
BFS-like (p=1, q=4)     [   0 1862    0 2582    0 1862    0 2582 1166 1986 2007 1986  476 1986
 1995  745  553 1995 1583 1013]
DFS-like (p=1, q=0.25)  [   0 1862 1701 1100  598 2138  548 1523 2449 1523  548  843 2339  843
 2339 1191 2241  500 2241 1957]

Setting context_size equal to walk_length gives one window per walk, so the windows are the full walks. The first walk of each setting, from node 0, is printed above. We then train one model per setting and seed, and evaluate it as before.

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
PQ_SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]

pq_accuracy = {}
for name, (p, q) in WALK_SETTINGS.items():
    pq_accuracy[name] = []
    for seed in PQ_SEEDS:
        mx.random.seed(seed)
        np.random.seed(seed)
        pq_model = make_model(p, q)
        train(pq_model)
        pq_accuracy[name].append(test_accuracy(np.array(pq_model.embedding.weight)))

pq_table = pd.DataFrame(walk_stats).T.round(2)
pq_table["test accuracy"] = [
    f"{np.mean(a):.3f} ± {np.std(a, ddof=1):.3f}" for a in pq_accuracy.values()
]
pq_table
distinct nodes steps back (%) hops start to end test accuracy uniform (p=1, q=1) 12.28 29.37 3.78 0.706 ± 0.007 BFS-like (p=1, q=4) 9.07 44.58 2.81 0.678 ± 0.010 DFS-like (p=1, q=0.25) 14.54 18.51 4.27 0.724 ± 0.006 
def style_axis(ax):
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for side in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_color(GRID)


def label_bars(ax, bars, values, errors, fmt):
    """Writes each value above its bar, or above its error bar."""
    errors = errors if errors is not None else [0] * len(values)
    for bar, value, error in zip(bars, values, errors):
        ax.annotate(
            format(value, fmt),
            (bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value + error),
            xytext=(0, 3),
            textcoords="offset points",
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            color=INK,
            fontsize=9,
        )


names = list(WALK_SETTINGS)
short_names = [n.replace(" (", "\n(") for n in names]
x = np.arange(len(names))
panels = [
    (
        "Distinct nodes in a walk of 20 nodes",
        [walk_stats[n]["distinct nodes"] for n in names],
        None,
        ".1f",
    ),
    (
        "Hops between first and last node",
        [walk_stats[n]["hops start to end"] for n in names],
        None,
        ".2f",
    ),
    (
        "Test accuracy (mean ± std, 3 seeds)",
        [np.mean(pq_accuracy[n]) for n in names],
        [np.std(pq_accuracy[n], ddof=1) for n in names],
        ".3f",
    ),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for ax, (title, values, errors, fmt) in zip(axes, panels):
    bars = ax.bar(x, values, 0.6, color=MLX_COLOR, yerr=errors, ecolor=INK, capsize=4)
    label_bars(ax, bars, values, errors, fmt)
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks(x, short_names, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(values) * 1.18)
    style_axis(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The walk statistics behave as the parameters suggest. With q = 4, the walks step back much more often, visit fewer distinct nodes and end closer to their start: they describe the immediate neighborhood of each node. With q = 0.25, they visit more nodes and travel further.

On Cora, the walks that travel further give the best test accuracy here, and the BFS-like walks the lowest. Papers on the same topic form groups larger than a node's direct neighbors, so a wider context helps to recognize them. Other graphs and tasks can favor the other end: the best p and q depend on the data, and should be chosen on a validation set.

items.title: Sampling the walks on the GPU or the CPU
items.text:
use_gpu selects the device of the walk sampler only: random_walk for uniform walks, and rejection_sampling for biased ones. The embedding lookups, the loss, the gradients and the optimizer updates run on MLX's default device, which is the GPU on Apple silicon.

We first time the sampling of the positive windows of every node (27,080 walks of 20 nodes) on each device. The timer reports the median over 10 calls, after 2 warm-up calls that compile the Metal kernels.

import statistics


def benchmark(fn, sync, warmup=2, repeats=10):
    """Median wall-clock time of fn() in ms. sync(out) waits for the result."""
    for _ in range(warmup):
        sync(fn())
    times = []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        sync(fn())
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return statistics.median(times) * 1000


all_nodes = mx.arange(num_nodes)
device_rows = {}
for name, (p, q) in [
    ("uniform (p=1, q=1)", (1.0, 1.0)),
    ("biased (p=1, q=0.25)", (1.0, 0.25)),
]:
    device_rows[name] = {}
    for device in ["GPU", "CPU"]:
        sampler = make_model(p, q, use_gpu=device == "GPU")
        ms = benchmark(lambda: sampler.pos_sample(all_nodes), sync=mx.eval)
        device_rows[name][f"{device} walks (ms)"] = round(ms, 1)
device_table = pd.DataFrame(device_rows).T
device_table["GPU speedup"] = (
    device_table["CPU walks (ms)"] / device_table["GPU walks (ms)"]
).map("{:.1f}x".format)
device_table
GPU walks (ms) CPU walks (ms) GPU speedup uniform (p=1, q=1) 0.6 2.6 4.3x biased (p=1, q=0.25) 2.3 17.5 7.6x

The device changes where the walks are sampled, not which walks are sampled: with the same seed, the CPU and the GPU return the same walks.

for name, (p, q) in [("uniform", (1.0, 1.0)), ("biased", (1.0, 0.25))]:
    walks = {}
    for device in ["GPU", "CPU"]:
        mx.random.seed(SEED)
        walks[device] = make_model(p, q, use_gpu=device == "GPU").pos_sample(all_nodes)
    print(
        f"{name:<8} walks identical on GPU and CPU: {mx.array_equal(*walks.values())}"
    )

uniform  walks identical on GPU and CPU: True
biased   walks identical on GPU and CPU: True

Sampling is only part of an epoch. To compare whole epochs, we also run training entirely on the CPU, by changing MLX's default device as well, and time 3 epochs in each configuration.

training_rows = {}
for label, use_gpu, device in [
    ("walks on GPU, training on GPU", True, mx.gpu),
    ("walks on CPU, training on GPU", False, mx.gpu),
    ("walks on CPU, training on CPU", False, mx.cpu),
]:
    mx.set_default_device(device)
    try:
        mx.random.seed(SEED)
        times, _ = train(make_model(use_gpu=use_gpu), num_epochs=3)
    finally:
        mx.set_default_device(mx.gpu)
    training_rows[label] = {"s/epoch": round(statistics.median(times), 3)}
pd.DataFrame(training_rows).T
s/epoch walks on GPU, training on GPU 0.136 walks on CPU, training on GPU 0.138 walks on CPU, training on CPU 1.228

The GPU samples walks faster than the CPU, and the gap is larger for biased walks, whose rejection sampling does more work per step (see the speedups in the first table). Over a whole epoch, however, the walks are a small part of the time when the rest of the training runs on the GPU: sampling them on the CPU makes an epoch only slightly slower. Most of the gain comes from running the training itself on the GPU, as the last row of the second table shows.

items.title: mlx-graphs vs PyG
items.text:
PyG has the same Node2Vec model, with the same arguments, sampling and loss, so we can train both on the same graph with the same hyperparameters and compare three things:

  1. Walk sampling: the time to sample the positive windows of every node with each library's pos_sample, with walks of 80 nodes (the length used in the Node2Vec paper), and a check that the walks follow the edges of the graph.
  2. Training: the time per epoch of each library's training loop, which includes the sampling, the loss, the gradients and the optimizer updates.
  3. Embedding quality: the logistic-regression test accuracy, so that the speeds are compared at equal quality.

Each library runs on its usual device on a Mac: mlx-graphs on the GPU, and PyG on the CPU. PyG's walk sampler has no GPU version on macOS, and the many small operations of Node2Vec training are faster on PyTorch's CPU backend than on MPS.

PyG's walk sampler. PyG's Node2Vec samples its walks with the random_walk operator of the optional pyg-lib package, which supports uniform walks only (p = q = 1) and raises an error for biased walks. When pyg-lib is not installed, Node2Vec refuses to start. In that case, the cell below registers a short PyTorch implementation of the same operator, with the same inputs, outputs and uniform-only restriction, so that PyG's Node2Vec runs unchanged on top of it. The printed line tells which sampler is used: timings with the fallback measure this PyTorch code, not pyg-lib.

import warnings

# With recent PyTorch versions, importing PyG warns that torch.jit.script is deprecated
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message=".*torch.jit.script.* is deprecated")

import platform
from importlib.metadata import version

import torch
import torch_geometric.nn.models.node2vec as pyg_node2vec_module
from torch_geometric.nn import Node2Vec as PyGNode2Vec
from torch_geometric.typing import WITH_PYG_LIB

if not WITH_PYG_LIB:

    @torch.library.custom_op("pyg::random_walk", mutates_args=())
    def random_walk(
        rowptr: torch.Tensor,
        col: torch.Tensor,
        seed: torch.Tensor,
        walk_length: int,
        p: float,
        q: float,
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """Uniform random walks (pyg-lib's pyg::random_walk, in plain PyTorch)."""
        if p != 1.0 or q != 1.0:
            raise RuntimeError("Uniform sampling required for now")
        degree = rowptr[1:] - rowptr[:-1]
        node, nodes, edges = seed, [seed], []
        rand = torch.rand(walk_length, seed.numel())
        for step in range(walk_length):
            deg = degree[node]
            edge = rowptr[node] + (rand[step] * deg).long()
            has_neighbors = deg > 0  # nodes without neighbors stay in place
            node = torch.where(
                has_neighbors, col[edge.clamp(max=col.numel() - 1)], node
            )
            nodes.append(node)
            edges.append(torch.where(has_neighbors, edge, -1))
        return torch.stack(nodes, dim=1), torch.stack(edges, dim=1)

    pyg_node2vec_module.WITH_PYG_LIB = True  # Node2Vec checks this flag at init

PYG_SAMPLER = "pyg-lib" if WITH_PYG_LIB else "PyTorch fallback"
print(f"{platform.platform()}, {platform.processor()}")
for package in ["mlx", "mlx_cluster", "torch", "torch_geometric"]:
    print(f"{package:<16}{version(package)}")
print(f"PyG walk sampler: {PYG_SAMPLER}, {torch.get_num_threads()} PyTorch CPU threads")

macOS-27.2.1-arm64-arm-64bit, arm
mlx             0.32.4
mlx_cluster     0.1.2
torch           2.15.0
torch_geometric 2.8.1
PyG walk sampler: PyTorch fallback, 6 PyTorch CPU threads

Both libraries get the same edges: we convert Cora's edge_index from mlx-graphs to PyTorch.

edge_index_torch = torch.from_numpy(np.array(graph.edge_index).astype(np.int64))


def make_pyg_model(p=1.0, q=1.0, **kwargs):
    config = dict(
        embedding_dim=EMBEDDING_DIM,
        walk_length=WALK_LENGTH,
        context_size=CONTEXT_SIZE,
        walks_per_node=WALKS_PER_NODE,
        num_negative_samples=NUM_NEGATIVE_SAMPLES,
    )
    config.update(kwargs)
    return PyGNode2Vec(edge_index_torch, num_nodes=num_nodes, p=p, q=q, **config)

items.title: Walk sampling
items.text:
Both samplers run on the same graph, from the same start nodes (every node, 10 times). Biased walks are timed for mlx-graphs only, since PyG's sampler doesn't support them.

SAMPLING_WALK_LENGTH = 80
all_nodes_torch = torch.arange(num_nodes)


def mlx_sampler(p, q):
    return make_model(p, q, walk_length=SAMPLING_WALK_LENGTH)


def pyg_sampler(p, q):
    return make_pyg_model(p, q, walk_length=SAMPLING_WALK_LENGTH)


mlx_uniform, mlx_biased = mlx_sampler(1.0, 1.0), mlx_sampler(1.0, 0.25)
pyg_uniform = pyg_sampler(1.0, 1.0)
sampling_ms = {
    "mlx-graphs uniform": benchmark(lambda: mlx_uniform.pos_sample(all_nodes), mx.eval),
    "mlx-graphs biased": benchmark(lambda: mlx_biased.pos_sample(all_nodes), mx.eval),
    "PyG uniform": benchmark(
        lambda: pyg_uniform.pos_sample(all_nodes_torch), lambda _: None
    ),
}
num_windows = mlx_uniform.pos_sample(all_nodes).shape[0]
print(
    f"{num_nodes * WALKS_PER_NODE:,} walks of {SAMPLING_WALK_LENGTH} nodes, "
    f"{num_windows:,} windows"
)
for name, ms in sampling_ms.items():
    print(f"{name:<20}{ms:7.1f} ms")
try:
    pyg_sampler(1.0, 0.25).pos_sample(all_nodes_torch)
except RuntimeError as error:
    print(f"PyG biased          not supported ({str(error).splitlines()[0]})")

27,080 walks of 80 nodes, 1,922,680 windows
mlx-graphs uniform      2.3 ms
mlx-graphs biased       9.3 ms
PyG uniform            25.1 ms
PyG biased          not supported (Uniform sampling required for now)

Speed only counts if the walks are valid. The cell below checks that every step of every window is an edge of the graph (Cora has no node without neighbors, so a walk never stays in place).

edge_codes = np.unique(src_np.astype(np.int64) * num_nodes + dst_np)


def invalid_steps(windows):
    windows = np.asarray(windows).astype(np.int64)
    steps = windows[:, :-1] * num_nodes + windows[:, 1:]
    return int((~np.isin(steps, edge_codes)).sum())


for name, windows in [
    ("mlx-graphs uniform", mlx_uniform.pos_sample(all_nodes)),
    ("mlx-graphs biased", mlx_biased.pos_sample(all_nodes)),
    ("PyG uniform", pyg_uniform.pos_sample(all_nodes_torch).numpy()),
]:
    print(f"{name:<20}{invalid_steps(windows)} invalid steps")

mlx-graphs uniform  0 invalid steps
mlx-graphs biased   0 invalid steps
PyG uniform         0 invalid steps

items.title: Training and embedding quality
items.text:
Each library trains its own Node2Vec model with uniform walks for 10 epochs, with Adam, the same learning rate and the same batch size, once per seed. The timer covers whole epochs. After training, the embeddings are scored with the logistic regression above.

Two details make the runs comparable. PyTorch initializes nn.Embedding with a standard deviation of 1, and MLX with 1/sqrt(embedding_dim), so we initialize PyG's embeddings at MLX's scale. And MLX's Adam uses bias_correction=True (see train above), which is what torch.optim.Adam does.

COMPARISON_SEEDS = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]


def train_pyg(model, num_epochs=NUM_EPOCHS):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE)
    loader = model.loader(batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True, num_workers=0)
    model.train()
    epoch_times, losses = [], []
    for _ in range(num_epochs):
        start, total, num_batches = time.perf_counter(), 0.0, 0
        for pos_rw, neg_rw in loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = model.loss(pos_rw, neg_rw)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            total, num_batches = total + loss.item(), num_batches + 1
        epoch_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
        losses.append(total / num_batches)
    return epoch_times, losses


runs = {"mlx-graphs": [], "PyG": []}
for seed in COMPARISON_SEEDS:
    mx.random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    mlx_model = make_model()
    times, losses = train(mlx_model)
    accuracy = test_accuracy(np.array(mlx_model.embedding.weight))
    runs["mlx-graphs"].append(dict(times=times, loss=losses[-1], accuracy=accuracy))

    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    pyg_model = make_pyg_model()
    torch.nn.init.normal_(pyg_model.embedding.weight, std=EMBEDDING_DIM**-0.5)
    times, losses = train_pyg(pyg_model)
    accuracy = test_accuracy(pyg_model.embedding.weight.detach().numpy())
    runs["PyG"].append(dict(times=times, loss=losses[-1], accuracy=accuracy))

    mlx_acc, pyg_acc = runs["mlx-graphs"][-1]["accuracy"], runs["PyG"][-1]["accuracy"]
    print(f"seed {seed}: test accuracy mlx-graphs {mlx_acc:.3f}, PyG {pyg_acc:.3f}")

seed 0: test accuracy mlx-graphs 0.705, PyG 0.731
seed 1: test accuracy mlx-graphs 0.714, PyG 0.712
seed 2: test accuracy mlx-graphs 0.700, PyG 0.709
seed 3: test accuracy mlx-graphs 0.735, PyG 0.707
seed 4: test accuracy mlx-graphs 0.689, PyG 0.710

items.title: Summary
items.text:
The time per epoch is the median over all seeds, without the first epoch of each run, which includes the compilation of the kernels. The loss and the accuracy are the mean and standard deviation over the seeds.

def epoch_seconds(library):
    return statistics.median(t for run in runs[library] for t in run["times"][1:])


def mean_std(values, fmt=".3f"):
    return f"{np.mean(values):{fmt}} ± {np.std(values, ddof=1):{fmt}}"


summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {

            sampling_ms["mlx-graphs uniform"],
            sampling_ms["PyG uniform"],

        "final loss": [mean_std([r["loss"] for r in runs[lib]], ".4f") for lib in runs],
        "test accuracy": [mean_std([r["accuracy"] for r in runs[lib]]) for lib in runs],

        ["mlx-graphs (GPU)", f"PyG (CPU, {PYG_SAMPLER} walks)"], name="library"
    ),
)
summary["uniform walks (ms)"] = summary["uniform walks (ms)"].round(1)
summary["biased walks (ms)"] = [
    f"{v:.1f}" if isinstance(v, float) else v for v in summary["biased walks (ms)"]
]
summary["training (s/epoch)"] = summary["training (s/epoch)"].round(3)
summary

fig.suptitle(
    "Node2Vec on Cora: mlx-graphs on the GPU, PyG on the CPU",
    x=0.01,
    ha="left",

fig.legend(
    *axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(),

Quality. Both libraries train the same model and reach the same test accuracy: the mean ± std ranges over the seeds overlap, and the differences between seeds of one library are as large as the difference between the two libraries. Their final losses are also close. The speed comparison is therefore made at equal quality.

Speed. These timings were measured on an Apple M5 Pro, with mlx-graphs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU. mlx-graphs samples walks and trains faster than PyG (see the speedups printed above). The gap is larger for the walks alone than for training, which also includes the embedding lookups, the loss and the optimizer. mlx-graphs also samples biased walks on the GPU, which PyG's sampler doesn't support.

Two caveats. Without pyg-lib, the PyG sampling time measures the PyTorch fallback above, not pyg-lib's C++ sampler, so install pyg-lib for a comparison with PyG's own sampler. And timings vary from run to run and from machine to machine, so run the notebook on your own machine to compare.

items.title: Going further
items.text:
• Try other values of p and q, or a larger embedding_dim or more walks_per_node. Tune them on the validation split (graph.val_mask, or the validation graph of RandomLinkSplit), not on the test split.
  • The same code runs on the other Planetoid graphs, PlanetoidDataset("CiteSeer") and PlanetoidDataset("PubMed"), or on any graph given as an edge_index.
  • Node2Vec embeddings can be concatenated with the node features and fed to a GNN, for example a GCNConv model as in the other tutorials.
  • For the details of the walk samplers, see the docstrings of mlx_cluster.random_walk and mlx_cluster.rejection_sampling.

items.title: Quantum-chemical property prediction with GNNs
items.text:
View on GitHub Download notebook

In this mlx-graphs tutorial we explore how to use and graph neural networks to predict quantum-chemical properties of small molecules. You may need to install mlx, mlx-graphs, tqdm and matplotlib to run it.

items.title: Loading the dataset
items.text:
We will be using the QM9 dataset as provided via TUDataset, which consists of about 130,000 small molecules consisting of 9 heavy atoms drawn from the elements C, H, O, N, F. Each molecule includes spatial information for the single low energy conformation (i.e., 3D coordinates of the atoms, specified in the latest 3 columns in the node_features of the graph) in addition to 13 other features. The dataset consists of 19 regression tasks, corresponding to different quantum-chemical properties of the molecules.

Let's start by loading the dataset and looking at some of its properties

from mlx_graphs.datasets import TUDataset
qm9 = TUDataset(name="QM9")

print(f"Number of graphs: {len(qm9)}")
print(f"Number of node features: {qm9.num_node_features}")
print(f"Number of edge features: {qm9.num_edge_features}")
print(f"Number of regression tasks: {qm9[0].graph_labels.shape[1]}")

Number of graphs: 129433
Number of node features: 16
Number of edge features: 4
Number of regression tasks: 19

We'll split the dataset into training and test sets and create dataloader for them

from mlx_graphs.loaders import Dataloader

# training and test splits
num_training_samples = 110_000

training_dataset = qm9[:num_training_samples]
test_dataset = qm9[num_training_samples:]

# dataloaders
batch_size = 128

train_loader = Dataloader(training_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
test_loader = Dataloader(test_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)

items.title: Graph Neural Network module
items.text:
To dive a bit deeper into the GNN logic and allow for more flexibility, we will implement node and edge processing blocks from scratch (as in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.01261.pdf) and then combine them through the GraphNetworkBlock provided by mlx-graphs.

Let's start with the edge features update model. It will concatenate the edge_features with the node_features of the coreesponding source and target nodes, pass them through a simple MLP (just a linear layer followed by a ReLU) and output the updated edge_features.

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
from mlx_graphs.nn import Linear
from mlx_graphs.utils import scatter

class EdgeModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        edge_features_dim: int,
        node_features_dim: int,
        output_dim: int,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = Linear(
            input_dims=2 * node_features_dim + edge_features_dim, # source + target features + edge features
            output_dims=output_dim,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        edge_index: mx.array,
        node_features: mx.array,
        edge_features: mx.array,
        graph_features = None
    ):
        source_nodes = edge_index[0]
        destination_nodes = edge_index[1]
        model_input = mx.concatenate(
            [
                node_features[destination_nodes],
                node_features[source_nodes],
                edge_features,
            ],
            1,
        )
        new_edge_features = self.linear(model_input)
        new_edge_features = nn.relu(new_edge_features)
        return new_edge_features

The node features update model will start by aggregating the edge_features corresponding to the edges incoming into each node, by computing their mean. Such aggregated edge features will be concatenated to the corresponding node_features and passed through an MLP to compute the updated node features.

class NodeModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        node_features_dim: int,
        edge_features_dim: int,
        output_dim: int,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = Linear(
            input_dims=node_features_dim + edge_features_dim,
            output_dims=output_dim,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        edge_index: mx.array,
        node_features: mx.array,
        edge_features: mx.array,
        graph_features = None
    ):
        target_nodes = edge_index[1]
        aggregated_edges = scatter(edge_features, target_nodes, out_size=node_features.shape[0], aggr="mean")
        model_input = mx.concatenate([node_features, aggregated_edges], 1)
        new_node_features = self.linear(model_input)
        new_node_features = nn.relu(new_node_features)
        return new_node_features

Now, the edge and node models we defined can be combined to create a basic graph neural network to sequentially update/transform edges and node features of the input graph.

To do that we can use the GraphNetworkBlock. In the model below we create two graph network blocks that we apply sequentially, we then pool the node features and pass them through a linear transformation to compute the predicted output. We use an output dimension of 1 for the entire model as we'll use it to learn a single regression task.

from mlx_graphs.nn import global_mean_pool, GraphNetworkBlock


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.gnn1 = GraphNetworkBlock(
            node_model=NodeModel(qm9.num_node_features, 64, 64), 
            edge_model=EdgeModel(qm9.num_edge_features, qm9.num_node_features, 64),
        )
        self.gnn2 = GraphNetworkBlock(
            node_model=NodeModel(64, 64, 64), 
            edge_model=EdgeModel(64, 64, 64),
        )
        self.output_linear = Linear(input_dims=64, output_dims=1)

    def __call__(
        self,
        edge_index: mx.array,
        node_features: mx.array,
        edge_features: mx.array,
        batch_indices: mx.array,
    ):

        node_features, edge_features, _ = self.gnn1(
            edge_index=data.edge_index,
            node_features=data.node_features,
            edge_features=data.edge_features,
        )
        node_features, _, _ = self.gnn2(
            edge_index=data.edge_index,
            node_features=node_features,
            edge_features=edge_features,
        )
        out = global_mean_pool(node_features, batch_indices)
        return self.output_linear(out)

items.title: Model training
items.text:
Now that we have our model we can simply define our loss function (MSE) and the forward function we're going to use to train our model along with an optimizer (we'll use AdamW in this example).

import mlx.optimizers as optim

model = Model()

mx.eval(model.parameters())

def loss_fn(y_hat, y, parameters=None):
    return nn.losses.mse_loss(y_hat, y, "sum")

def forward_fn(model, graph, labels):
    y_hat = model(graph.edge_index, graph.node_features, graph.edge_features, graph.batch_indices)
    loss = loss_fn(y_hat, labels, model.parameters())
    return loss, y_hat

loss_and_grad_fn = nn.value_and_grad(model, forward_fn)
optimizer = optim.AdamW(learning_rate=1e-3)

We're now ready to train our GNN model. Let's select the "Lowest unoccupied molecular orbital energy" as the target regression task.

from tqdm import tqdm

mx.set_default_device(mx.gpu)
regression_task = 4

len_training_loader = int(len(training_dataset)/batch_size + 1)
len_test_loader = int(len(test_dataset)/batch_size + 1)
epochs = 20

epoch_training_losses = []
epoch_test_losses = []
for epoch in range(epochs):
    # training loop
    with tqdm(train_loader, total=len_training_loader, unit="batch") as tepoch:
        tepoch.set_description(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}")
        training_loss = 0.0
        for idx, data in enumerate(tepoch):
            (loss, y_hat), grads = loss_and_grad_fn(
                model=model,
                graph=data,
                labels=mx.expand_dims(data.graph_labels[:, regression_task], 1),
            )
            optimizer.update(model, grads)
            mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state)
            training_loss += loss.item()/data.num_graphs
            tepoch.set_postfix(training_loss=training_loss / (idx+1), test_loss=0)
        epoch_training_losses.append(training_loss/(idx+1))

    # testing loop
    with tqdm(test_loader, total=len_test_loader, unit="batch", leave=False) as test_epoch:
        test_epoch.set_description(f"Testing")
        test_loss = 0.0
        for idx, data in enumerate(test_epoch):
            y_hat = model(data.edge_index, data.node_features, data.edge_features, data.batch_indices)
            loss = loss_fn(y_hat, mx.expand_dims(data.graph_labels[:, regression_task], 1))
            test_loss += loss.item()/data.num_graphs
            test_epoch.set_postfix(test_loss=test_loss / (idx+1))
        epoch_test_losses.append(test_loss/(idx+1))

items.title: Notes and next steps
items.text: While this is an illustrative tutorial, we hope it gives some insights into mlx-graphs. Next steps could involve implementing more complex and specialized models (e.g., exploiting invariances and equivariances in the geometries of the molecules) or normalizing features and target properties, which can highly improve performance as well.

items.title: Temporal Graph Networks: mlx-graphs vs PyG
items.text:
View on GitHub Download notebook

Many graphs are not static: they are streams of timestamped events, such as a user editing a Wikipedia page, a student taking a course, or a payment between two accounts. A Temporal Graph Network (TGN, Rossi et al., 2020) learns from such streams by keeping a memory vector for every node. Each new event sends a message to its two nodes, and a GRU updates their memories. To predict a future event, TGN embeds the involved nodes with a graph attention layer over their most recent interactions, and scores the pair.

In this tutorial, we train the same TGN with mlx-graphs and with PyTorch Geometric (PyG) on the JODIE Wikipedia dataset. We then compare the average precision (AP) of the predicted links and the time per epoch. The model is PyG's examples/tgn.py, with the same hyperparameters in both frameworks.

The PyG part needs a few extra dependencies:

pip install torch torch_geometric scikit-learn pandas matplotlib

import time

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
import mlx.optimizers as optim
import numpy as np

from mlx_graphs.datasets import JODIEDataset
from mlx_graphs.loaders import TemporalDataLoader
from mlx_graphs.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from mlx_graphs.nn import TGNMemory, TransformerConv
from mlx_graphs.nn.models.tgn import (
    IdentityMessage,
    LastAggregator,
    LastNeighborLoader,
    TimeEncoder,
)

# Same hyperparameters as PyG's examples/tgn.py
EPOCHS = 10
BATCH_SIZE = 200
LR = 1e-4
DIM = 100  # memory, time encoding and embedding sizes
NUM_NEIGHBORS = 10
SEED = 0

items.title: The dataset
items.text:
JODIE Wikipedia has 157,474 edits by 8,227 users of 1,000 pages over one month. Each event is a (src, dst, t, msg) tuple: a user, a page, a timestamp in seconds, and a 172-dimensional feature vector of the edit text. mlx-graphs stores the stream in a TemporalData object.

dataset = JODIEDataset("wikipedia")
data = dataset[0]
print(data)
print(
    f"{data.num_nodes} nodes, {data.num_events} events, "
    f"message size {data.msg.shape[1]}"
)

Loading jodie_wikipedia data ... Done
TemporalData(src=[157474], dst=[157474], t=[157474], msg=[157474, 172], y=[157474])
9227 nodes, 157474 events, message size 172

The events are split by time: the first 70% are used for training, the next 15% for validation and the last 15% for testing. A TemporalDataLoader iterates over the events in mini-batches of 200, in chronological order, and draws a random negative destination for every event. The LastNeighborLoader keeps the 10 most recent neighbors of every node, which form the subgraph the attention layer looks at.

train_data, val_data, test_data = data.train_val_test_split(
    val_ratio=0.15, test_ratio=0.15
)

train_loader = TemporalDataLoader(
    train_data, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0
)
val_loader = TemporalDataLoader(val_data, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0)
test_loader = TemporalDataLoader(
    test_data, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0
)
neighbor_loader = LastNeighborLoader(data.num_nodes, size=NUM_NEIGHBORS)

print(
    f"train: {train_data.num_events}, val: {val_data.num_events}, "
    f"test: {test_data.num_events} events"
)

items.title: The model in mlx-graphs
items.text:
The model has three parts:

  • TGNMemory holds one memory vector per node, and updates it from the messages of the past events with a GRU. IdentityMessage builds a message from the two memories, the time since the last update and the event features, and LastAggregator keeps the most recent message of each node.
  • GraphAttentionEmbedding embeds the nodes with a TransformerConv over the recent interactions. Each edge carries the encoding of its relative time and its event features.
  • LinkPredictor scores a (source, destination) pair from the two embeddings.

The memory is a state, not a parameter: nn.value_and_grad and the optimizer only see the weights of the modules. The time encoder is shared between the memory and the attention layer. It is passed to the attention layer at call time, so that it appears only once in the parameters of the model.

class GraphAttentionEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim, msg_dim, time_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = TransformerConv(
            in_dim,
            out_dim // 2,
            heads=2,
            dropout=0.1,
            edge_features_dim=msg_dim + time_dim,
        )

    def __call__(self, x, last_update, edge_index, t, msg, time_enc: TimeEncoder):
        rel_t = (last_update[edge_index[0]] - t).astype(x.dtype)
        edge_features = mx.concatenate([time_enc(rel_t), msg], axis=-1)
        return self.conv(edge_index, x, edge_features)


class LinkPredictor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin_src = nn.Linear(dim, dim)
        self.lin_dst = nn.Linear(dim, dim)
        self.lin_final = nn.Linear(dim, 1)

    def __call__(self, z_src, z_dst):
        return self.lin_final(nn.relu(self.lin_src(z_src) + self.lin_dst(z_dst)))


class TGN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_nodes, msg_dim, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.memory = TGNMemory(
            num_nodes,
            msg_dim,
            dim,
            dim,
            message_module=IdentityMessage(msg_dim, dim, dim),
            aggregator_module=LastAggregator(),
        )
        self.gnn = GraphAttentionEmbedding(dim, dim, msg_dim, dim)
        self.link_pred = LinkPredictor(dim)

    def __call__(self, n_id, edge_index, e_id, src, pos_dst, neg_dst):
        z, last_update = self.memory(n_id)
        z = self.gnn(
            z,
            last_update,
            edge_index,
            data.t[e_id],
            data.msg[e_id],
            self.memory.time_enc,
        )
        return self.link_pred(z[src], z[pos_dst]), self.link_pred(z[src], z[neg_dst])


def loss_fn(model, *args):
    pos_out, neg_out = model(*args)
    return nn.losses.binary_cross_entropy(
        pos_out, mx.ones_like(pos_out)
    ) + nn.losses.binary_cross_entropy(neg_out, mx.zeros_like(neg_out))

For every mini-batch, the neighbor loader returns the nodes n_id involved (the batch's nodes and their recent neighbors), the edges between them and their event ids. assoc maps the global ids of the batch's nodes to their position in n_id.

After the loss is computed, the batch's events are written to the memory and to the neighbor loader. The model therefore never sees an event before predicting it. memory.detach() then cuts the gradient through the memory, as PyG does after the optimizer step.

assoc = np.zeros(data.num_nodes, dtype=np.int64)


def prepare(batch):
    n_id, edge_index, e_id = neighbor_loader(batch.n_id)
    assoc[np.array(n_id)] = np.arange(n_id.size)

    def local(nodes):
        return mx.array(assoc[np.array(nodes)].astype(np.int32))

    return (
        n_id,
        edge_index,
        e_id,
        local(batch.src),
        local(batch.dst),
        local(batch.neg_dst),
    )


def train(model, optimizer):
    model.train()
    model.memory.reset_state()  # start with a fresh memory
    neighbor_loader.reset_state()  # and an empty graph
    loss_and_grad = nn.value_and_grad(model, loss_fn)

    total_loss = 0.0
    for batch in train_loader:
        loss, grads = loss_and_grad(model, *prepare(batch))
        model.memory.update_state(batch.src, batch.dst, batch.t, batch.msg)
        neighbor_loader.insert(batch.src, batch.dst)
        optimizer.update(model, grads)
        model.memory.detach()
        mx.eval(model.parameters(), optimizer.state, loss)
        total_loss += loss.item() * batch.num_events
    return total_loss / train_data.num_events


def test(model, loader):
    model.eval()  # also flushes the pending messages into the memory
    mx.random.seed(12345)  # same negative destinations at every epoch

    aps, aucs = [], []
    for batch in loader:
        pos_out, neg_out = model(*prepare(batch))
        y_pred = np.array(mx.sigmoid(mx.concatenate([pos_out, neg_out]))).reshape(-1)
        y_true = np.concatenate([np.ones(pos_out.shape[0]), np.zeros(neg_out.shape[0])])
        aps.append(average_precision_score(y_true, y_pred))
        aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y_true, y_pred))

        model.memory.update_state(batch.src, batch.dst, batch.t, batch.msg)
        neighbor_loader.insert(batch.src, batch.dst)
    return float(np.mean(aps)), float(np.mean(aucs))

items.title: Training with mlx-graphs
items.text:
Every epoch replays the training events from the start, then evaluates on the validation and test events, which follow them in time. We time the training and the evaluation separately.

def run_epochs(train_epoch, evaluate):
    history = []
    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        loss = train_epoch()
        train_s = time.perf_counter() - start
        start = time.perf_counter()
        (val_ap, val_auc), (test_ap, test_auc) = evaluate()
        eval_s = time.perf_counter() - start
        history.append(
            dict(
                epoch=epoch,
                loss=loss,
                val_ap=val_ap,
                test_ap=test_ap,
                test_auc=test_auc,
                train_s=train_s,
                eval_s=eval_s,
            )
        )
        print(
            f"Epoch {epoch:02d}  loss {loss:.4f}  val AP {val_ap:.4f}  "
            f"test AP {test_ap:.4f}  "
            f"test AUC {test_auc:.4f}  train {train_s:.1f} s  eval {eval_s:.1f} s"
        )
    return history


mx.random.seed(SEED)
mlx_model = TGN(data.num_nodes, data.msg.shape[1], DIM)
# bias_correction=True gives the update rule of torch.optim.Adam
mlx_optimizer = optim.Adam(learning_rate=LR, bias_correction=True)

mlx_history = run_epochs(
    lambda: train(mlx_model, mlx_optimizer),
    lambda: (test(mlx_model, val_loader), test(mlx_model, test_loader)),
)

items.title: The same model in PyG
items.text:
The PyG version below is PyG's examples/tgn.py, with the same data, splits and hyperparameters. It runs on the CPU: PyG's TGN does many small indexing operations per batch, which are slower on the MPS backend.

One detail: without the optional torch-scatter package, PyG falls back to its own scatter_argmax, which gives nodes without messages the index dim_size - 1 instead of an out-of-range one. Its LastAggregator then copies an unrelated message to every node without messages instead of zeros. mlx-graphs follows the torch-scatter behavior. For a like-for-like comparison, we patch the fallback when torch-scatter is not installed.

import torch
import torch_geometric.nn.models.tgn as pyg_tgn_module
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score as sk_ap
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score as sk_auc
from torch_geometric.datasets import JODIEDataset as PyGJODIEDataset
from torch_geometric.loader import TemporalDataLoader as PyGTemporalDataLoader
from torch_geometric.nn import TGNMemory as PyGTGNMemory
from torch_geometric.nn import TransformerConv as PyGTransformerConv
from torch_geometric.nn.models.tgn import IdentityMessage as PyGIdentityMessage
from torch_geometric.nn.models.tgn import LastAggregator as PyGLastAggregator
from torch_geometric.nn.models.tgn import LastNeighborLoader as PyGLastNeighborLoader

try:
    import torch_scatter  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:

    def scatter_argmax(src, index, dim=0, dim_size=None):
        res = src.new_empty(dim_size)
        res.scatter_reduce_(0, index, src, reduce="amax", include_self=False)
        out = index.new_full((dim_size,), fill_value=src.size(0))
        nonzero = (src == res[index]).nonzero().view(-1)
        out[index[nonzero]] = nonzero
        return out

    pyg_tgn_module.scatter_argmax = scatter_argmax

torch.manual_seed(SEED)
pyg_data = PyGJODIEDataset(".pyg_data/JODIE", name="wikipedia")[0]
pyg_train, pyg_val, pyg_test = pyg_data.train_val_test_split(
    val_ratio=0.15, test_ratio=0.15
)
pyg_train_loader = PyGTemporalDataLoader(
    pyg_train, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0
)
pyg_val_loader = PyGTemporalDataLoader(
    pyg_val, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0
)
pyg_test_loader = PyGTemporalDataLoader(
    pyg_test, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, neg_sampling_ratio=1.0
)
pyg_neighbor_loader = PyGLastNeighborLoader(pyg_data.num_nodes, size=NUM_NEIGHBORS)

class PyGGraphAttentionEmbedding(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, msg_dim, time_enc):
        super().__init__()
        self.time_enc = time_enc
        edge_dim = msg_dim + time_enc.out_channels
        self.conv = PyGTransformerConv(
            in_channels, out_channels // 2, heads=2, dropout=0.1, edge_dim=edge_dim
        )

    def forward(self, x, last_update, edge_index, t, msg):
        rel_t = last_update[edge_index[0]] - t
        edge_attr = torch.cat([self.time_enc(rel_t.to(x.dtype)), msg], dim=-1)
        return self.conv(x, edge_index, edge_attr)


class PyGLinkPredictor(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin_src = torch.nn.Linear(in_channels, in_channels)
        self.lin_dst = torch.nn.Linear(in_channels, in_channels)
        self.lin_final = torch.nn.Linear(in_channels, 1)

    def forward(self, z_src, z_dst):
        return self.lin_final((self.lin_src(z_src) + self.lin_dst(z_dst)).relu())


msg_dim = pyg_data.msg.size(-1)
memory = PyGTGNMemory(
    pyg_data.num_nodes,
    msg_dim,
    DIM,
    DIM,
    message_module=PyGIdentityMessage(msg_dim, DIM, DIM),
    aggregator_module=PyGLastAggregator(),
)
gnn = PyGGraphAttentionEmbedding(DIM, DIM, msg_dim, memory.time_enc)
link_pred = PyGLinkPredictor(DIM)
pyg_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
    set(memory.parameters()) | set(gnn.parameters()) | set(link_pred.parameters()),
    lr=LR,
)
criterion = torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
pyg_assoc = torch.empty(pyg_data.num_nodes, dtype=torch.long)


def pyg_forward(batch):
    n_id, edge_index, e_id = pyg_neighbor_loader(batch.n_id)
    pyg_assoc[n_id] = torch.arange(n_id.size(0))
    z, last_update = memory(n_id)
    z = gnn(z, last_update, edge_index, pyg_data.t[e_id], pyg_data.msg[e_id])
    pos_out = link_pred(z[pyg_assoc[batch.src]], z[pyg_assoc[batch.dst]])
    neg_out = link_pred(z[pyg_assoc[batch.src]], z[pyg_assoc[batch.neg_dst]])
    return pos_out, neg_out


def pyg_train_epoch():
    memory.train()
    gnn.train()
    link_pred.train()
    memory.reset_state()
    pyg_neighbor_loader.reset_state()

    total_loss = 0.0
    for batch in pyg_train_loader:
        pyg_optimizer.zero_grad()
        pos_out, neg_out = pyg_forward(batch)
        loss = criterion(pos_out, torch.ones_like(pos_out)) + criterion(
            neg_out, torch.zeros_like(neg_out)
        )
        memory.update_state(batch.src, batch.dst, batch.t, batch.msg)
        pyg_neighbor_loader.insert(batch.src, batch.dst)
        loss.backward()
        pyg_optimizer.step()
        memory.detach()
        total_loss += float(loss) * batch.num_events
    return total_loss / pyg_train.num_events


@torch.no_grad()
def pyg_test(loader):
    memory.eval()
    gnn.eval()
    link_pred.eval()
    torch.manual_seed(12345)

    aps, aucs = [], []
    for batch in loader:
        pos_out, neg_out = pyg_forward(batch)
        y_pred = torch.cat([pos_out, neg_out]).sigmoid()
        y_true = torch.cat([torch.ones(pos_out.size(0)), torch.zeros(neg_out.size(0))])
        aps.append(sk_ap(y_true, y_pred))
        aucs.append(sk_auc(y_true, y_pred))
        memory.update_state(batch.src, batch.dst, batch.t, batch.msg)
        pyg_neighbor_loader.insert(batch.src, batch.dst)
    return float(np.mean(aps)), float(np.mean(aucs))

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
The table below summarizes the two runs: the test AP and AUC after the last epoch, the best validation AP, and the median time per epoch (the median is less sensitive than the mean to an epoch slowed down by other programs).

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)

rows = []
for name, history in [("mlx-graphs", mlx_history), ("PyG", pyg_history)]:
    last = history[-1]
    rows.append(
        {
            "framework": name,
            f"test AP (epoch {EPOCHS})": round(last["test_ap"], 4),
            f"test AUC (epoch {EPOCHS})": round(last["test_auc"], 4),
            "best val AP": round(max(h["val_ap"] for h in history), 4),
            "train s/epoch": round(np.median([h["train_s"] for h in history]), 2),
            "eval s/epoch": round(np.median([h["eval_s"] for h in history]), 2),
        }
    )
summary = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("framework")
summary
test AP (epoch 10) test AUC (epoch 10) best val AP train s/epoch eval s/epoch framework mlx-graphs 0.9568 0.9531 0.9605 4.72 0.76 PyG 0.9544 0.9501 0.9605 11.90 2.17 
speedup_train = (
    summary.loc["PyG", "train s/epoch"] / summary.loc["mlx-graphs", "train s/epoch"]
)
speedup_eval = (
    summary.loc["PyG", "eval s/epoch"] / summary.loc["mlx-graphs", "eval s/epoch"]

print(
    f"mlx-graphs trains {speedup_train:.1f}x faster and evaluates "
    f"{speedup_eval:.1f}x faster than PyG."
)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

COLORS = {"mlx-graphs": "#2a78d6", "PyG": "#eb6834"}
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#1f1f1e", "#6b6a64", "#e6e5e0"

fig, (ax_ap, ax_time) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
epochs = np.arange(1, EPOCHS + 1)

for name, history in [("mlx-graphs", mlx_history), ("PyG", pyg_history)]:
    ap = [h["test_ap"] for h in history]
    ax_ap.plot(
        epochs,
        ap,
        color=COLORS[name],
        linewidth=2,
        marker="o",
        markersize=5,
        label=name,
    )

names = ["mlx-graphs", "PyG"]
x = np.arange(2)
width = 0.36
for offset, column, label, alpha in [
    (-width / 2, "train s/epoch", "train", 1.0),
    (width / 2, "eval s/epoch", "evaluation", 0.55),
]:
    values = [summary.loc[n, column] for n in names]
    bars = ax_time.bar(
        x + offset,
        values,
        width - 0.02,
        color=[COLORS[n] for n in names],
        alpha=alpha,
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=2,
    )
    for bar, value in zip(bars, values):
        ax_time.annotate(
            f"{label}\n{value:.1f} s",
            (bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, value),
            xytext=(0, 3),
            textcoords="offset points",
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            color=INK,
            fontsize=9,
        )

ax_ap.set_title("Test AP per epoch", loc="left", color=INK)
ax_ap.set_xlabel("epoch", color=MUTED)
ax_ap.set_xticks(epochs)
ax_ap.set_xlim(0.5, EPOCHS + 0.5)
ax_ap.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
ax_time.set_title("Median seconds per epoch (lower is better)", loc="left", color=INK)
ax_time.set_xticks(x, names)
ax_time.set_ylim(0, max(summary["train s/epoch"]) * 1.3)
for ax in (ax_ap, ax_time):
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for side in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_color(GRID)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Accuracy. Both models reach a test AP of about 0.95 to 0.96 after 10 epochs, and the gap between them is within the variation between random seeds. The curves differ most in the first epochs, because the two models start from different random weights. The parity tests of mlx-graphs go further: with the same weights, the memory, the losses and the gradients match PyG batch after batch.

Runtime. These timings were measured on an Apple M5 Pro, with mlx-graphs on the GPU and PyG on the CPU. mlx-graphs is several times faster than PyG at both training and evaluation (see the speedups printed above). Timings vary from run to run and from machine to machine, so run the notebook on your own machine to compare.

items.title: Going further
items.text:
• The same code trains on the two other JODIE datasets, JODIEDataset("mooc") and JODIEDataset("lastfm").
  • mlx_graphs.metrics also provides ranking metrics for link prediction (LinkPredMRR, LinkPredNDCG, LinkPredHitRatio, ...), with the same API as torch_geometric.metrics.
  • examples/tgn_jodie.py is a command-line version of the mlx-graphs part of this tutorial.
